name: Green Cove Springs

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE CITY'S OWN WORDS: Green Cove Springs is the only town in the service area whose government publishes 'Delay installing new sod or other high-water use landscaping until conditions improve' on its official water conservation page — while running its own electric, water, wastewater and reclaimed water utilities, having just raised water, wastewater and reclaimed rates on 17 September 2025, and holding residents to one watering day a week under the SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage. Everywhere else you have to argue that grass costs money. Here the city says it for you. Build the page around that quote and the utility bill. THE SECOND MOVEMENT is that this is two towns, and the offer differs: in the 300-acre NRHP historic district — 78 contributing buildings, 7,000 sq ft R-1 lots, live-oak canopy, Mandarin/Cassia spodosol with the water table 30 inches down and three active city stormwater projects on Clay Street, Ferris Street and Oakridge — the sale is shade tolerance and drainage, because nothing will grow under those oaks and the ground stays wet. In the new R-1A subdivisions west and north — 50-foot lots created only in March 2023, 10-foot rear yards, brand-new construction feeding off a First Coast Expressway segment finished 29 June 2026 — the sale is a small, perfect, dog-proof back yard that is finished the day the builder leaves. Name Magnolia Point specifically and tell them their $17M reclaimed water project is on hold, so they are still irrigating on restricted water. WHY THIS IS DIFFERENT FROM THE TOWN NEXT DOOR: Middleburg is unincorporated well-water acreage with no rules and no municipal utility; Hibernia is $129k-income river estates with no town at all; Penney Farms is an 81-year-old-median retirement campus. Green Cove Springs is the only one of the five with a city hall, a city utility bill, a code with an impervious-surface cap, a historic district, a county seat's institutional buyers and a genuine young-family growth curve. Write it as a civic page, not a lifestyle page. And be precise about the impervious-surface cap (40% low density, 50% medium, Sec. 113-4) — no competitor in Clay County will mention it, and mentioning it is how you win the $10-12/sq ft jobs.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: NO artificial-turf ordinance. I read the Green Cove Springs Land Development Code (Municode, codified 2026): the words 'artificial turf,' 'synthetic turf' and 'synthetic grass' appear NOWHERE in the code — the only 'artificial' reference is to artificially lighted communication towers. There is also NO local historic-preservation chapter and NO certificate-of-appropriateness requirement, despite the NRHP historic district — the listing is honorary, so a historic-district homeowner does not need architectural board approval for a back yard. That is a meaningful contrast with Fernandina Beach, and worth saying explicitly. TWO REAL CONSTRAINTS TO RESPECT: (1) Sec. 113-4, IMPERVIOUS SURFACE COVERAGE — maximum impervious ratio is 40% in Residential low density, 50% in Residential medium, 70% in high density and commercial, 100% in the Downtown Core, 80% Primary Corridor, 70% Secondary Corridor, 50% Transition. Subsection (c) excludes porous paving materials used 'in accordance with the construction manual.' A large turf install on a low-density lot that already has a house, drive, patio and pool deck can bump the 40% cap, so a permeable turf system over open-graded base should be documented against the construction manual rather than assumed. Flag this on the page — it makes you look like the only installer who has read the code. (2) Sec. 113-277, DROUGHT-TOLERANT PLANT STANDARDS — required landscaping must use native, non-invasive drought-tolerant plants, and 'mulches and drought tolerant groundcovers shall replace narrow turf areas where irrigation is impractical.' Artificial turf is not named as an approved substitute, so on commercial, industrial, civic, multifamily and common-area jobs treat turf as amenity area beyond the required landscape, not as the required landscape. Also relevant: Sec. 113-3 requires development be designed 'to avoid unnecessary impervious surface cover.' HOA/CDD: Magnolia Point and Magnolia West have HOAs with amenity centres; the historic grid largely does not. New subdivisions (Rookery and the R-1A product) will carry covenants — check each, none known to ban turf.
facts.water_and_rules: UNIQUE AMONG THE FIVE: Green Cove Springs runs its OWN municipal utilities — ELECTRIC, water, wastewater AND reclaimed water — not CCUA, not JEA, not Clay Electric. City Hall, 321 Walnut Street, 904-297-7500. The City Council approved increases to water, wastewater and reclaimed water rates on 16 Sept 2025, effective 17 Sept 2025. CURRENT STATUS AS OF 2026-09-07: SJRWMD PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE. The City's own water conservation page states landscape irrigation is limited to ONE DAY PER WEEK, only between 6 p.m. and 8 a.m., with odd/no-numbered addresses on Saturday, even on Sunday, nonresidential on Tuesday; no more than 3/4 inch per zone and no more than one hour per zone; and 'restrictions apply to private wells and pumps, ground or surface water and water from public and private utilities.' THE QUOTE TO PUT ON THE PAGE: among the City's own outdoor conservation tips is 'Delay installing new sod or other high-water use landscaping until conditions improve, if possible.' The city government is telling residents not to lay sod. Nobody selling turf in northeast Florida has a better third-party endorsement than a city conservation page saying that. REBATES — honest answer: NO for artificial turf. The City directs residents to the SJRWMD Water Conservation Rebate Program (launched October 2024), whose eligible items are Florida Water Star certification for new residential construction, EPA WaterSense-labelled smart irrigation controllers, irrigation conversions to rotary nozzle or micro-irrigation, irrigation evaluations and timer modification, landscape soil amendments for new construction, indoor fixture retrofits, and an H2OSAV subscription — cost-share up to 50% with per-item caps. Artificial turf is not on the list, and applicants are local governments, small utilities, HOAs/POAs and multi-family properties, not individual homeowners. Say that plainly; it converts better than a vague rebate hint. Background driver: 2022's Florida Senate Bill 64 requires utilities to stop discharging treated wastewater to surface waters such as the St. Johns River by 2032, which is why the city is chasing reclaimed expansion and is in talks with CCUA to interconnect.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO at 29.9919,-81.6784: CASSIA FINE SAND map unit, dominant component MANDARIN at 80% — SOMEWHAT POORLY DRAINED, hydrologic group A, taxonomic class Sandy siliceous thermic OXYAQUIC ALORTHODS. This is a spodosol: fine sand over a cemented spodic horizon (the 'hardpan' local excavators complain about). Minimum annual water table depth 77 cm — about 30 inches / 2.5 feet. Slopes 0 to 2 percent. No mapped flooding or ponding at that point. WHAT THAT MEANS ON THE JOB: unlike Middleburg's free-draining Ortega sand, Green Cove Springs has a wet-season table within two and a half feet of the surface and a subsurface layer that perches water. Do not assume percolation. Base design has to tie into surface drainage or a positive outfall, especially in the historic grid — and the City's own project list confirms the problem is real: it is currently running the Clay Street Stormwater Upgrades, the Ferris Street Storm Basin Project and the Oakridge Stormwater Project, all in and around the old town. That trio of named projects is your credibility line with a historic-district homeowner. Shade: the old grid is heavily canopied — Augusta Savage Friendship Park at Walburg Street and Pine Avenue is described by the City as 'a beautiful oak-shaded lot,' which is exactly the condition where St. Augustine grass thins to dirt. Riverfront: the St. Johns River is the eastern edge; the city has a Riverfront Residential zoning category, and Vera Francis Hall Park backs onto Governors Creek.
facts.housing_stock: CHECKED 2026-09-07. ACS 2024 5-yr (Green Cove Springs city, GEOID 16000US1227400): population 10,044 (up from 9,786 in 2020, which was itself up 41.7% from 6,908 in 2010 — the fastest-growing place in this batch); MEDIAN AGE 37.3, the youngest of the five by seven years; median household income $75,142; median home value $371,000; median year built 1998; 3,532 occupied units but only 2,296 owner-occupied — 65% ownership, the LOWEST of the five, with median gross rent just $1,114. This is genuinely a TWO-MARKET TOWN and the page must treat it as two: (1) THE HISTORIC GRID. Green Cove Springs Historic District, NRHP 1991 (ref 91000281), 300 acres, 78 contributing buildings plus 1 structure, bounded by Bay Street, the CSX tracks, Center Street, Orange Avenue, St. Elmo Street and St. Johns Road. Founded 1854 as White Sulfur Springs, county seat since 1871, and a Gilded Age winter resort — the city's own history pages document The Clarendon, the Qui-Si-Sana, The Oakland, The Muldrow, the Tyler House and the Mohawk Hotel. Kirkpatrick-Wilcox House is the photographed landmark. Zoning here is R-1: minimum lot 7,000 sq ft, 70 ft wide, 20 ft front yard, 10 ft rear yard, 10 ft side yards, max lot coverage 35% — deep old lots with mature canopy and 1900s-1940s frame houses. (2) THE NEW SUBDIVISIONS. The city created a brand-new R-1A small-lot category by Ord. O-21-2022 effective 7 March 2023: minimum lot 5,000 sq ft, 50 ft wide, 7'6" side yards, 10 ft rear yard, 35% coverage. R-2 detached is the same 5,000 sq ft / 50 ft. That is the new-build product now going in west and north — 50-foot lots, 10-foot rear yards, backyards in the 400-900 sq ft range. Named developments: Magnolia West (amenity centre and playground at 30.006,-81.731), Magnolia Point (gated golf community off Harbor Road), and the Rookery subdivision, whose developers are funding Phase 1 of Gustafson Regional Park. Also notable: enclosed garages are required for all residential dwelling units (Sec. 117-5), and ADUs became permitted by Ord. O-05-2025 on 1 April 2025.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $75,142; median age 37.3 (young families, not retirees); 2020 racial composition 70.1% white non-Hispanic, 13% Black, 10% Hispanic/Latino; 21.4% under 18 and 21.9% aged 65+. 35% of occupied units are renter-occupied at a median gross rent of $1,114 — a real working-class rental base in the old grid alongside $370k+ new construction on the edges. County-seat employment: the Clay County Courthouse, county administration, the school district and Kindred Hospital-North Florida are here, plus the Reynolds Park industrial estate on the former naval station. Famous former residents give the town outsized name recognition: Charles E. Merrill (co-founder of Merrill Lynch), Harlem Renaissance sculptor Augusta Savage, and Olympic swimmer Caeleb Dressel. The buyer profile splits cleanly: historic-district owners restoring 1900s houses with shade and drainage problems, and 2020s subdivision buyers on 50-foot lots who want a usable back yard and a dog that isn't covered in mud.
facts.golf: MAGNOLIA POINT GOLF AND COUNTRY CLUB, 3570 Clubhouse Drive, Green Cove Springs (30.0039,-81.7097) — the town's one golf community, gated, off Harbor Road. Magnolia Park sits on Harbor Road directly across from the Magnolia Point entrance. THE ANGLE NOBODY ELSE WILL KNOW: the City's $17,045,000 Magnolia Point Reclaimed Water System project — designed and permitted with Florida DEP State Revolving Fund money to bring reclaimed irrigation water to the neighbourhood and save an estimated 73.9 million gallons of Floridan Aquifer water a year — is CURRENTLY ON HOLD pending alternate projects and funding (city project page, 2026). Reclaimed water is exempt from the watering-day restrictions; potable and well water is not. So until that project resumes, Magnolia Point homeowners are irrigating on restricted water at one day a week under Phase III. That is a specific, checkable, dated reason for a Magnolia Point homeowner to call this week. Adjacent courses: Eagle Harbor Golf Club (2217 Eagle Harbor Parkway) and The Golf Club at Fleming Island (2260 Town Center Boulevard) ~7-8 mi north; Country Club of Orange Park (2525 Country Club Boulevard); and the Penney Retirement Community's 9-hole synthetic-greens course 8 mi west in Penney Farms — the closest working proof that synthetic greens perform in Clay County.

Bennett Elementary (29.989,-81.699); Spring Park Elementary, 3530 County Road 315 (30.012,-81.733); Clay County Center for Community Education; Learning Resource Center. County: CLAY COUNTY FAIRGROUNDS (29.978,-81.742) — high-traffic event ground, ideal for a visible demo/putting installation. Industrial and institutional: REYNOLDS PARK industrial estate (29.975,-81.660) with Reynolds Airpark; Kindred Hospital-North Florida (29.988,-81.683); the Clay County Courthouse campus; Clay County Historical Society Library and the Green Cove Springs Branch Library; Green Cove Springs Marina; Modlins Trucking. HOA common areas: Magnolia Point Golf and Country Club (3570 Clubhouse Drive) entry, clubhouse and pool surrounds; Magnolia West Amenity Center and Magnolia West Playground (30.006,-81.731); the Rookery amenity package. Downtown Redevelopment / CRA projects (Rivers House interior buildout, Walnut Street) are the route to streetscape and civic work.
facts.landmarks: SPRING PARK, 200 Spring Street — the mineral spring locally called the 'Original Fountain of Youth,' with the CITY POOL continuously fed with water straight from the spring, plus playground, gazebo and picnic facilities. THE CITY PIER at the east end of Walnut Street — 500 feet long with 12 boat slips. Clay County Courthouse (NRHP 1975). St. Mary's Episcopal Church (NRHP 1978). Princess Mound (NRHP 1990). Holly Cottage (NRHP 2010, GCS vicinity). Augusta Savage Friendship Park at Walburg Street and Pine Avenue; the Augusta Savage Arts and Community Center at 1107 MLK Jr. Blvd and 415 Lemon Street; the Augusta Savage Museum and Mentoring Building; Thomas Hogans Memorial Gym, 415 Lemon Street. Vera Francis Hall Park, 1400 Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard, backing onto Governors Creek. Magnolia Park on Harbor Road. GUSTAFSON REGIONAL PARK — brand new, Phase 1 (two tennis courts, parking, bathrooms) developer-funded by the Rookery developers, construction began spring 2026 and estimated complete July 2026; Phase 2 is a $400,000 city/FRDAP-funded 1,500-ft nature trail east along Green Cove Avenue connecting at Oakridge Avenue. St. Johns River Trail. CLAY COUNTY FAIRGROUNDS (29.978,-81.742) on the west side. Reynolds Park industrial estate and REYNOLDS AIRPARK (FAA identifier FL60, 29.972,-81.657) on the former Naval Air Station Lee Field / NAS Green Cove Springs, where roughly 500 mothball-fleet vessels were moored on the St. Johns after WWII. Green Cove Springs Marina. Florida Military Museum (29.980,-81.653). Christmas on Walnut Street and the 3rd Saturday Market in the Park are the town's signature events. And the growth driver: the FIRST COAST EXPRESSWAY (SR 23) now terminates at SR 16 on the city's eastern edge — Phase 2 from SR 21 to US 17 opened 9 August 2025 with the final segment completed 29 June 2026, and Phase 3 to I-95 with a replacement Shands Bridge is due 2031-32.

name: Penney Farms

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE PROOF THAT ALREADY EXISTS ON THE GROUND: 'Penney Farms already plays on artificial greens.' The Penney Retirement Community says on its own website that it is home to what it calls the only 9-hole synthetic greens golf course in Florida — nine holes under mature live oaks draped in Spanish moss, no greens fees for residents, no tee times, carts allowed on the course. Every other page on this website has to ARGUE that synthetic putting surfaces work in northeast Florida heat, sand and rain. This page gets to point at a course that has been doing it in Clay County for years. That is the most valuable single sentence in the whole research set and it should be quoted, attributed to PRC, and linked — then reused as social proof on the Middleburg, Green Cove Springs and Fleming Island pages: 'the only synthetic-greens golf course in Florida is fifteen minutes from here.' THE SECOND HALF OF THE LEAD is the soil, and it explains why this town went synthetic before anyone else: LEON FINE SAND, poorly drained, hydrologic group A/D, wet-season water table about TWELVE INCHES down, on ground with 0-2% slope. Grass here doesn't just burn in a drought, it drowns in August. Combine that with a median age of 81.1 and the argument writes itself: level, mud-free, non-slip, cane-and-walker-safe ground is a safety product, not a landscaping product, for a campus that advertises a Governor's Gold Seal and a CMS five-star rating. WHY THIS PAGE IS COMPLETELY DIFFERENT FROM THE TOWN NEXT DOOR: do not write it as a residential lead-gen page. There are FORTY-SIX owner-occupied housing units in the entire town — residents hold life-lease arrangements with PRC, not deeds, and the median household income is $52,500 on fixed retirement income. Green Cove Springs eight miles east is a growing municipal-utility county seat with young families on new 50-foot lots. Middleburg is well-water acreage with no HOA. Penney Farms is a single 192-acre institution founded by J.C. Penney in 1922, inside a 600-acre National Register historic district with 24 contributing buildings, where the client is a non-profit board and a facilities director. Write it as an institutional case-study page addressed to PRC — synthetic green refurbishment and expansion, courtyard and quadrangle turf under the oaks, cart-path shoulders, and safe therapy surfaces outside the rehab and memory care buildings — with the town's Recreation Center and Martina C. Kohler Park as the civic add-ons. One landed PRC project here is worth more across the rest of the site than every residential lead this town will ever produce.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Penney Farms is an incorporated TOWN with a council-manager government, but it is very small (642-821 residents) and its code of ordinances is NOT published on Municode — I could not verify any municipal landscaping or turf provision online, and the page should not claim one either way. Contact the town directly before quoting a job inside the corporate limits. What IS verified: there is NO artificial-turf prohibition in the Clay County Code of Ordinances, and Clay County's Chapter 18.5 Article III landscaping standards apply only to nonresidential paved areas and to residential buildings inside the Branan Field Corridor and Greater Lake Asbury District — neither of which covers Penney Farms. Clay County Chapter 18.5 Division 2 irrigation restrictions do apply. THE REAL GATEKEEPER IS NOT GOVERNMENT — IT IS THE PENNEY RETIREMENT COMMUNITY. PRC owns and controls the 192-acre campus and effectively the housing stock (only 46 of 300 occupied units are owner-occupied), so campus standards, the board of directors and the facilities department decide what happens to the grounds. Treat PRC as the client, not the HOA. SECOND GATEKEEPER: the MEMORIAL HOME COMMUNITY HISTORIC DISTRICT, listed on the National Register 3 February 1999, 600 acres with 24 contributing buildings and 2 structures, bounded by SR 16, Caroline Boulevard, Wilbanks Avenue and Studio Road. NRHP listing on its own imposes no design control on private work, but any project touching a contributing building, or any work involving federal or state funding or permitting, triggers historic review — and the community will care about appearance regardless. Specify a natural-looking, muted, multi-tone turf for anything in the quadrangle and say why.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: CLAY COUNTY UTILITY AUTHORITY serves the Penney Farms area (CCUA headquarters is at 3176 Old Jennings Rd, Middleburg); confirm per meter, and note the PRC campus is a single large institutional customer, which is exactly why a water-consumption argument lands harder here than in any single house. CURRENT STATUS AS OF 2026-09-07: SJRWMD PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE — irrigation limited to ONE DAY PER WEEK. Odd/no-numbered addresses Saturday, even Sunday, NONRESIDENTIAL TUESDAY (the PRC campus and the town's civic properties fall under the nonresidential Tuesday schedule). No watering 8 a.m.-6 p.m.; max 3/4 inch per zone; max one hour per zone; applies to private wells and pumps as well as utility water. Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-79 penalties: category 2 civil infraction first, category 10 second and subsequent, up to $500 if contested and lost, each day a separate offense, one written warning. NOTE THE EXEMPTION THAT MATTERS TO A GOLF COURSE: Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-72 defines 'landscape irrigation' to EXCLUDE 'golf course greens, tees, fairways, primary roughs, and vegetation associated with recreational areas such as playgrounds, football, baseball and soccer fields.' So a grass course could legally keep watering — which makes PRC's decision to run synthetic greens a choice about cost and maintenance labour, not a compliance workaround. That is a stronger story, not a weaker one: they went synthetic because it is better, not because they had to. REBATES: none for artificial turf. The SJRWMD Water Conservation Rebate Program (launched October 2024) funds Florida Water Star certification, WaterSense smart controllers, irrigation conversions to rotary or micro-irrigation, irrigation evaluations and timer modification, landscape soil amendments, indoor fixture retrofits and H2OSAV subscriptions at up to 50% cost-share — and the eligible applicants ARE local governments, small utilities, HOAs/POAs and multi-family properties, which for once includes an institution like PRC. Turf still is not an eligible item, but a smart-controller and irrigation-evaluation rebate is a legitimate thing to mention when proposing a partial turf conversion to the campus.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO at 29.9769,-81.8106: LEON FINE SAND, 0 to 2 percent slopes — 89% of the map unit, POORLY DRAINED, hydrologic group A/D, taxonomic class Sandy siliceous thermic AERIC ALAQUODS. MINIMUM ANNUAL WATER TABLE DEPTH 31 CM — ABOUT 12 INCHES. That is the worst drainage of the five by a wide margin and it is the technical heart of the page. Leon is the classic Florida flatwoods spodosol: fine sand over a dark cemented spodic horizon that perches water, on ground with essentially no slope (0-2%). WHAT THAT MEANS ON THE JOB: in the wet season water sits within a foot of the surface. Grass here does not just dry out in drought, it DROWNS in summer, stays soggy, scalps under a mower and rots at the crown. A turf base cannot rely on percolation at all — you excavate to the spodic layer or above it, install an open-graded aggregate base with geotextile separation, crown the surface and daylight the base laterally into a swale or drain. Put that on the page in plain words: 'Penney Farms sits on Leon fine sand with a hardpan and a wet-season water table about a foot down. That is why lawns here stay soggy and why we build the base to drain sideways.' It is checkable, it explains a problem every long-time resident has lived with, and it is the correct engineering. Shade: mature LIVE OAKS DRAPED IN SPANISH MOSS across the campus and over the golf course — PRC's own description — which is exactly the canopy under which turfgrass will not establish. Safety dimension unique to this town: with a median age of 81, walking surfaces matter. Level, non-slip, mud-free, cane-and-walker-friendly ground is a health-and-safety argument here, not an aesthetic one.
facts.housing_stock: CHECKED 2026-09-07. ACS 2024 5-yr (Penney Farms town, GEOID 16000US1255875): population 642 (the 2020 census counted 821, up from 749 in 2010 — cite both and note the ACS is a five-year estimate); MEDIAN AGE 81.1 — one of the oldest communities in Florida and by far the oldest in this batch; median household income $52,500 (lowest of the five); median home value $230,800; MEDIAN YEAR STRUCTURE BUILT 1954 — the oldest housing stock in the batch by forty years. 300 occupied units, of which ONLY 46 ARE OWNER-OCCUPIED — 15% ownership, because most residents hold life-lease / residency agreements with the Penney Retirement Community rather than deeds. Median gross rent $1,946, the highest in the batch, which is the retirement-community fee structure showing up in the census. Only 102 single-unit detached and 4 mobile homes. The town spans 1.46 square miles near the geographic centre of Clay County, about 8 miles west of Green Cove Springs. THE HOUSING IS THE INSTITUTION: J.C. Penney founded the place in 1922 as an experimental suburban farming village, and after the 1929 crash refocused it as a retirement community for Christian clergy in honour of his Baptist preacher father. The PENNEY RETIREMENT COMMUNITY has operated since 1926 on a 192-acre campus at 3495 Hoffman Street, housing Christian laypeople, clergy and missionaries. The MEMORIAL HOME COMMUNITY HISTORIC DISTRICT (NRHP, listed 3 February 1999) covers 600 acres bounded by SR 16, Caroline Boulevard, Wilbanks Avenue and Studio Road, with 24 contributing historic buildings and 2 contributing structures. Product types: 1920s-1950s masonry and frame cottages and quadrangle buildings, mid-century apartments, and modern healthcare and assisted-living buildings (memory care, nursing, long-term care, rehab/PT/OT/speech). Yards are small, communal courtyards and cottage strips rather than private back gardens, with golf-cart circulation throughout — the town motto is 'Unity in Community.'
facts.who_lives_there: MEDIAN AGE 81.1. Retired clergy, missionaries, and Christian lay people — a residency-qualified, non-profit, 501(c)(3) community, twelve-time recipient of Florida's Governor's Gold Seal Award for Excellence in Long-Term Care and a CMS five-star rated facility. Median household income $52,500 on fixed retirement income; median gross rent $1,946 reflecting community fees; 85% of occupied units are NOT owner-occupied. What this means commercially and you should be blunt about it internally: THERE IS ALMOST NO SINGLE-FAMILY HOMEOWNER MARKET IN PENNEY FARMS. Forty-six owner-occupied units in the entire town. Do not build this page as a residential lead-gen page — build it as an institutional and reputational page. Residents mostly cannot authorise a landscaping change on a building they do not own, and they are on fixed incomes. The buyer is the PRC organisation, the town, and the surrounding rural SR 16 corridor. The secondary value of this page is enormous, though: the credibility it lends every other page on the site.
facts.golf: THIS IS THE SINGLE BEST FACT IN THE ENTIRE FOUR-COUNTY RESEARCH SET. The Penney Retirement Community states on its own website that it is 'home to the only 9-hole synthetic greens golf course in Florida.' A whole town's golf course is already artificial. The course sits on campus (mapped in OpenStreetMap at roughly 29.981,-81.806 to 29.981,-81.808), and PRC describes it as 'a beautiful environment graced with mature live oaks draped in Spanish Moss,' with a clubhouse that stores clubs and keeps loaner sets for visitors, several daily 'best ball' times plus open play with no tee time required, golf carts permitted on the course (most residents use carts to get around the community), and NO GREENS FEES for residents. The emphasis, in PRC's words, is on fellowship and activity rather than competition. Everything to do on this page flows from that sentence. Nearest conventional courses: Magnolia Point Golf and Country Club, 3570 Clubhouse Drive, Green Cove Springs, about 8 miles east; Eagle Harbor Golf Club and The Golf Club at Fleming Island about 15 miles northeast. Also verify before publishing: PRC's claim of being the ONLY 9-hole synthetic greens course in Florida is their own marketing claim — quote it as their claim, attributed, rather than asserting it as independent fact.
facts.commercial_targets: THE WHOLE PAGE IS A COMMERCIAL PAGE — build it that way. (1) PENNEY RETIREMENT COMMUNITY, 3495 Hoffman Street, 904-284-8200, admissions/main 904-284-5994. The single biggest opportunity: resurfacing and expanding the existing 9-hole synthetic greens course, adding a practice putting green and chipping area by the clubhouse, cart-path shoulders, and low-maintenance turf in the courtyards and quadrangle where live oaks make grass impossible. Also on campus: memory care, nursing, long-term care and rehab/PT/OT/speech buildings — level, non-slip, fall-forgiving outdoor walking and therapy surfaces are a direct clinical and liability argument to a facility that markets its Governor's Gold Seal and CMS five-star ratings. Add the clubhouse, the P.E.T. workshop (residents build mobility carts), music and club spaces, and staff/visitor entry areas. (2) THE TOWN OF PENNEY FARMS — council-manager government: Penney Farms Recreation Center (29.978,-81.820) and Martina C. Kohler Park (29.981,-81.813). Two small municipal jobs that produce photographs and a reference letter. (3) Shadowlawn Elementary School (30.016,-81.814) just north. (4) The SR 16 rural corridor east toward Green Cove Springs — acreage owners, and the Clay County Fairgrounds 6 miles east. Realistically, one excellent PRC project here is worth more as marketing across the other 40 town pages than a year of residential leads in this town.
facts.landmarks: THE PENNEY RETIREMENT COMMUNITY CAMPUS, 3495 Hoffman Street, Penney Farms FL 32079 (904-284-8200) — 192 acres, operating since 1926, founded by J.C. Penney in 1922 as an experimental farming village and refocused after the 1929 crash as a home for retired clergy in memory of his father. THE 9-HOLE SYNTHETIC GREENS GOLF COURSE on campus under live oaks and Spanish moss — the landmark. THE MEMORIAL HOME COMMUNITY HISTORIC DISTRICT (NRHP 1999), 600 acres bounded by SR 16, Caroline Boulevard, Wilbanks Avenue and Studio Road, 24 contributing buildings and 2 structures — the quadrangle of 1920s memorial cottages is the visual signature. THE PAVILION at PRC (recent press release on their site). Penney Farms Recreation Center (29.978,-81.820). Martina C. Kohler Park (29.981,-81.813). Shadowlawn Elementary School is the nearest public school (30.016,-81.814). State Road 16 runs through, connecting to Green Cove Springs 8 miles east and to the First Coast Expressway. Penney Farms residents drive golf carts as everyday transport — the cart, not the car, is the local image. Also nearby for orientation: Camp Blanding to the southwest (Clay County's highest point at 259 feet), Ronnie Van Zant Memorial Park 6 miles north in Lake Asbury, and the Clay County Fairgrounds 6 miles east.

name: Middleburg

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: 'You're on a well. The county still tells you when you can water — and right now it's one day a week.' That is the Middleburg page and no other town in the service area can use it the same way. Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-77 applies the irrigation ordinance to every person in the county including private wells and pumps, the SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage has residents down to Saturday-or-Sunday-only, and Sec. 18.5-79 makes a second violation a category 10 civil infraction with up to $500 exposure and every day a separate offense. Middleburg is the town where the largest number of people wrongly believe the rules don't apply to them, and where Ortega fine sand — hydrologic group A, water table 4+ feet down, pure quartz Quartzipsamments that hold no water at all — punishes one-day-a-week watering harder than any soil on the coast. Then pivot to the second half of the lead: NOBODY IS ASKING PERMISSION HERE. Most of Middleburg is unincorporated acreage with no HOA, no CDD, no architectural review board and 45% manufactured housing — you can build a 900 sq ft backyard putting green, a fenced dog run, or a full turf lawn behind a doublewide on two acres without a single approval. WHY THAT'S DIFFERENT FROM THE TOWN NEXT DOOR: Fleming Island and Hibernia, ten miles east, are $116k-$129k income, master-planned, covenant-controlled and on city or CCUA water where turf is a luxury upgrade. Green Cove Springs is a municipal utility town with a historic grid and an impervious-surface cap. Middleburg is well water, sand, acreage, dogs, and no permission — which means the products are pet turf, dog runs, backyard chipping-and-putting greens on big lots, and full-yard replacement for people sick of watering sand. PRICE HONESTLY: median home value is $254,600 and median income $74,634, so most of this page's traffic is $7-8/sq ft work. Put the $10-12 offer in a clearly separated block aimed at The Ravines, Lake Asbury and acreage putting greens — don't price the whole page as if it were Ponte Vedra.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Middleburg is UNINCORPORATED — there is no town council, no municipal ordinance, and no architectural review board. Clay County code governs. Clay County Code of Ordinances (codified through Ord. 2026-12, Supp. 86), Chapter 18.5 VEGETATION: Article III (Landscaping) applies to paved ground surface areas of all NONRESIDENTIAL buildings countywide, plus ALL RESIDENTIAL BUILDINGS within the BRANAN FIELD CORRIDOR and the GREATER LAKE ASBURY DISTRICT (Sec. 18.5-51) — both of which sit in the Middleburg orbit, so a house in Lake Asbury has landscape obligations a house on CR 218 does not. Sec. 18-5.54: screening plus internal landscaping must total not less than 10 percent of the total developed area. Sec. 18.5-52(6) defines 'ground cover' as LOW GROWING PLANTS such as liriope or English ivy 'or like material' — living plants — and Sec. 18.5-53(3) requires that 'all landscaped areas shall be provided with an irrigation system or a readily available water supply.' PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: artificial turf almost certainly does NOT count toward the required 10% landscape on a commercial job in unincorporated Clay County. Sell commercial turf as the amenity area BEYOND the code minimum, never as a substitute for it, and say so up front — it builds credibility with the site engineer. There is NO artificial-turf prohibition anywhere in the county code. HOA reality: outside the platted subdivisions most of Middleburg has no HOA at all, which is the single biggest permission advantage this town has over Fleming Island, Nocatee or Ponte Vedra. Inside The Ravines, Ridaught Landing and the Lake Asbury communities expect standard covenants — check them, but none are known to ban synthetic turf. Note also Florida's Florida-Friendly Landscaping statute (F.S. 373.185) limits what HOAs can forbid, but it protects Florida-Friendly LANDSCAPING, which does not automatically include artificial turf — do not overclaim it.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: CLAY COUNTY UTILITY AUTHORITY (CCUA) — and CCUA's headquarters is physically in Middleburg at 3176 Old Jennings Rd (904-272-5999). Several subdivisions are on their own private package plants instead (The Ravines, Ridaught Landing, Meadowlakes). A large share of rural Middleburg is on PRIVATE WELLS. CURRENT STATUS AS OF 2026-09-07: SJRWMD PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE is in effect — landscape irrigation cut to ONE DAY PER WEEK. Odd/no address = Saturday; even = Sunday; nonresidential = Tuesday. No watering 8 a.m.-6 p.m. Max 3/4 inch per zone, max one hour per zone. CRITICAL SELLING POINT: the restrictions apply to private wells and pumps, ground and surface water — Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-77 applies to 'each person located within the county,' so the common Middleburg belief that 'I'm on a well, it doesn't apply to me' is wrong. Normal (non-shortage) schedule under Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-73: DST — odd Wed+Sat, even Thu+Sun, nonresidential Tue+Fri; EST — one day only. PENALTIES, Sec. 18.5-79: first violation is a category 2 civil infraction, second and subsequent a category 10, up to $500 if you contest and lose, EACH DAY a separate offense, one written warning maximum, enforceable by law enforcement. REBATES — the honest answer: NO. The SJRWMD cost-share rebate program (launched Oct 2024) covers only Florida Water Star certification, EPA WaterSense smart controllers, irrigation conversions to rotary/micro, irrigation evaluations, landscape soil amendments, indoor fixture retrofits and H2OSAV subscriptions — artificial turf is NOT an eligible item, and the program is open to local governments, small utilities, HOAs/POAs and multi-family properties, NOT individual single-family homeowners. CCUA does offer bill credits for NEW SOD installation and for verified leaks — which is a nice rhetorical hook: the utility gives you a water-bill credit because new sod drinks so much. Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-74(2) also grants new landscape a 60-day establishment window (daily watering for 30 days, then every other day for 30 more) — that is the water bill artificial turf eliminates.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO at 30.0655,-81.8595: ORTEGA FINE SAND, 0 to 5 percent slopes — 85% of the map unit, moderately well drained, hydrologic group A, taxonomic class Thermic uncoated Typic QUARTZIPSAMMENTS (essentially clean quartz sand with almost no clay or organic matter). Minimum annual water table depth 130 cm (~51 inches / 4.3 ft) — the second-deepest in this batch. No flooding, no ponding. What that means on the job: percolation is excellent, so a standard 3-4 inch open-graded base drains without engineering heroics — but the same sand holds essentially no water or nutrients, which is exactly why St. Augustine and Bahia in Middleburg go straw-coloured between waterings and why one day a week under Phase III will kill it. Terrain: the Black Creek ravine system is the local exception — Black Creek Ravines Conservation Area (30.069,-81.836) has genuine slope, and the North Fork Black Creek at Middleburg cuts through the historic core, so riverside and ravine-adjacent lots have real grade, erosion and shade issues that flat-lot competitors will misprice. Shade: mature live oak and longleaf/slash pine canopy over the older Main Street area and the acreage lots — dense enough that turfgrass simply will not fill in under it. Dogs: with 87% owner-occupancy, acreage, and no HOA, this is the highest-density dog-run and pet-turf opportunity of the five.
facts.housing_stock: CHECKED 2026-09-07. ACS 2024 5-yr (Middleburg CDP, GEOID 16000US1245350): population 11,644 (DOWN from 12,881 in the 2020 census — the only shrinking place in this batch); median year structure built 1994; median home value $254,600 (lowest of the five); 4,558 occupied units, 3,976 owner-occupied (87% ownership). THE DEFINING NUMBER: 2,066 mobile/manufactured homes vs 2,857 single-unit detached — roughly 45% of the housing stock is manufactured housing. This is NOT a manicured-subdivision town on average. Middleburg CDP covers 19.62 sq mi of land for ~12,900 people (2020) — genuinely rural density, big parcels, well-and-septic common outside platted subdivisions. Housing splits into three products: (1) manufactured/modular homes on 1-10 acre wooded parcels along Blanding Blvd (SR 21), CR 218 and CR 220 — no HOA, no architectural review, huge open yards; (2) 1980s-2000s platted subdivisions with modest HOAs, several running their OWN package utilities — The Ravines (Ravines Rd / Ravine Hill Dr / Ravines Lakes Rd, ~30.056,-81.851, with a Ravines Water Treatment Plant and Ravines Waste Water Treatment Plant), Ridaught Landing (~30.096,-81.79, which has a water plant, a wastewater plant AND a REUSE water treatment plant — reclaimed irrigation, exempt from watering-day limits), Meadowlakes (Meadowlakes Water Treatment Plant, 30.044,-81.800); (3) newer Lake Asbury / Bradley Creek Parkway growth on the east side toward Green Cove Springs. Historic core: Middleburg Historic District (NRHP 1990, ref 90000313), 60 acres along Main Street, Palmetto Street and Wharf Street beside Black Creek — Clark-Chalker House (3891 Main St), Haskell-Long House (3858 Main St), Frosard W. Budington House (3816 Main St), George Randolph Frisbee Jr. House (2125 Palmetto St), Edenfield House (2160 Wharf St). Backyards: no standard — expect anything from a 60x100 rear yard in Ridaught Landing to two open acres behind a doublewide on CR 218.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $74,634 (ACS 2024 5-yr) — essentially level with Green Cove Springs, and well below Clay County's overall $76,679 and Fleming Island's $116,611. Median age 44.7. Predominantly white (86.4% per 2020 census), 5.4% Hispanic, 2.8% Black. 55.2% married-couple households. Heavy commuter town: over half of Clay County workers commute to another county and the county has the third-longest average commute in Florida at ~33 minutes — Middleburg is the far end of that commute. Large military/veteran presence (Camp Blanding to the southwest, NAS Jacksonville and Cecil Field to the north). Practical read for pricing: this is a $7-8/sq ft town at the median. The $10-12/sq ft work exists but is concentrated in The Ravines, the Lake Asbury side, and acreage owners building backyard putting greens — not distributed across the CDP.

name: Hibernia

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE GROUND AND THE NAME, NOT THE WATER BILL. Hibernia is the only address in this batch where the household median is $129,325 with 97% ownership and zero mobile homes, and it is the only one sitting on BLANTON FINE SAND — well drained, hydrologic group A, water table 65 inches down, the deepest and cleanest profile of the five. Open the page with that: 'Hibernia sits on some of the best-draining sand in northeast Florida. It is the ground a golf architect would ask for — and it is why the putting greens we build here can have real contour instead of being a flat mat on a lawn.' Then anchor it in the place: this is the 1790 Hibernia Plantation, George Fleming's Spanish land grant, and St. Margaret's Episcopal Church and Cemetery has been on the National Register since 1973 — the oldest listing in Clay County. These are river-bluff estate lots on the west bank of the St. Johns below Fleming Island, a mile from The Golf Club at Fleming Island and three from Eagle Harbor, owned by people who have lived there thirty years and are members somewhere. The product is the tournament-quality backyard green with a fringe and a chipping approach, plus deep-shade lawn replacement under the plantation live oaks where nothing has ever grown, plus pool and lanai surrounds. WHY THAT'S DIFFERENT FROM THE TOWN NEXT DOOR: Fleming Island proper — one mile north — is 1998-2005 master-planned CDD product on platted lots inside Eagle Harbor, Pace Island and Fleming Island Plantation, with covenants and a landscape committee. Hibernia is the unplatted historic river frontage: bigger, older, wealthier, largely covenant-free, and it does not need anyone's permission. Green Cove Springs seven miles south is a municipal-utility county seat with an impervious cap; Middleburg ten miles west is well-water acreage with 45% manufactured housing. Hibernia is the one page in the batch that should never mention price and should lead entirely with permanence, drainage engineering and golf. SECONDARY, NOT PRIMARY: the Phase III one-day-a-week restriction applies to private wells and river withdrawals here too (Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-77) — use it as a supporting paragraph for the owner with two irrigated acres, not as the headline. HONEST NOTE FOR THE BUILD: Hibernia has no census geography of its own; every income and housing figure above is Census Tract 307.01, which also covers south Fleming Island. Do not put a precise 'Hibernia median income' figure on the public page — describe the corridor.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Hibernia is UNINCORPORATED — no town government, no municipal code, no architectural review board of its own. Clay County code applies: Chapter 18.5 Article III landscaping standards apply to nonresidential paved areas countywide (and to residential buildings only within the Branan Field Corridor and Greater Lake Asbury District, neither of which covers Hibernia), and Division 2 landscape irrigation rules apply to everyone. There is NO artificial-turf prohibition anywhere in the Clay County code. The real gatekeepers here are PRIVATE COVENANTS, not government. Fleming Island's master-planned communities — Eagle Harbor, Fleming Island Plantation, Pace Island — carry HOAs and in places CDD-funded amenity standards; the historic Hibernia Road / river-frontage parcels are largely unplatted and covenant-free. That is a genuinely useful distinction to make on the page: tell the reader that if their address is on Hibernia Road or the river side of US 17 they very likely need no approval at all, and that if they are inside an Eagle Harbor or Plantation village they should send you the covenant and you will read it. Note also that the NRHP listing of St. Margaret's Episcopal Church and Cemetery (1973) is honorary and imposes no design control on neighbouring private property. Florida's Florida-Friendly Landscaping statute (F.S. 373.185) constrains what HOAs may prohibit, but it protects Florida-Friendly landscaping, which does not automatically include artificial turf — do not overclaim it.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: CLAY COUNTY UTILITY AUTHORITY (CCUA) for most of the corridor, with some private package systems (the Fleming Oaks water and wastewater plants at 30.075,-81.704 serve part of the area). River-adjacent estate properties commonly irrigate from private wells or from the St. Johns/Doctors Lake. CURRENT STATUS AS OF 2026-09-07: SJRWMD PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE — one irrigation day per week. Odd/no address Saturday, even Sunday, nonresidential Tuesday; no watering 8 a.m.-6 p.m.; max 3/4 inch per zone; max one hour per zone. Clay County Code Sec. 18.5-77 applies these limits to every person in the county INCLUDING private wells, pumps, ground and surface water — so pulling from the river or a shallow well is not an exemption, and the estate owners with the biggest irrigated areas are the ones with the most exposure. Penalties under Sec. 18.5-79: category 2 civil infraction on a first violation, category 10 on a second, up to $500 if contested and lost, each day a separate offense, one written warning only. Exemptions that matter here (Sec. 18.5-74): micro-spray, micro-jet, drip and bubbler systems any time; hand-held hose with an automatic shut-off nozzle any time; reclaimed water any time; and recycled water from wet detention ponds any time provided they are not augmented. Reclaimed availability is patchy in this corridor — confirm per address rather than assuming. REBATES: none for artificial turf. The SJRWMD cost-share rebate program (Oct 2024) covers Florida Water Star certification, WaterSense smart controllers, irrigation conversions, irrigation evaluations, soil amendments, indoor retrofits and H2OSAV, up to 50% cost-share, and applicants are local governments, small utilities, HOAs/POAs and multi-family properties — not single-family homeowners, and not synthetic turf. CCUA offers bill credits for new sod installation and verified leaks, not for turf.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO at 30.0650,-81.6978: BLANTON FINE SAND, 0 to 5 percent slopes — 80% of the map unit, WELL DRAINED (the only 'well drained' rating of the five), hydrologic group A, taxonomic class Loamy siliceous semiactive thermic GROSSARENIC PALEUDULTS. Minimum annual water table depth 165 cm — about 65 inches / 5.4 feet, the DEEPEST in this batch by a wide margin. No flooding, no ponding at that point. WHAT THAT MEANS ON THE JOB: this is the best turf ground in the whole batch. Deep clean sand over a loamy subsoil more than four feet down means excavation is easy, percolation is genuine, and a properly compacted open-graded base will stay stable — which is exactly the profile that lets you build a putting green with real undulation, tiered shelves and a fringe collar rather than a flat mat. Use that in the copy: 'Hibernia sits on Blanton fine sand — the same deep, well-drained sand a golf architect would ask for.' Caveats specific to the river bluff: parcels dropping toward the St. Johns have real grade, so retaining and edge detailing matter; and the mature live oak, magnolia and cypress canopy along the old plantation frontage — the same canopy that shades St. Margaret's churchyard — is dense enough that turfgrass will not hold under it. Nearby water features shape drainage: Black Creek and Peters Creek converge at Camp Chowenwaw just south, and Jessie Island and Little Jessie Island sit offshore.
facts.housing_stock: CHECKED 2026-09-07. HONEST CAVEAT FIRST: Hibernia is an unincorporated community with NO census place geography, so there is no place-level ACS data. The best available proxy is CENSUS TRACT 307.01, Clay County (which covers Hibernia and the southern end of Fleming Island): ACS 2024 5-yr population 8,280; MEDIAN HOUSEHOLD INCOME $129,325 — by far the highest in this batch and above Fleming Island CDP's $116,611; median home value $384,000; median age 48.9; 3,315 occupied units with 3,225 owner-occupied (97.3% ownership); 3,183 single-unit detached and ZERO mobile homes; median year structure built 1995. Treat the tract as indicative of the corridor, not of the historic hamlet itself. What is actually there: Hibernia sits at roughly 30.065,-81.698 on the WEST BANK OF THE ST. JOHNS RIVER, off US 17, at the southern end of what is now Fleming Island. It is the original 1790 Hibernia Plantation — Irish immigrant George Fleming (1760-1821) received a 1,000-acre Spanish land grant for military service and named it after the Latin for Ireland; his son Col. Lewis Michael Fleming (1798-1862) inherited it, and after the Civil War Lewis's second wife Margaret Seton turned the damaged plantation house into a tourist resort. The Hibernia post office ran 1849-1931. The housing product today is a mix: genuine large-lot and riverfront estate parcels along Hibernia Road and the river bluff, established 1990s-2000s Fleming Island homes inland (Fleming Island Plantation, Eagle Harbor, Pace Island are the master-planned names on the island proper), and smaller riverside enclaves — Cypress Bluff Court, Cypress Glen Drive, Bartram Plantation, Edgewater Landing, Black Creek Village nearby. Backyards here are the largest of the five in a high-income context: think half-acre to multi-acre river lots with dock frontage, not 50-foot builder lots. Some are served by private package utilities (Fleming Oaks Water Treatment Plant and Fleming Oaks Waste Water Treatment Plant at ~30.075,-81.704).
facts.who_lives_there: Tract 307.01 median household income $129,325; median home value $384,000; median age 48.9; 97% owner-occupancy and zero mobile homes — the wealthiest, most settled, most owner-controlled of the five places in this batch and one of the wealthiest ZIP-code areas in the Jacksonville region (Fleming Island ranked #1 in the Jacksonville area by ZIP in 2021 and #2 in 2013). Established professional and executive households, empty-nesters and second-generation Fleming Island owners; a strong medical employment cluster right there (Baptist Clay Medical Campus, Jacksonville Orthopaedic Institute). Older skew than Green Cove Springs by more than eleven years, with the disposable income and the length-of-tenure that supports a permanent installation rather than a cheap fix. THIS IS THE $10-12/SQ FT AUDIENCE in this batch — and the only one of the five where you should lead with craftsmanship and permanence rather than water bills.
facts.golf: Hibernia has no course of its own — it is a hamlet, not a development — but it is a mile or less from two clubs and the page should say so precisely. THE GOLF CLUB AT FLEMING ISLAND, 2260 Town Center Boulevard (30.0701,-81.7162) — roughly 1.2 miles from the St. Margaret's site, with its own driving range mapped just west of the course. EAGLE HARBOR GOLF CLUB, 2217 Eagle Harbor Parkway, Fleming Island (30.1107,-81.7278) — the island's flagship club, about 3.5 miles north, centre of the Eagle Harbor community. COUNTRY CLUB OF ORANGE PARK, 2525 Country Club Boulevard (30.1747,-81.7663) — about 8 miles north. MAGNOLIA POINT GOLF AND COUNTRY CLUB, 3570 Clubhouse Drive, Green Cove Springs — about 7 miles south. Practical read: a Hibernia or south-Fleming-Island client is very likely a member at Eagle Harbor or Fleming Island, plays several times a week, and is the single best backyard-putting-green prospect in the entire four-county service area — high income, big lot, no CDD small-lot constraint, and Blanton fine sand that is already close to a USGA-spec base profile.
facts.commercial_targets: Churches with large campuses and shaded, hard-to-grow grounds — HIBERNIA BAPTIST CHURCH (playgrounds, children's ministry areas, courtyards), Sacred Heart Catholic Church, Fleming Island Methodist, St. Luke's, and St. Margaret's Episcopal (a historic churchyard where turfgrass fails under oaks — a small, high-visibility, high-reference job). PLANTATION SPORTS COMPLEX (30.0887,-81.7201) — the Fleming Island Plantation multi-field complex, the biggest field-conversion target in the corridor. EAGLE HARBOR SOCCER COMPLEX, 4387 Lakeshore Drive (30.1159,-81.7246). Healthcare: Baptist Clay Medical Campus and Jacksonville Orthopaedic Institute & Rehabilitation Center — courtyards, healing gardens, rehab surfaces and shaded entry areas, and a rehab facility is a natural buyer of an even, fall-forgiving walking surface. Schools nearby: Fleming Island High School, St. Johns Classical Academy (30.101,-81.727), Heritage Christian Academy (30.119,-81.704), Doctors Inlet Elementary. Clubs: The Golf Club at Fleming Island, Eagle Harbor Golf Club, Country Club of Orange Park — practice greens, chipping areas, driving-range tee lines and clubhouse surrounds. HOA common areas: Eagle Harbor, Fleming Island Plantation and Pace Island amenity centres, pool decks and entry monuments. County: Camp Chowenwaw Park and Island Forest Park.
facts.landmarks: ST. MARGARET'S EPISCOPAL CHURCH AND CEMETERY (30.0673,-81.6964) — listed on the National Register in 1973, the OLDEST NRHP listing in Clay County, built by the Fleming family on the Hibernia Plantation grounds. It is the single most recognisable thing in Hibernia and any local will place it instantly. HIBERNIA BAPTIST CHURCH (30.0656,-81.7091) — one of the largest congregations in Clay County and the name most people actually associate with the word 'Hibernia' today. Sacred Heart Catholic Church and its columbarium (30.0627,-81.7088); Fleming Island Methodist Church; St. Luke's Church. THE GOLF CLUB AT FLEMING ISLAND and its driving range (30.070,-81.716). CAMP CHOWENWAW PARK (30.041,-81.715) — the Clay County park on the former Girl Scout camp at the confluence of Black Creek and Peters Creek, a genuine local touchstone. Back it with the one hard technical fact that separates you from every satellite-photo bidder: Albany fine sand here is hydrologic group A/D with the seasonal water table as shallow as 21 INCHES, so bases have to be built to shed water sideways to a positive outfall, not down into sand that is already full. Chapter 18.5 Article III landscaping standards apply to nonresidential paved areas countywide, and to residential buildings only inside the Branan Field Corridor and the Greater Lake Asbury District — NEITHER of which covers Virginia Village, so a residential job here has no county landscape obligation at all. Chapter 18.5 Division 2 irrigation restrictions do apply. HOA: no HOA over the general US 17 / CR 226 area. facts.water_and_rules: Provider: this far south on US 17 the corridor is a mix of CLAY COUNTY UTILITY AUTHORITY service and PRIVATE WELLS AND SEPTIC — verify per address; do not assert a single provider on the page. A rural US 17 landowner on a well is fully covered. The SJRWMD Water Conservation Rebate Program (Oct 2024) funds Florida Water Star certification, WaterSense smart controllers, irrigation conversions, irrigation evaluations, landscape soil amendments, indoor fixture retrofits and H2OSAV at up to 50% cost-share, for local governments, small utilities, HOAs/POAs and multi-family properties — artificial turf is not eligible and individual homeowners are not applicants.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA SSURGO at 29.9206,-81.6823: ALBANY FINE SAND, 0 to 5 percent slopes — 85% of the map unit, SOMEWHAT POORLY DRAINED, hydrologic group A/D (the dual rating is the tell: it behaves like free-draining sand until the water table rises, then it behaves like clay), taxonomic class Loamy siliceous subactive thermic GROSSARENIC PALEUDULTS. MINIMUM ANNUAL WATER TABLE DEPTH 53 CM — about 21 INCHES. That is the second-shallowest in this batch and it is the single most important technical fact about installing turf in Virginia Village. WHAT THAT MEANS ON THE JOB: in the wet season the water table can sit less than two feet below grade, so a base that relies on downward percolation WILL saturate and pump fines. This is a place where you excavate deeper, use an open-graded aggregate base with a geotextile separation layer, crown the surface, and daylight the base to a positive outfall or a French drain rather than trusting the sand. Say that on the page in plain language — 'in Virginia Village the water table can come up to within two feet of your back door in August, so we build the base to shed water sideways, not down' — because it is true, it is checkable, and no competitor bidding off a satellite photo will price it. AIRPARK-SPECIFIC: on a taxiway-adjacent lot, base compaction has to tolerate an occasional aircraft tyre and prop wash, and the surface must not shed loose infill that could become FOD near an open hangar — specify a stabilised or non-migrating infill and a proper edge restraint, and put that in writing. Grass clippings and blown sand are an existing nuisance around hangars; turf removes both.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE WATER TABLE AND THE ABSENCE OF AN HOA — the drainage build IS the product, and the freedom to just do it is the closer. Palm Valley shares a ZIP code with Ponte Vedra Beach and shares nothing else. Ponte Vedra Beach is the ocean side: dune sand that drains too fast, salt burn, club money, golf. Palm Valley is the marsh side one mile west: a tidal water table, salt-marsh muck under the sand, 1.43 square miles of open water inside a 12-square-mile CDP, and a canopy of unclearred live oaks and cabbage palms over lots that have been there since the moonshine days. The homeowner's actual complaint is not 'my lawn looks bad', it is 'my backyard is a mud pit, the dog tracks it inside, and it breeds mosquitoes'. So this page must be the ENGINEERING page: publish the base spec — 3–4 inches of compacted open-graded stone over geotextile, engineered positive fall, French drain or swale tie-in, permeable backing rated well above site infiltration — and lead with photos of standing water before and dry turf after. Then the closer that no other page in the batch can use: A LARGE SHARE OF PALM VALLEY HAS NO HOA. Say it plainly. In Nocatee a mile west, 100% of homes need Architectural Review Committee approval and a 30–60 day wait. On Palm Valley Road and Roscoe Boulevard, many owners can sign today. Third pillar: these are big, deep, wooded acreage lots — which means the two highest-margin add-ons actually fit here, unlike on a 50-foot Nocatee lot. A full 600–1,000 sq ft short-game complex with a chipping pad and a bunker, and a genuinely large dog run for people who own boats and labradors. Fourth, a compliance angle nobody else will write: St. Johns County prohibits fertilizer within 10 feet of any surface water body, and in Palm Valley a huge share of lots touch a tidal creek, canal or the marsh — turf needs no fertilizer at all, which turns a regulatory headache into a feature. Finally, the drought: since 11 May 2026 Phase III has limited irrigation to one day a week AND BANNED NEW SOD, so an owner whose shaded, waterlogged lawn finally gave up this summer is not legally allowed to replace it with grass.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE STANDOUT FACT: a large share of Palm Valley — the older unplatted acreage along Palm Valley Road, Roscoe Boulevard and Canal Boulevard — is NOT IN ANY HOA. That is genuinely unusual this close to the ocean in St. Johns County, and it is a real commercial advantage: no ARC packet, no committee meeting, no 30-to-60-day approval wait. The page should say so directly, because it is the exact opposite of Nocatee's 100% CDD/HOA coverage a mile west. Inside the gated enclaves — Marsh Landing Country Club, Sawmill Lakes, Odom's Mill, The Preserve, Seven Mile Drive, Isle of Palms — a conventional ARC applies and the standard Florida packet (site plan, product spec, infill and backing detail, drainage plan, licensed and insured contractor) is expected. Palm Valley sits OUTSIDE the Ponte Vedra Zoning District overlay that governs the Ponte Vedra Boulevard corridor across A1A, so PVZAB is generally not your approval path here — St. Johns County Growth Management is. Countywide LDC rules that do apply: Florida-Friendly landscaping on new development (at least half native species, at least half the irrigated area low-volume) and an Impervious Surface Ratio cap set by the Comprehensive Plan, whose definition of impervious includes 'compacted materials utilized for parking or roadways' — since Palm Valley lots frequently sit inside wetland buffers and county Natural Resources review (LDC Article IV), documenting turf permeability is more important here than anywhere else in the batch. State preemption: Fla. Stat. § 125.572 (HB 683, ch. 2025-140, effective 1 July 2025) bars the county from prohibiting DEP-compliant synthetic turf on single-family residential parcels of one acre or less — note that many Palm Valley acreage parcels EXCEED one acre, so the statutory shield does not automatically cover the whole property.
facts.water_and_rules: Potable water is St. Johns County Utility Department; a substantial share of the older acreage properties along Palm Valley Road and Roscoe Boulevard irrigate from PRIVATE SHALLOW WELLS — and on the marsh side those wells can pull brackish. The SJRWMD shortage orders apply to private wells and pumps, not just utility customers, so 'I'm on a well' is not the exemption owners assume. St. Johns County has been under PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE since 11 May 2026, driven by an Extreme Drought (D3) classification — the highest recorded in Florida since 2000. Phase III terms: ONE irrigation day per week; no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m.; odd or no address SATURDAY, even address SUNDAY, non-residential TUESDAY; maximum 3/4 inch and one hour per zone; NO NEW SOD INSTALLATION AND NO NEW PLANTINGS; aesthetic water uses prohibited; street and pressure washing restricted. Reclaimed water is exempt from the one-day cap; micro-spray, micro-jet, drip and bubbler are allowed anytime. Normal (non-shortage) schedule: odd Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, non-residential Tue/Fri during daylight saving; one day each in Eastern Standard Time; avoid 10 a.m.–4 p.m.; one hour per zone. New landscaping normally gets 30 days unrestricted then 30 days alternating — currently moot under the sod ban. St. Johns County fertilizer rule: max 5 lb nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per year, and NOTHING WITHIN 10 FEET OF A SURFACE WATER BODY — that ten-foot rule bites hard in Palm Valley specifically, where a very large share of lots touch tidal creek, marsh, canal or the ICW. Enforcement: SJC Code Enforcement (904) 209-0734 or the SJC Connect app. No artificial turf rebate exists from SJRWMD, JEA or St. Johns County — do not claim one.
facts.soil_and_yard: THIS IS THE PAGE'S PRODUCT. Palm Valley is the low, wet, west-facing half of San Pablo Island — fine coastal quartz sand over salt-marsh organic muck, a high and tidally influenced water table, and 1.43 sq mi of open water inside a 12.18 sq mi CDP. (Landform, water area and setting are sourced; the soil-profile and water-table mechanics are installer field knowledge — confirm per-parcel via USDA Web Soil Survey and check FEMA flood zone.) The result on the ground is a yard that is spongy underfoot after any rain, holds standing water in the low quarter for days, grows moss and dollarweed instead of St. Augustine, and turns to mud along every path the dog takes. Layer on DENSE SHADE: the Palm Valley Road and Roscoe Boulevard corridor is Old Florida canopy — sprawling live oaks, cabbage palms and Spanish moss over lots that have never been cleared — so the same sub-4-hour sun problem as Riverside applies, but with the water table three feet down instead of ten. Slope is almost nil. Mosquito pressure is real (Anastasia Mosquito Control District serves St. Johns County) and standing water in a dead lawn is a breeding site, which is a legitimate, non-cosmetic argument for eliminating it. Salt aerosol reaches here but is milder than on the oceanfront. The honest technical conclusion the page should make: on a Palm Valley lot the turf is the cheap part — the deliverable is 3–4 inches of compacted open-graded stone over geotextile, engineered positive fall, a French drain or swale tie-in, and a permeable backing rated well above the site's infiltration rate. Publish those numbers.
facts.housing_stock: IMPORTANT GEOGRAPHIC FACT THE PAGE MUST GET RIGHT: Palm Valley is a census-designated place on San Pablo Island, EAST OF THE INTRACOASTAL AND WEST OF A1A, running north from Palm Valley Boulevard to Butler Boulevard (JTB), with Nocatee to the west across the ICW, Ponte Vedra Beach to the east, the Jacksonville Beaches north and St. Augustine Beach south. In other words Palm Valley is the MARSH-AND-INTRACOASTAL half of the same 32082 ZIP whose ocean half is Ponte Vedra Beach — same postal address, completely different yard. 12.18 sq mi of land plus 1.43 sq mi of water; 9,803 housing units; population 19,796–22,486 depending on vintage (21,827 at the 2020 census, up from 20,019 in 2010). Median home value $690,800 with 75–81.4% owner-occupied and only 1,676 renter-occupied units. The stock is a genuine SPLIT, and that split is the sales strategy: (a) older, pre-1980s Old Florida frame and block houses on deep, wooded, often unplatted acreage strung along Palm Valley Road (CR 210), Roscoe Boulevard and Canal Boulevard — many with NO HOA AT ALL, boats, docks, workshops and dogs; and (b) 1980s–2020s gated and platted enclaves including Marsh Landing Country Club, Sawmill Lakes, Odom's Mill, The Preserve, Seven Mile Drive, Isle of Palms and Harbour Island, with conventional associations. NeighborhoodScout flags Sawmill Lakes/Palm Valley as leading neighbourhood income growth in the area over the past five years — the money is moving in and rebuilding.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $116,625 and per capita income $90,258 — Palm Valley ranks 109th of Florida's 956 incorporated cities, towns and CDPs for median household income (89th percentile) and 51st for per capita income (95th percentile). Median home value $690,800. Median age 51.2, with about 27% aged 65-plus and only 13.2% under 15 — older than Nocatee, marginally younger than Ponte Vedra Beach. Poverty just 4.17%. 9,284 employed; leading sectors Professional/Scientific/Technical Services (1,310), Health Care & Social Assistance (1,246) and Retail Trade (977); leading occupations Management (2,090), Sales (1,754) and Business/Financial Operations (853). 87.5% white non-Hispanic, 98.7% US citizens, two cars per household, 24.1-minute average commute. THE CHARACTER READ, which matters more than the numbers: Palm Valley is where people who love the water live — boat owners, fishermen, dock people, dog people — as opposed to the golf-and-club identity of Ponte Vedra Beach across A1A. The high per-capita number combined with older unplatted acreage means a lot of quiet, low-debt, long-tenure owners with real budget and no committee to ask.
facts.golf: Golf is present but it is NOT the differentiator here, and the page should treat it as a secondary section rather than the lead. MARSH LANDING COUNTRY CLUB is the one that is genuinely in this corridor — a private championship 18 threaded through Intracoastal marsh, tidal creeks, pines and lagoons, with 10 lighted Har-Tru courts, a large fitness facility and a resort pool; its marsh-front lots are the premium residential target in Palm Valley. Everything else is a short drive: TPC Sawgrass (THE PLAYERS Stadium Course and Dye's Valley), Sawgrass Country Club and The Plantation at Ponte Vedra just east across A1A; Ponte Vedra Inn & Club's Ocean and Lagoon courses; the Sawgrass Marriott; Jacksonville Beach Golf Club north over JTB. So Palm Valley homeowners have full access to the same golf as Ponte Vedra Beach — but they usually have the LOT SIZE to build a proper 600–1,000 sq ft short-game complex, which the tighter beach and Nocatee lots often will not take. Position the green as the upsell on a drainage job, not the headline.
facts.commercial_targets: Smaller and more specialised than Jacksonville's, and the page should target accordingly. MARSH LANDING COUNTRY CLUB — clubhouse landscape, pool deck, the 10 lighted Har-Tru tennis courts' surrounds, fitness-facility flooring, cart-path aprons and practice areas; the single best commercial logo in this CDP. HOA COMMON AREAS in Sawmill Lakes, Odom's Mill, The Preserve, Isle of Palms and Harbour Island — entry medians, amenity lawns, mail kiosks, pool decks. MARINE AND DOCK BUSINESSES along the Intracoastal — boat yards, marinas, dock-builder yards, and the Palm Valley boat ramp area; dock and boat-lift landing surfaces and marina walkway edges are a niche almost nobody bids. WATERFRONT RESTAURANTS — Palm Valley Fish Camp and Palm Valley Outdoors have outdoor deck and lawn areas where mud is a genuine operating problem. SCHOOLS: Ocean Palms Elementary, Landrum Middle and Ponte Vedra High serve this corridor; Palm Valley Academy is just west in Nocatee. PET: veterinary practices, groomers and boarding along A1A and CR 210, plus the dog-owning residential base. Also short-term rental and second-home managers along Roscoe — low-maintenance is a direct operating-cost argument for them.
facts.landmarks: Palm Valley Road (CR 210) and the PALM VALLEY BRIDGE over the Intracoastal — the fixed-span bridge everyone uses as the local reference point. Roscoe Boulevard running along the ICW under the oaks. Canal Boulevard. The Palm Valley Fish Camp restaurant on the Intracoastal and Palm Valley Outdoors Bar & Grill — the two names every local will recognise instantly. The Palm Valley boat ramp. Marsh Landing Country Club's gate on A1A. Sawmill Lakes. The Guana Tolomato Matanzas National Estuarine Research Reserve to the south. Butler Boulevard (JTB) forming the north edge. The name's origin is a good local detail: settlers named it Palm Valley for the abundant palms, and the early economy was ranching, farming, logging and SELLING PALM FRONDS, followed by MOONSHINE PRODUCTION DURING PROHIBITION — the Intracoastal creeks were a bootlegging route. That is far more interesting than anything Nocatee can claim and it is documented.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE BUILDER-GRADE BACKYARD THAT NEVER WORKED — the 25-by-30-foot rectangle between the pool cage and the preserve fence, on compacted engineered fill, that has taken two rounds of St. Augustine and killed both. facts.ordinance_or_hoa: HOA AND CDD ARE UNIVERSAL HERE — 100% coverage, which is the opposite of Hilliard and much of Palm Valley. Nocatee is governed through Community Development Districts (the Nocatee CDD and the Tolomato CDD structure) plus a per-neighbourhood HOA with an Architectural Review Committee. Approval is neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood ARC, and the page should say exactly that rather than assert a rule that does not exist. What is verifiable is the general Florida ARC pattern — a complete packet (site plan, product spec sheet, infill and backing details, drainage plan, contractor licence and insurance) materially improves approval odds, and drainage, realism and neighbourhood consistency are the three decision factors committees actually weigh. THE LEGAL LEVER: Fla. Stat. § 125.572, created by HB 683 (2025), ch. 2025-140, effective 1 July 2025, requires DEP to adopt minimum synthetic-turf standards for single-family residential properties of one acre or less — material type, colour, permeability, stormwater management, potable water conservation, water quality, proximity to trees — and preempts local governments from prohibiting compliant installations. CRITICAL CAVEAT FOR THIS PAGE SPECIFICALLY: that statute binds GOVERNMENTS, not HOAs. A Nocatee ARC can still say no by covenant. Do not overstate it. Countywide, the St. Johns County LDC requires Florida-Friendly landscaping on new development (at least half native species, at least half the irrigated area on low-volume irrigation) and applies an Impervious Surface Ratio cap whose definition includes 'compacted materials' — so submit permeability documentation with the ARC packet. The realistic service offer: 'we prepare and submit your ARC packet' is worth more in Nocatee than anywhere else in the four counties.
facts.water_and_rules: THIS IS THE MOST SPECIFIC, MOST CHECKABLE LOCAL WATER DETAIL IN THE ENTIRE BATCH AND THE PAGE SHOULD LEAD ITS UTILITY SECTION WITH IT. Nocatee is served with RECLAIMED WATER BY JEA under a Reclaimed Water Conservation Schedule established in spring 2025 with SJRWMD support, created specifically because reclaimed pressure in Nocatee was failing. Under that schedule NOCATEE IS DIVIDED INTO FOUR WATERING ZONES, each with assigned watering days keyed to the number of irrigation days SJRWMD currently allows — AND TWO DAYS EACH WEEK WHEN RECLAIMED WATER SERVICE IS SIMPLY NOT AVAILABLE. Potable service in the area is St. Johns County Utility Department. Layer on the drought: St. Johns County has been under a PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE since 11 May 2026 (Extreme Drought D3, highest in Florida since 2000) — one irrigation day per week, nothing 8 a.m.–6 p.m., odd Saturday / even Sunday / non-residential Tuesday, max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone, and NO NEW SOD INSTALLATION OR NEW PLANTINGS. Reclaimed water is exempt from the one-day-per-week cap, which is why Nocatee residents assume they are fine — but the JEA zone schedule and the two no-service days mean their reclaimed lawn is still not getting what St. Augustine needs, and pressure at the far end of a zone is often too low to run a full cycle. St. Johns County also came online with the $191.8M SR 207 Water Reclamation Facility on 11 May 2026, the largest capital project in county history — evidence of just how tight reuse capacity has been. County fertilizer cap: 5 lb N per 1,000 sq ft per year, nothing within 10 ft of surface water. Enforcement: SJC Code Enforcement (904) 209-0734 or the SJC Connect app. No turf rebate exists — do not claim one.
facts.soil_and_yard: Nocatee was built on 13,323 acres of former pine flatwoods and silviculture land, and that history is why these lawns fail. (Land history is sourced; the soil mechanics below are installer field knowledge — verify per-lot with USDA Web Soil Survey.) Northeast Florida flatwoods sit on spodosols — fine quartz sand over a cemented spodic hardpan typically 12–30 inches down — which perches water after every summer storm and then goes bone dry in spring. Mass grading for a DRI of this size means most lots are engineered fill, compacted to a density that roots cannot penetrate, with a thin veneer of topsoil and sod laid over it. Add the stormwater system: ponds, berms, swales and preserve edges are everywhere in Nocatee by design, so a large share of backyards back to water or to a preserve line and sit at the low point of the drainage. THE PRACTICAL SYMPTOM the page should describe in the homeowner's own words: a 25-by-30-foot backyard that is standing water for two days after a storm, then a mud pit, then bare dirt where the dog runs the fence line, with St. Augustine that has been replaced twice and died twice. Slope is minimal, so the fix is base engineering — open-graded stone, geotextile, positive fall, a tie-in to the existing drain or swale — not turf selection. Shade is LOW here compared with Jacksonville or Palm Valley; these are young landscapes with young trees, so the real issue is water and compaction, not canopy. That is a genuinely different technical story from the oak-shade pages and should be written as one.
facts.housing_stock: This is a POSTAL COMMUNITY, not a town, and the distinction matters for the page: 32081 is the inland Ponte Vedra ZIP west of the Intracoastal, and it is overwhelmingly Nocatee. Nocatee is a 13,323-acre (27.29 sq mi) master-planned community in northern St. Johns County, approved as a Development of Regional Impact in 2001, under construction since 2005, developed by The PARC Group (founded by Roger O'Steen in 1989). Population went from 4,524 in 2010 to 22,503 in 2020 — a 397% increase in one decade — and the wider 32081 ZIP now counts about 31,654. Roughly 50 neighbourhoods, some age-restricted. THE HOUSING NUMBERS ARE THE STORY: median construction year 2015; 66.3% of all homes built between 2010 and 2019; 82.2% owner-occupied. NeighborhoodScout describes 32081 real estate as among the newest in the nation. This is production building — Dream Finders, David Weekley, ICI, Toll Brothers, Pulte, Providence, Riverside — on 40, 50, 65, 75 and 90-foot lots, with courtyard and zero-lot-line plans throughout. The backyards are the commercial fact: on the common 50–65 ft product the usable rear yard is frequently 20–35 feet deep before you hit a preserve line, a retention pond bank or a rear easement, and much of that is taken by a pool cage or lanai. That is a 400–900 sq ft turf job repeated across thousands of near-identical lots. At the top end, St. Johns County luxury new construction runs from the upper $700s past $12 million with a median near $1.2M, but the 32081 volume is the middle. Nocatee is reportedly around 96% sold with fewer than 400 homes remaining — worth knowing: the new-build wave is ending and the RETROFIT wave (2012–2018 homes now on their second failed lawn) is beginning.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $156,501 for ZIP 32081 and $131,738 for Nocatee proper — very high, but earned rather than inherited, and structurally different from Ponte Vedra Beach. Median age 40.8–40.9 versus 53.1 at the beach, and Nocatee skews heavily to FAMILIES WITH SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN, which is why 30% of the beach is over 65 and this place is not. 81.3% white. These are dual-income professionals — Jacksonville finance, healthcare, tech, Mayo Clinic, Baptist, remote executives — who moved for the A-rated St. Johns County schools. Behaviourally this is the opposite customer from the beach retiree: they research online, they compare quotes, they ask about warranty and pet safety and lead content, they are active on the Nocatee community Facebook groups and Nextdoor, and they buy what their neighbour bought. Referral velocity here is the highest in the service area — one visible install on a cul-de-sac generates the next three.
facts.golf: BE HONEST: NOCATEE ITSELF HAS NO GOLF COURSE, and pretending otherwise will get the page caught. This is the single biggest golf difference between 32081 and 32082 and it is an OPPORTUNITY, not a weakness.
