Median household income $62,417, per capita income $33,987, with a 16.2% poverty rate that runs well above state and national figures. Only 9.4% hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Veterans make up 13.8% of the population, more than double the national rate. Racially homogeneous (about 94.3% white; diversity index 11). And extremely stable: only about 4% of residents moved in the past year versus roughly 12% nationally, so word-of-mouth and neighbour referrals compound here in a way they will not in Nocatee or Wildlight.
facts.golf: None in the CDP, and nothing close. This is a genuine golf desert — the nearest courses are the Amelia Island / SR 200 cluster roughly 25-30 minutes northeast (The Golf Club at North Hampton, Amelia National, Fernandina Beach Golf Club, Amelia River Club) or the Jacksonville north- and west-side public courses. There is no golf community, no course frontage and no club culture to sell against here. Be honest about that on the page. The one usable inversion: for the retired golfer on a half-acre in Nassau Village-Ratliff, the nearest decent practice green is a 30-minute drive each way, which is precisely the argument for a compact 300-500 sq ft chipping and putting green at home — but pitch it as convenience for a fixed-income retiree, not as country-club prestige.
facts.commercial_targets: Genuinely thin inside the CDP — it is 14.7 square miles of scattered rural residential with essentially no verified commercial anchor of its own. Do not pad. The honest play is to point commercial capacity at the adjacent Callahan cluster: Callahan Ball Park (seven baseball/softball fields, a football stadium, two soccer fields, batting cages, mid-upgrade with county funds), Callahan Elementary / Intermediate / Middle and West Nassau County High School, the Callahan library branch, and Nassau County School District as an account. Local-scale opportunities that do fit the CDP itself: churches along the county roads, small independent kennels, boarding and grooming operations, and equine/livestock properties (the lots explicitly accommodate small livestock) — pet turf and wash-down runs are the realistic recurring commercial product here, not stadium fields. Verify any named business independently before it goes on the page.
facts.landmarks: Thin, and the page should not invent any. Verified: the CDP sits within the Callahan-Hilliard Census County Division of Nassau County with a 32011 (Callahan) mailing address, 14.68 square miles at roughly 30.5108N, -81.8088W, and includes the Ratliff and Keene areas. Residents orient to Callahan for daily life — the weekly farmers market, small-town diners and seasonal festivals, the historic Callahan Train Depot and Railroad Day, the Callahan library branch — and to the US 1 / US 301 corridor and the Duval County line for commuting. Children attend the Callahan school cluster. Realistically, a Nassau Village-Ratliff page should name Callahan landmarks and the surrounding road network rather than claim landmarks the CDP does not have.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: 'Backyard putting greens built to the standard of the course you already play — and the ARB paperwork to get them approved.' Why this and nowhere else: Sawgrass is the only place in the service area where the customer's reference point for a green is the Stadium Course they can see from their kitchen, and where THE PLAYERS Championship sets the visual bar every March. Two concrete, town-specific hooks the page should carry that no neighbouring town page can honestly use: (1) THE GOLF-COURSE CLAUSE. FS 720.3045 protects backyard turf that isn't visible from the street, a neighbour, common area — or a community golf course. In Sawgrass a huge share of lots are fairway-front, so the statute does NOT automatically protect them and the architectural review board really is the decision-maker. Being the installer who arrives with the completed ARB submittal (plot plan, permeability data, PFAS/heavy-metal validation, base and infill spec, warranty, 12x12 sample) is worth more than any discount and is exactly how you justify $10–12/sq ft. (2) SHADE, NOT DROUGHT. These are 1975–1995 houses under 45 years of live oak canopy; the failure mode is a lawn that will not grow in shade plus root competition, not a lawn that burns. That is the opposite of the South Ponte Vedra pitch and unrelated to Nocatee's tiny-yard pitch. Bonus proof point: DEP Rule 62-308.100's 10-foot waterbody setback and tree-drip-line/arborist rule are precisely the two things a cheap installer gets wrong on a Sawgrass lagoon-and-oak lot — say so, and the $7/sq ft competitor disqualifies himself.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THIS IS THE MOST REGULATED PLACE IN THE BATCH AND THE PAGE MUST SAY SO. (1) State preemption now helps: FS 125.572 (HB 683, signed 16 June 2025) plus DEP Rule 62-308.100, EFFECTIVE 19 MAY 2026, bar local governments from prohibiting or inconsistently regulating compliant synthetic turf on single-family lots of 1 acre or less. (2) But the preemption applies to LOCAL GOVERNMENTS, NOT HOAs — private associations keep their own authority. (3) FS 720.3045 (HB 437, 2023) stops an HOA restricting items — artificial turf named explicitly — that are NOT visible from the parcel frontage, an adjacent parcel, an adjacent common area, OR A COMMUNITY GOLF COURSE. That golf-course clause bites harder in Sawgrass than anywhere else in northeast Florida: on a fairway-front lot the statutory protection evaporates and the ARB genuinely controls the decision. (4) DEP Rule 62-308.100 hard requirements that shape Sawgrass jobs: turf must be permeable and free of intentionally added PFAS and heavy metals; NO in-ground irrigation of turf areas; not in a swale, ditch, stormwater pond or littoral zone; NO CLOSER THAN 10 FEET from a natural or man-made waterbody measured from the ordinary/mean high water line (this kills naive lagoon-front designs); not inside a tree drip line unless a certified arborist certifies it is not harmful (this is the constraint on every mature-oak Sawgrass backyard); anchored at all edges and seams to withstand wind and flooding. (5) Practically: expect a home-improvement application, plot plan, product spec sheet with lead/heavy-metal validation, base and infill spec, seam adhesive spec, warranty documentation and a 12"x12" physical sample to the ARB. Selling the ARB package as a service is the differentiator.
facts.water_and_rules: Potable water in Ponte Vedra Beach 32082 is served by one of three St. Johns County providers (St. Johns County Utility, JEA, City of St. Augustine) — the county publishes no service-area map and directs residents to 904-209-2700 to confirm by address. VERIFY BY ADDRESS before making any claim on the page; my read is that JEA serves much of Ponte Vedra Beach but I could not confirm it in this pass. Restrictions as of the check date are severe: SJRWMD/St. Johns County have been in a PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE since 11 May 2026 — landscape irrigation limited to ONE DAY PER WEEK, no irrigation 8am–6pm, applying to utility water, private wells and pumps, and surface water alike. New sod installation is restricted, and pressure washing and aesthetic water uses are curtailed. Normal (non-drought) SJRWMD schedule: DST — odd addresses Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, non-residential Tue/Fri; EST — one day each. Max 3/4 inch per zone, one hour per zone. Reclaimed water is exempt from the once-weekly cap. NO TURF-REMOVAL OR TURF-INSTALL REBATE was found for any St. Johns County or SJRWMD program in this pass — do not claim a rebate exists on the page.
facts.soil_and_yard: Coastal-ridge and relict-dune sand east of A1A — fast-draining, low organic content, salt-influenced, and the reason lawns here need constant irrigation and fertiliser to hold colour. West of A1A the ground transitions toward flatwoods soils with a shallow seasonal water table and a spodic hardpan that perches water after summer storms. The dominant yard problem in Sawgrass is not drought, it is SHADE: 45–50 years of live oak, laurel oak and slash pine canopy over lawns that were sodded in full sun in 1980, plus root competition that St. Augustinegrass cannot win. Second problem is the lagoon/fairway edge — a large fraction of lots slope to a golf lagoon or retention feature, which stays soggy and scalps. NOTE: soil-series characterisation here is general regional knowledge (NE Florida flatwoods spodosols and coastal dune sands), not read off a county soil survey in this pass — flag as unverified if used as a factual claim.
facts.housing_stock: Two adjacent gated communities totalling roughly 2,400 acres and ~3,300 residences, all built late 1970s through the 1990s — this is the OLDEST high-end stock in the batch and nothing like a new-build subdivision. SAWGRASS COUNTRY CLUB (east of A1A, ~1,250 acres, 1,409 residences) is the only gated residential community east of A1A in Ponte Vedra Beach, so every owner is on the beach side; mix of estate homes, patio homes, townhomes and six condo neighborhoods, quoted range roughly $200Ks (condos) to well over $2M (oceanfront/estate). SAWGRASS PLAYERS CLUB / TPC SAWGRASS (west of A1A, ~1,200+ acres, ~1,900 residences across 16 named sub-subdivisions incl. Salt Creek, Oakbridge, Cypress Creek, The Coves) plus Vicars Landing retirement apartments. Lots are irregular and golf/lagoon-oriented rather than gridded — typical single-family parcels run roughly 1/4 to 1/2 acre with genuinely usable rear yards, but a large share of them are fairway-front or lagoon-front, which changes the job. Patio-home and townhome products have small walled courtyards. Census: Sawgrass CDP pop. 4,734; median home/condo value ~$994,568 (2024 est.). HOA prevalence is 100% — master association plus a sub-association and architectural review board for nearly every one of the 16 Players Club subdivisions and each Country Club village.
facts.who_lives_there: Older, asset-rich, low-turnover. Median age 57.4 — the oldest of the five places by a wide margin. Census-reported median household income $121,519 (2019–2023 ACS) understates real wealth badly here: per-capita income is ~$99,099 and average individual income ~$97,687 against ~$1M median home values, because a large share of residents are retired and living on assets, not W-2 wages. NeighborhoodScout puts the area in the top ~15% of US neighborhoods by income and higher than 97% of neighborhoods nationally. Practical read: seasonal residents, retirees, PGA TOUR and Fidelity/financial-services executives, second-home owners. They pay cash, they hire on reputation and referral inside the gate, and they will not chase a price — but they will absolutely reject a contractor who does not know how to file an ARB submittal.
facts.golf: The densest concentration of famous golf in Florida outside Orlando, and it is INSIDE the community, not adjacent. TPC SAWGRASS — Players Stadium Course (host of THE PLAYERS Championship; the island-green 17th) and Dye's Valley Course. PGA TOUR Global Home / headquarters is physically here (1 PGA TOUR Blvd). SAWGRASS COUNTRY CLUB — 27 holes designed by Ed Seay (three nines: East, West, South). SAWGRASS MARRIOTT GOLF RESORT & SPA. Immediately adjacent: Ponte Vedra Inn & Club (Ocean Course and Lagoon Course), Marsh Landing Country Club, and Palm Valley Golf Club (9-hole executive with a 10,000 sq ft practice putting green) a few minutes south in Nocatee. No other town in this batch can claim a championship course inside its own gates.
facts.commercial_targets: Sawgrass Marriott Golf Resort & Spa (resort courtyards, event lawns, pool decks, practice green). TPC Sawgrass clubhouse and practice facilities. PGA TOUR Global Home campus. Vicars Landing retirement community (pet relief areas, low-maintenance courtyards, resident putting green — a very strong fit). Sawgrass Country Club Beach Club (oceanfront pool deck, salt-exposed lawn). Sawgrass Village retail common areas. Ponte Vedra Inn & Club and The Lodge & Club. The 16 Players Club sub-association common areas, playgrounds and pool surrounds — one ARB relationship can generate a dozen jobs. Schools nearby: Ocean Palms Elementary, Alice B. Landrum Middle, Ponte Vedra High School. Ponte Vedra Athletic Association fields. Veterinary and pet-boarding businesses along A1A and JTB.
facts.landmarks: The island green 17th at TPC Sawgrass. The TPC Sawgrass clubhouse (one of the largest in the world). PGA TOUR Global Home on PGA TOUR Blvd. Sawgrass Marriott Golf Resort & Spa. Sawgrass Village shopping centre (Publix, CVS, boutiques). The Sawgrass Beach Club with 1,600 feet of private oceanfront. Vicars Landing. The A1A gatehouses that split Country Club (east) from Players Club (west). THE PLAYERS Championship in March, when the whole town's landscaping is judged by 200,000 visitors.

facts.strongest_angle: Atlantic Beach is the ONLY city in the entire service area that publishes a written artificial turf specification and requires a city inspection of the stone base before the turf goes down. Lead the whole page on that, because it reframes the transaction. Every competitor in this market quotes a price per square foot; on this page Timeless Grass & Greens quotes a code-compliant cross-section — 2 inches of #57 stone under 2 inches of #89, four inches minimum, 100 inches-per-hour ASTM-certified permeability, no paver sand, no screenings, no fines, light compaction only — and produces the permeability documentation, cross-section drawing and tree-relative site plan the city's review actually demands, then leaves the base exposed for inspection instead of burying a failing job. Any installer who shows up with paver sand fails here, publicly, on an inspection. That is a moat, and it is worth $10–12/sq ft on its own. Then deliver the payoff the homeowner cares about: because Atlantic Beach counts genuinely permeable turf as PERVIOUS, a compliant install does not consume the 45% impervious cap that a patio, a driveway extension or a pool (which now counts, since Ord. 90-19-238 in 2019) would eat into — in a city that tightened that cap precisely because of flooding. Turf is the only way to turn a dead, shaded, root-bound yard into usable space without spending impervious allowance. No neighbor can run this page: Neptune Beach and Jacksonville Beach have no published turf spec, Butler Beach has no municipal government at all, and Mayport is federal land. Support it with a second section on Selva Marina and Atlantic Beach Country Club — ~0.36-acre on-course lots, an Ed Seay 1958 layout redeveloped by Erik Larsen in 2014, and the 18th green where Nicklaus made his first tournament double eagle in 1966 — as the batch's one true backyard-putting-green neighborhood.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: This is by far the richest regulatory field of any town in the service area, and it is the page. The City of Atlantic Beach publishes formal 'Artificial Turf Installation Guidelines.' Turf is expressly permitted, and — critically — if it is genuinely permeable it counts as PERVIOUS for lot-coverage purposes. The spec: ASTM-certified permeability with a minimum 100 inches per hour; a minimum 4-inch permeable, free-draining aggregate base, specified as 2 inches of #57 stone as the lower drainage layer over-laid with 2 inches of #89 stone, or clean angular crushed rock with little to no fines. Expressly PROHIBITED base materials: paver sand, crushed fines, stone screenings, decomposed granite containing fines, and any compacted material that reduces permeability. Light compaction only — compaction that restricts air or water movement through the base is prohibited. No turf in any city right-of-way, and installation must not interfere with drainage patterns or push runoff onto adjacent properties. Tree rules: keep turf outside drip lines where possible, and if installing under a dripline stay a minimum 18–24 inches from the trunk, cap subbase depth under trees at 3 inches, lightly compact only, keep materials permeable to water AND oxygen, and cause no pooling at tree bases. Turf is allowed in privately owned stormwater retention/drainage areas only if designed storage volume and drainage function are fully preserved, without obstructing structures, overflow paths or maintenance access — and the city may require engineering documentation proving it. Products must be free of hazardous materials and heavy metals. City review requires manufacturer product specifications, permeability testing documentation, installation details/cross-section drawings, and a site plan showing turf locations relative to trees and property lines. And the enforcement teeth: the aggregate subbase MUST be inspected and approved by the city BEFORE turf is installed, with the base left exposed and accessible until approval is granted. Separately, Ordinance 90-19-238 (adopted February 25, 2019) reduced the impervious cap in all conventional residential zoning districts from 50% to 45%, made swimming pools count as impervious, and triggers on-site stormwater storage for any modification adding more than 250 sq ft of impervious area. Statewide, FS 125.572 (Ch. 2025-140) directs FDEP to set minimum synthetic-turf standards for single-family lots of 1 acre or less and will preempt inconsistent local regulation once adopted — so track that, but the Atlantic Beach spec is the governing document today.
facts.water_and_rules: The City of Atlantic Beach Public Utilities Department produces and distributes its own potable water and handles its own wastewater — NOT JEA. Customer service at City Hall, 800 Seminole Road, (904) 247-5816; utilities office at 902 Assisi Lane. SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage applies (mid-May 2026, Duval included): irrigation ONE day per week, never 8 a.m.–6 p.m., residential odd addresses Saturday, even Sunday, non-residential Tuesday, maximum 3/4 inch and one hour per zone, restrictions extended to private wells and pumps, and tightened limits on irrigating new plantings including sod. Micro-irrigation and hand-held hoses exempt. No turf rebate identified — do not claim one.
facts.soil_and_yard: Barrier-island sand over a high water table, and the city's own legislative record proves the drainage problem rather than leaving it to inference: Atlantic Beach cut its residential impervious cap specifically to address citywide stormwater and flooding, and now requires on-site stormwater storage whenever a modification adds more than 250 sq ft of impervious surface. Mature live oaks throughout Old Atlantic Beach and Selva Marina create heavy shade and protected root zones — which is precisely why the city's turf guidelines carry explicit tree rules. Practical read: shaded, root-bound, poorly draining yards where grass has already failed and where any hardscape fix costs the homeowner impervious allowance.
facts.housing_stock: A 1920s resort town that grew into the largest-lot beach city of the batch. Incorporated 1926, developed after Henry Flagler's railroad and the 250-room Continental Hotel (dance pavilion, tennis courts, fishing pier). Distinct products: Old Atlantic Beach near the ocean — small historic cottage lots; Saltair (from 1949) — mid-century, midsize homes; Royal Palms (from 1960) — smaller mid-century homes; and Selva Marina (from 1955) — the standout, large homes wrapped around the golf course with listing lot sizes around 0.36 acre, plus Selva Marina Garden. Also the historically Black Donner neighborhood, with a different income profile — the city is not uniform and the page shouldn't pretend it is. 13,513 residents (2020) on 3.68 sq mi of land (13.17 sq mi total). 6,434 housing units: 64.8% detached single-family, 16.1% attached (duplex/townhouse). 73.9% homeownership. Median property value $630,200 (2024), median gross rent $2,305. Bottom line for turf: the biggest, most varied backyards of the three Duval beach cities — real square footage, and real putting-green room in Selva Marina.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $118,935 (recent estimate; $92,056 at the 2020 census — use the range). Per capita income $75,977, poverty 7.75%. Median age 48.9 (2026 estimate) / 47.9 (2020 census) — older and more established than Jacksonville Beach. 73.4–79.5% White, ~9.1% Black, ~8.8% Hispanic. 2026 population estimate around 13,190. Second largest of the Jacksonville Beaches communities. Profile: settled, high-income, older owners with the largest yards on the Duval coast — plus a country-club membership that maps almost exactly onto the premium buyer.
facts.golf: Atlantic Beach Country Club, 1600 Selva Marina Drive — PRIVATE, 18 holes, 6,815 yards, par 71. Originally Selva Marina Country Club, designed by Ed Seay and opened in 1958; new owners bought it in January 2014, renamed it, and Erik Larsen (formerly of Arnold Palmer's design company) led a complete redevelopment rebuilding bunkers and runoff areas for a more natural, dunes-like feel. The club hosted the Greater Jacksonville Open, and Jack Nicklaus recorded his first double eagle in tournament competition on the 18th hole there in 1966 — a specific, checkable, locally-loved fact worth putting on the page. The Selva Marina residential community wraps the course with clay tennis courts and a pool. This is the ONLY genuine on-course golf neighborhood among the five towns in this batch.
facts.commercial_targets: Atlantic Beach Country Club (1600 Selva Marina Dr) — practice facility, short-game and chipping areas, clubhouse surrounds; and its membership is the precise residential buyer for a $10–12/sq ft backyard green. Jack Russell Park, 850 Seminole Road — 12 acres of city-owned athletic fields, tennis and racquetball courts, a direct municipal procurement path. Kathryn Abbey Hanna Park — 447 acres, city-owned. Beaches Town Center courtyards, restaurant patios and hotel outdoor space. Atlantic Beach Elementary. Donner Park and community center. Pet businesses and groomers along Atlantic Boulevard and Mayport Road. (Dutton Island and Tideviews preserves are commonly cited as Atlantic Beach city parks but I did not confirm them in these sources — verify before naming.)
facts.landmarks: Beaches Town Center, where Atlantic Boulevard meets the ocean (shared with Neptune Beach) — Ragtime Tavern, Coop 303, Poe's Tavern, two oceanfront hotels, brick courtyards. Kathryn Abbey Hanna Park at the city's northern tip — 447 acres with 1.5 miles of beach, a lagoon, hiking and biking trails, camping, surfing and fishing. Jack Russell Park, 850 Seminole Road — 12 acres with tennis courts, racquetball courts and athletic fields (note: this is in ATLANTIC Beach, not Jacksonville Beach — locals will catch the error). Atlantic Beach City Hall, 800 Seminole Road. Selva Marina Drive and the Atlantic Beach Country Club clubhouse at 1600. The historic Continental Hotel site. The Donner neighborhood.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH ACREAGE AND ISOLATION, NOT LUXURY. Hilliard's page must not read like the beach pages — the median home is $239,500 and one in four residents is below the poverty line. The genuinely different lead is: 'You own an acre. There is no golf course within half an hour, no HOA telling you what you can build, and under the current Phase III order you are not allowed to lay new sod anyway.' That combination exists nowhere else in the service area. The three offers that fit: (1) a real short-game complex — green, fringe, chipping pad, practice bunker — built on ground you already have, because the nearest course is a 30-mile drive; (2) heavy-duty pet and kennel turf for dog people, hunting dogs and rural vet/boarding businesses, where mud and worn-out patches under a pole barn are the actual problem; (3) small, defined turf zones — the area right around the pool, the play zone, the shop apron — rather than whole-yard replacement nobody here will fund. Also lead with the WELL: most of these properties irrigate from a private well, and the SJRWMD shortage order applies to private wells too, so 'I have my own water' is not the exemption people assume. STRATEGIC HONESTY FOR THE CLIENT: Hilliard sits roughly 10.3 miles north of Callahan and 27 miles west-northwest of Fernandina Beach. The yellow boundary as described runs north of Callahan and meets the Atlantic above Fernandina Beach — which puts Hilliard ON or JUST OUTSIDE that arc, most likely just outside. Build the page, but rank it low-priority: treat it as a US 1 extension page that captures northern Nassau searches, not a core money town. Confirm the boundary call with the client before spending on it.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Hilliard's ordinances are published at townofhilliard.com/ordinances. I found NO artificial turf ordinance, no landscape code and no design standards touching synthetic grass — genuinely thin, and I am saying so rather than inventing one. HOA coverage is minimal to nonexistent across most of 32046. The rule that actually matters is state law: Florida HB 683 (2025), ch. 2025-140, effective 1 July 2025, created Fla. Stat. § 125.572, which requires the Florida DEP to adopt minimum standards for synthetic turf installation on single-family residential properties one acre or less (material type, colour, permeability, stormwater management, potable water conservation, water quality and proximity to trees) and bars local governments from prohibiting compliant installations or enforcing inconsistent regulations. Caveat worth stating plainly on the page: many Hilliard parcels are LARGER than one acre, so the statutory protection does not automatically cover the whole property — and the statute does not override private covenants where they exist.
facts.water_and_rules: Water provider inside the town limits is the Town of Hilliard Public Works water & sewer utility; account setup and questions go through Town Hall at (904) 845-3555. Outside the incorporated limits, which is most of the addresses in the 32046 ZIP, properties are on PRIVATE WELLS AND SEPTIC. This matters more than people assume: SJRWMD's water shortage orders explicitly apply to private wells and pumps, not just utility customers. Nassau County is inside the SJRWMD district and is covered by the Phase III Extreme Water Shortage Declaration issued 11 May 2026 — irrigation limited to ONE DAY PER WEEK, nothing between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., odd addresses Saturday, even addresses Sunday, non-residential Tuesday, no more than 3/4 inch per zone and one hour per zone. The declaration also bans NEW SOD INSTALLATION AND NEW PLANTINGS outright. Micro-spray, micro-jet, drip and bubbler are exempt. Normal (non-drought) schedule is Wed/Sat odd, Thu/Sun even during daylight saving, one day in EST. NO REBATE: I found no Florida utility or SJRWMD rebate that pays for artificial turf. Do not put a rebate claim on this page. The savings story is the well pump running less, the sod bill you never pay again, and the fact that under Phase III you legally cannot re-sod a dead yard.
facts.soil_and_yard: At 66 ft elevation Hilliard is far higher and better drained than anywhere else in this batch — this is Nassau County upland, sandy loam over the inland ridge rather than the coastal quartz sand and hardpan you fight at the beaches. (Elevation is sourced; soil series characterisation is installer field knowledge and should be confirmed against USDA Web Soil Survey for a specific parcel.) Practical consequences: less standing water and less muck than Palm Valley or Nocatee, but more organic matter, more root competition from pines and hardwoods, and more weed pressure from adjoining woods and pasture. Large lots mean long runs of base material and real haul costs — price mobilisation separately, Hilliard is 35+ miles from Jacksonville and 27+ miles from Fernandina. Shade comes from planted pines and mixed hardwood rather than the sprawling coastal live oaks. Dogs, livestock and farm traffic mean the edges and seams take abuse; spec heavier face weight and more nails than a beach install.
facts.housing_stock: Small rural town, 5.51 sq mi, elevation 66 ft — the highest, driest ground in this batch. 2,967 residents at the 2020 census (3,034 in the 2024 ACS-based estimate), and it SHRANK from 3,086 in 2010. Median property value $239,500 (2024) — roughly one-third of Ponte Vedra Beach. Homeownership only 58.5%, and 63.8% of owners carry a mortgage. Dominant stock is 1970s–2000s frame ranch and modest single-story homes on large, deep, unlandscaped lots along US 1 and CR 108, plus a very heavy share of manufactured/mobile homes on 1–5 acre parcels once you leave the incorporated grid. Almost no HOA — this is the least-covenanted place in the whole service area. New-build is scattered infill and owner-built, not subdivision production. Backyards are enormous (often measured in acres, not feet) and typically contain a pole barn, a shop, a boat, dogs and sometimes chickens or horses. Nothing here resembles the 25-ft builder backyard in Nocatee. HONEST NOTE: this is a genuinely thin market. Population ~3,000, poverty rate 25.2%, median household income $65,096. Full-yard turf at $10–12/sq ft is not the product here.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $65,096 (2024, up 8.6% y/y), average household income $69,338, median age 34.6 — young families, not retirees. Poverty rate 25.2%, which is high and should temper any premium positioning. Top employment sectors are Other Services (238), Construction (202) and Health Care (141) — tradespeople who will price-check you and may DIY. Average commute 32.6 minutes with 80.6% driving alone: most working residents commute to Yulee, Callahan, west Jacksonville or the port. THE IMPORTANT NUANCE: the FAA's Jacksonville Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZJX) is in Hilliard and is a major employer. Air traffic controllers are federal GS/ATC-scale earners well into six figures with stable, recession-proof income and long shifts. That is a small, identifiable, high-income pocket sitting inside an otherwise low-income rural town — a controller on 2 acres who wants a putting green and a dog run is the realistic premium customer here, not the town at large. Rayonier timberland/logging and tree farming remain significant local industries.
facts.golf: There is effectively no golf in Hilliard, and that is the whole point. No course in town, none in Callahan 10 miles south. The nearest real golf is on Amelia Island (Amelia River Golf Club, the Omni Amelia Island courses, Fernandina Beach Municipal) at 27 miles / roughly 33 miles by road, or the Jacksonville Northside courses. That drive is the pitch: a Hilliard golfer spends 45–60 minutes round-trip before he hits a ball. The backyard practice green is not a luxury upgrade here, it is a substitute for a course that does not exist within half an hour. Sell short-game complexes — green plus chipping pad plus a bunker — on the acre they already own.
facts.commercial_targets: Realistically short, and worth saying so. Hilliard Middle-Senior High (the Flashes' athletic fields, batting cages, bullpens, weight-room flooring), Hilliard Elementary playground surfacing, the Hilliard YMCA, town ball fields and the Town of Hilliard parks, Hilliard Airpark landside areas, and the small daycares and churches along US 1. Veterinary and boarding/kennel businesses on the US 1 corridor are the best pet-turf commercial lead. Do not promise a deep commercial pipeline in a town of 3,000 — the honest commercial play from Hilliard is northern Nassau County generally (Callahan, Bryceville, Yulee) rather than Hilliard alone.
facts.landmarks: Hilliard Middle-Senior High School, 1 Flashes Avenue — the mascot is the 'Flashes', named for Hilliard's former standing as the statistical lightning capital of Florida. Hilliard Elementary School, 27568 Ohio Street. The US 1 / CR 108 intersection, the town water tower and the CSX Nahunta Subdivision tracks running through the middle of town. Hilliard Airpark (01J) for small aircraft. Hilliard Town Hall. The Hilliard Mansion. The FAA Jacksonville Air Route Traffic Control Center. Ralph E. Simmons Memorial State Forest on the St. Marys River just north/east of town. Jeb Bush named Hilliard '2003 Rural Community of the Year' for standing up a YMCA chapter. MLB's Howie Kendrick and NFL running back Daniel Thomas are from here — a local-recognition detail worth one line.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE MARSH-AND-SHADE PROBLEM, NOT WITH LUXURY. This is the only page in this batch that is a market area rather than an address — it is the volume page. Every gated community below it gets a page that leads with money; Intracoastal West should lead with a defect the reader is looking at right now: the mainland side of the Intracoastal is flat Pomona sand with a high water table, backed by tidal marsh, retention ponds and oak canopy, on 25–40ft-deep production-builder backyards where St. Augustine has failed in the same three spots for a decade. That is the hook, and it is true in Windsor Parke, Pablo Bay, Hunters Ridge and Isle of Palms alike. Layer the Phase III one-day-a-week reality on top and the page converts on frustration, not aspiration. Structurally this page should be the HUB: name the 50+ subdivisions for long-tail search, then link out to Queen's Harbour, Glen Kernan, Pablo Creek Reserve and Deerwood as the high-ticket children. The difference from every neighbour: Ponte Vedra sells prestige, Nocatee sells new-build tidiness, Atlantic Beach sells walkable surf-town character — Intracoastal West sells the fix for a specific, visible, recurring failure in a yard the owner already dislikes.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Duval is a CONSOLIDATED city-county — there is no separate town hall for any of these places; the City of Jacksonville Municipal Code governs all of them, so one permitting relationship covers the whole batch. State law changed the landscape on 2025-07-01: CS/CS/CS/HB 683 (Ch. 2025-140) created § 125.572, Fla. Stat., directing the Florida DEP to adopt minimum statewide standards for synthetic turf on single-family residential lots of one acre or less and PROHIBITING local governments from banning compliant turf on those lots. Separately, § 720.3045, Fla. Stat., bars an HOA from restricting artificial turf that is not visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel, an adjacent common area, or a community golf course. HONEST GAPS: (1) the DEP implementing rule (reported as F.A.C. 62-308.100) was still in development at the check date, so the preemption is not yet fully operative — do not tell a customer local rules are dead; (2) the Jacksonville Municode zoning-definitions page returned HTTP 403 and I could not confirm whether Jacksonville has a turf-specific ordinance or an impervious-surface-ratio trigger. Verify impervious surface / stormwater treatment thresholds with the City of Jacksonville Planning and Development Department before publishing any permitting claim.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: JEA (potable, reuse and reclaimed) for essentially all of it. As of the 2026-09-07 check, the St. Johns River Water Management District has Duval County under a Phase III Extreme Water Shortage: landscape irrigation limited to ONE day per week, prohibited entirely between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., maximum ¾ inch per zone and maximum one hour per zone. Odd-numbered / no-number addresses water Saturday; even-numbered addresses water Sunday; non-residential water Tuesday. Duval escalated fast in 2026 — Phase I was declared in February 2026 (Duval plus parts of Alachua, Baker, Bradford, Marion), Phase II by late April 2026 covering all JEA customers including reuse and reclaimed, and Phase III by the time of the SJRWMD page check. Exemptions that matter: drip and micro-irrigation, hand watering with an adjustable shut-off nozzle, and new plantings during their establishment period. JEA reclaimed-water customers normally run an odd Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun schedule, but Phase II/III collapses that to one day. SJRWMD irrigation hotline: 386-329-4545. HONEST GAP: I found NO artificial-turf rebate from JEA or SJRWMD. Do not put a rebate claim on this page. The sellable fact is the restriction itself, not a cheque.
facts.soil_and_yard: USDA zone 9a/9b. Over 80% of Duval County is poorly drained, acidic sandy soil of the Pomona series with organic matter under 1.2%, and a seasonally high water table is common across Jacksonville — the exact combination that makes St. Augustine sod either drown or starve depending on the month. Add the Intracoastal-specific problems: tidal marsh margins with brackish influence and salt spray on the eastern streets, retention-pond backyards that pond after summer thunderstorms, and dense live oak / laurel oak / slash pine canopy on the older preserve-backed lots where turfgrass never fills in. Slope is essentially nil — this is flat coastal terrace, so drainage has to be engineered into the base, not relied on from grade. Base build and a drainage plan are the whole job here; a turf installer who leads with 'we solve the soggy shady patch behind your lanai' is describing something every homeowner in these subdivisions has stared at.
facts.housing_stock: Not a subdivision — a 50+ neighborhood market area on the MAINLAND side of the Intracoastal Waterway, bounded roughly by Atlantic Blvd north, JTB (SR 202) south, and running along the Kernan / Hodges / San Pablo Blvd spine. Frankel Realty's own index for the area lists 50+ named subdivisions including Ashton Hills, Bay Pointe, Beach Haven, Bentwater Place, Brighton Bay, Broadwater, Covenant Cove, Covington Creek, Crosswater at Pablo Bay, Cypress Village, Danforth, Egret's Glade, Glen Kernan, Golden Glades, Grand Reserve, Harbor Lights, Heather Glen, Highland Glen, Holiday Harbor, Hunters Green, Hunters Ridge, Ibis Point, Indian Springs, Isle of Palms, Jacksonville Golf & CC, Johns Creek, Kensington, Kensington Gardens, Marina San Pablo, Mira Vista at Harbortown, Marsh Sound, Osprey Point, Pablo Bay, Pablo Creek Reserve, Palermo, Riverbrook, San Pablo Creek, Seabreeze, Seven Pines / Seven Pines Island, Somerset, St Andrews Place, Tamaya, Terra Costa, The Woods, Villages of Pablo, Villini at Glen Kernan, Vista Pointe, Vizcaya, Waterside, Waverly Place, Windsor Parke, Windsor Pointe, and Wolf Creek. Era and type therefore run the full spread: 1970s–80s waterfront ranches on the older Intracoastal-front streets (Isle of Palms, Holiday Harbor, Beacon Hills Harbor), heavy 1990s–2000s production-builder single-family on 55–75ft lots (Windsor Parke, Pablo Bay, Hunters Ridge, Kensington), 2000s–2020s gated master-plans (Tamaya, Seven Pines), plus townhomes and condos. Listings in the area span under $100,000 to over $4,600,000 — the widest price band of any single page in this batch. Backyards are the story: the bulk of the mid-market 1990s–2000s product sits on ~0.15–0.25 acre with a rear yard roughly 25–40ft deep, often backing to preserve, retention pond or tidal marsh. HOA prevalence is high in anything built after ~1990; the older waterfront streets are frequently HOA-free. Almost none of it is historic — Riverside-style pre-war stock does not exist here.
facts.who_lives_there: ZIP 32224: 42,252 people, median household income $88,259 (2024), median home value $458,100, 52% bachelor's degree or higher, median age 32.1 — that age is depressed by the University of North Florida student body on Kernan Blvd, so read it as 'college town grafted onto an affluent suburb', not as a young market. ZIP 32225: 57,441 people, 22,906 households, median household income $90,559 (2024), median age 38.8, 44.5% bachelor's or higher (about 25% above the Jacksonville metro's 36.5%). Momentum Realty's resident guide describes the mix as professionals, growing families, retirees, healthcare workers, military families, boaters and multi-decade locals. Practically: Mayo Clinic Florida staff, Naval Station Mayport families, UNF faculty, and beach-adjacent professionals who wanted 5 minutes to the ocean without oceanfront pricing. This is the $7–8/sq ft volume page, and the funnel that feeds the four gated pages below it.
facts.golf: Inside or immediately adjacent: Queen's Harbour Yacht & Country Club (Mark McCumber, 18 holes, private), Glen Kernan Club (Robert C. Walker 1999, reimagined 2024 by Jim Furyk, private), Jacksonville Golf & Country Club (private, off Baymeadows/Hodges), Windsor Parke Golf Club (semi-private, inside the Windsor Parke subdivision on Hodges Blvd), and the Hayt Golf Learning Center on the UNF campus. Deerwood Country Club and the Ponte Vedra Beach clubs sit just outside the area's southern and eastern edges. Golf density here is the reason a putting-green-led offer works even in mid-market subdivisions.
facts.commercial_targets: Duval County Public Schools serving the area: Chets Creek Elementary, Alimacani Elementary, Abess Park Elementary, San Pablo Elementary, Kernan Trail Elementary, Neptune Beach Elementary, Kernan Middle, Landmark Middle, Duncan U. Fletcher Middle and Fletcher High, Sandalwood High. UNF Athletics facilities (Hodges Stadium, Harmon Stadium, UNF Arena, Hayt Golf Learning Center) — the Hayt in particular is a putting-surface prospect. Mayo Clinic Florida campus courtyards and healing gardens. Windsor Parke Golf Club and Jacksonville Golf & Country Club practice areas and tee surrounds. Tamaya and Seven Pines amenity centers (new-build master-plans still adding common-area features). St. Johns Town Center retail courtyards and the pet-friendly patios along Town Center Pkwy. HOA common areas across 50+ subdivisions is the single largest repeatable commercial pool in this batch.
facts.landmarks: Mayo Clinic Florida, 4500 San Pablo Rd. University of North Florida, 1 UNF Drive on Kernan Blvd — with Hodges Stadium (12,000 capacity; soccer, track and field, cross country, rugby league), UNF Arena, Harmon Stadium and the Hayt Golf Learning Center. Castaway Island Preserve on San Pablo Rd (boardwalks and marsh water access). The Brumos Collection automobile museum just off San Pablo Rd. St. Johns Town Center. Atlantic Beach Town Center, roughly 7 minutes from the Queen's Harbour gate. The three named boulevards — Kernan, Hodges, San Pablo — are how locals actually give directions here.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE BACKYARD PUTTING GREEN AT TOUR-QUALITY SPEED, SOLD TO PEOPLE WHO PLAY FAZIO AND DYE COURSES EVERY WEEK. This is the $10–12/sq ft page — the one place in the batch where the customer's baseline for a green is set by Long Point (Fazio, 1987, member-owned), Oak Marsh (Pete Dye, Beau Welling renovation completed 2025, Golf Digest Top 75 Resort Course) and the brand-new Little Sandy short course and 18-hole putting course. A homeowner who just played the renovated Oak Marsh does not want 'a green'; they want stimp, contour, a fringe collar and a chipping approach. Say so in that language, name those courses, and price accordingly. The second half of the lead is the constraint that keeps competitors out: virtually every address is behind a gate with an architectural review board and a $1,550–$1,910 annual HOA, so the page promises ARB-ready drawings, color/pile/infill specs to community standard, and a crew that can work inside a gated resort community's contractor rules. Third: salt spray, marsh edge and permanent maritime-forest shade — conditions where turfgrass has never worked and irrigation now gets one day a week under SJRWMD Phase III (non-residential common areas: Tuesday only). This page is club money, championship golf and gate access. Fernandina Beach is permits and Victorian shade. Yulee is 50-foot builder lots. Never share a template.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Jurisdiction splits and the page must say so: inside Fernandina Beach city limits the city's Land Development Code and, in the historic districts, the Historic District Council govern. South of the city line the island is UNINCORPORATED NASSAU COUNTY — county land development code, no city Certificate of Appropriateness. On top of that, virtually every south-island address sits inside a gated community with an architectural review board: the Amelia Island Plantation Community Association and the individual villa/neighborhood associations, Amelia Surf & Racquet Club, Summer Beach, The Amelia Island Club. Practically, an ARB submittal is mandatory and the reviewable variables are turf color, pile height, blade shape, infill, edging/border treatment and how the install meets existing landscape beds. Florida law (§373.185, Ch. 720) bars HOAs from unreasonable prohibitions on water-conserving landscaping but does NOT clearly name synthetic turf as protected and does not override local zoning — so the honest position is 'we prepare the ARB package,' not 'your HOA can't stop you.' Nassau County also maintains an Amelia Island Tree Commission dealing with tree protection on unincorporated Amelia Island; SCOPE UNVERIFIED (the county's PDF would not parse on the check date) — confirm before making claims about tree or root-zone permitting. Coastal construction control line and dune-protection rules apply oceanfront.
facts.water_and_rules: Same SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage as the rest of Nassau County, effective 11 May 2026: one irrigation day per week, none between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone. Residential odd/no address = Saturday, even = Sunday, NON-RESIDENTIAL = TUESDAY — and that non-residential Tuesday is the line that matters here, because resort, club and HOA common-area irrigation falls under it. Phase III also prohibits aesthetic water use and requires commercial, industrial and institutional users to suspend certain non-essential uses. Baseline in a normal year is still only two days a week in summer, one in winter, no irrigation 10 a.m.–4 p.m. Providers are the City of Fernandina Beach utility inside city limits and JEA/private systems elsewhere on the island — verify per address. No artificial-turf rebate exists in this district; do not imply one.
facts.soil_and_yard: Barrier-island sand throughout, but the island is not uniform: the Nassau County comprehensive plan describes Amelia Island as poorly drained on the west (Amelia River / marsh) side and better-drained, higher sand elsewhere. Conditions that drive spec here: salt spray and onshore wind on dune-side lots, where turfgrass burns and irrigation runs constantly; deep maritime-forest shade under live oak and pine on interior Plantation lots (Oak Marsh's own signature is 'century-old moss-draped oaks'); tidal marsh edges with high water tables and salt intrusion on west-facing lots; and sugar-sand base that drains fast but holds no nutrient. Where the water table is high near the marsh, base depth and drainage design — not the turf product — is what separates a good install from a failure in year three. Shell and root plates limit trenching.
facts.housing_stock: Not a census place — a 13-mile-long, ~4-mile-wide barrier island (the southernmost Sea Island) containing Fernandina Beach (the only incorporated city) plus the unincorporated communities of Amelia City, American Beach and Franklintown. As a MARKET, 'Amelia Island' means the resort and club product on the island's southern two-thirds. The anchor is Amelia Island Plantation: 1,350+ acres behind 24-hour gates, 3.5 miles of beachfront, 900+ single-family homes and 1,200+ condos/villas, priced $615,000 to $15,000,000. Named single-family neighborhoods: Dunes Row, Dunes Court, Heron Oaks, Little Dunes, Long Point (Oak Point, Sound Point, The Pointe, Marsh Point Road), Marsh Creek Village, Ocean Club Drive, Sea Marsh Village. Named villa/condo communities include Beachside Villas, Beach Walker Villas, Piper Dunes, Sea Dunes, Spyglass Villas and Windsong. Also gated: Amelia Surf & Racquet Club (oceanfront condos, two oceanfront pools, clay tennis, private dune walkover) between the Ritz-Carlton and the Omni; Summer Beach. Product is largely 1970s–2000s resort-era custom homes and villas on wooded, irregular maritime-forest lots — courtyard back yards, small pool decks, dune-side terraces and marsh-front lots, NOT rectangular suburban rear yards. HOA prevalence is effectively total and fees are heavy: Plantation HOA dues roughly $1,550–$1,910 a year, condo fees roughly $623–$2,076 a month.
facts.who_lives_there: Second-home owners, retirees, club members and short-term-rental investors, layered over the year-round Fernandina Beach population (city-wide median age 58.6, median household income $97,903, median home value $555,400 — the south-end resort addresses run far above that, into eight figures at the top). A meaningful share of the housing is rented nightly or weekly, which changes the pitch: an absentee owner buys turf as an operating-cost and turnover-risk decision, not a lifestyle one. The island also carries very large visitor volume — the Shrimp Festival alone draws 150,000+.
facts.golf: The densest golf concentration in the batch and the reason this page exists. At the Omni Amelia Island Resort & Spa: OAK MARSH — Pete Dye, 6,471 yards, par 72, tidal marshes, century-old moss-draped oaks, small greens, 14 holes with water; renovation by Beau Welling completed 2025; on Golf Digest's Top 75 Resort Courses in the US and named by Travel & Leisure Golf among Florida's 50 Finest. LONG POINT — Tom Fazio, 1987, PRIVATE and member-owned for The Amelia Island Club, 12 Long Point Drive; tight rolling fairways through marsh, oak-and-pine forest and oceanfront dunes. LITTLE SANDY — new Beau Welling 10-hole short course plus an 18-hole putting course, walk-ins, family-oriented. Off-resort: THE GOLF CLUB OF AMELIA ISLAND — Mark McCumber and Gene Littler, 18 holes, 4700 Amelia Island Parkway, adjacent to the Ritz-Carlton. AMELIA RIVER CLUB — private, 18 holes, TifEagle greens. Plus Amelia River Golf Club (public, Tom Jackson, 4477 Buccaneer Trail) and the municipal 27-hole Fernandina Beach Golf Club at the north end, and Amelia National (Fazio, gated) and The Golf Club at North Hampton (Arnold Palmer Signature) just off-island. Racquet Park at the Plantation carries 23+ tennis courts.
facts.commercial_targets: The highest-value commercial list in the batch. Omni Amelia Island Resort & Spa — 404-room hotel plus Oak Marsh, Long Point and the new Little Sandy short course and 18-hole putting course; resort practice areas, event lawns, pool decks, and non-residential Tuesday-only irrigation make this the flagship prospect. The Ritz-Carlton, Amelia Island — event lawns, terraces, pet-relief areas. The Amelia Island Club and The Golf Club of Amelia Island (4700 Amelia Island Parkway). Amelia River Club. Amelia Island Plantation Community Association common areas, entry features, villa courtyards and the Racquet Park surrounds. Amelia Surf & Racquet Club. Vacation-rental and villa management companies handling the 1,200+ condo/villa units. Wedding and event venues on resort property. Dog-friendly resort properties and boarding/grooming businesses serving island visitors.
facts.landmarks: The Ritz-Carlton, Amelia Island (4750 Amelia Island Parkway); the Omni Amelia Island Resort & Spa (404-room hotel); Amelia Island Plantation's gates and 9 miles of trails and boardwalks; Racquet Park; Amelia Island State Park at the southern tip (horseback riding on the beach); Nassau Sound and the south-end bridge; American Beach and the NaNa dune; Fort Clinch State Park and the Amelia Island Lighthouse at the north end; the Amelia Island Museum of History; Fernandina Beach Municipal Airport. Events a local names instantly: the Amelia Island Concours d'Elegance and the Isle of Eight Flags Shrimp Festival (first weekend of May, 150,000+ visitors).

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH DRAINAGE AND DOGS, NOT LUXURY. Oceanway is Jacksonville's growth frontier built on the worst soil in the batch: Leon-type fine sand over a spodic hardpan within 30 inches, water table 6–18 inches down for months, four rivers and creeks, and 'unprecedented' Irma flooding in living memory. These are $250k–$400k production homes on 40–60 ft lots with a fenced back yard, a dog, and a lawn that turns to mud from June to October and dust in April. The page should sell the engineering — excavation depth, permeable base spec, positive drainage away from the house, no runoff onto the neighbour, and a stated 10-ft standoff from ponds and swales because the DEP rule requires it — and should sell pet turf hard to a demographic that is 13–19% veterans with dogs. The aspirational upsell is a compact 2–3 hole backyard putting green precisely BECAUSE there is no golf here to live on; the nearest real course is 20 minutes away in Yulee. This is the technical-proof page. It is deliberately not Fleming Island's HOA-approval page, not Orange Park's shade page, and not Baldwin's acreage page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Since 19 May 2026, Florida DEP Rule 62-308.100 (adopted under s. 125.572, F.S., created by Ch. 2025-140, Laws of Florida) means Jacksonville cannot prohibit compliant synthetic turf on a single-family residential lot of 1 acre or less, or regulate it inconsistently with the state standard. Jacksonville has no artificial-turf-specific ordinance of its own. The binding constraints here are (a) the rule itself and (b) private CDD/HOA architectural review at Villages of Westport, Bainebridge Estates, Alta Lakes etc. — the rule expressly does NOT address HOA requirements or deed restrictions. Rule provisions that bite hardest in this area: turf may not be installed in a swale, ditch, stormwater pond or a pond's littoral zone (exactly where CDD lots drain); it must not increase runoff volume, direction or rate to adjacent properties; in-ground irrigation may not be used over turf and a local government may require heads removed and pipe capped; 10 ft setback from any natural or man-made waterbody without a seawall/bulkhead; and — critical for the septic-served rural parcels — the installation "must provide for access to the septic tank for routine pumpout." Note the preemption covers single-family only: it does not cover condos, duplexes, parks, athletic fields or commercial property.
facts.water_and_rules: JEA is the water/sewer utility (with reclaimed water in some newer subdivisions); a substantial number of older rural parcels in 32219/32226 are on private wells and septic. Rules come from the St. Johns River Water Management District. As of the 2026 checks, SJRWMD has a Phase III Extreme Water Shortage declaration in force covering Duval: landscape irrigation limited to ONE day per week, prohibited 8 a.m.–6 p.m., odd/no address Saturday, even address Sunday, nonresidential Tuesday, max ¾ inch and one hour per zone. JEA has applied the schedule to all its water customers including reclaimed (SJRWMD's own order language does not restrict reclaimed, so there is a real inconsistency worth checking before quoting it as fact on the page). Normal (non-drought) rule: 2 days/week in Daylight Saving Time (odd Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, nonresidential Tue/Fri), 1 day/week in Eastern Standard Time, no watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m. Jacksonville's own FAQ adds a local wrinkle — addresses ending in letters N–Z count as odd, A–M as even. No rebate: neither JEA nor the City offers any incentive for artificial turf, and UF/IFAS does not classify synthetic turf as Florida-Friendly Landscaping.
facts.soil_and_yard: Coastal flatwoods — the hardest drainage picture in this batch. Dominant soils are Leon-series-type fine sands: USDA describes Leon as "poorly drained and very poorly drained," with a spodic (Bh) hardpan within 30 inches of the surface that restricts downward movement, and a water table at 6–18 inches for 1–4 months a year (longer in depressions). The region is defined by four waterways — the St. Johns, Broward River, Trout River and Dunn Creek — and Oceanway took what Wikipedia records as "unprecedented" flooding in Hurricane Irma in September 2017. New CDD subdivisions sit on engineered fill above that natural grade with retention ponds; older rural lots are flat, wet and sit directly on the hardpan. Sun exposure is generally good (new subdivisions are cleared), so the shade problem is smaller here than in Orange Park — the problem is water. Base depth, permeable subgrade and positive drainage are the entire technical sale.
facts.housing_stock: Three distinct stocks in one service area, which is the whole point. (1) Pre-1980 rural remnant: Wikipedia describes Oceanway as "once dotted with small farms and isolated houses" until growth took off in the early 1980s — frame houses, block ranches and manufactured homes on half-acre-to-multi-acre lots along Pecan Park Rd, Braddock Rd, Starratt Rd, Cisco Dr, and out toward New Berlin and Cedar Bay. Many are on private well and septic. (2) 1990s–2000s subdivisions that filled in behind First Coast High School (opened 1990, expanded 2006 "to accommodate the explosive growth in North Jacksonville"). (3) 2015–present production-builder CDD communities: Villages of Westport (~2,000 acres between Lem Turner Rd and Dunn Ave, Lennar and others, its own CDD), Bainebridge Estates (CDD fees vary by section), Alta Lakes. New-build lots are standard NE Florida production widths — roughly 40/50/60 ft fronts — giving compact rectangular back yards; the typical turf job is 800–2,000 sq ft of usable back yard, frequently backing onto a CDD stormwater pond or preserve. HOA/CDD prevalence is high in the new sections, near zero on the older rural parcels. ZIP-level ACS (Census Reporter): 32218 pop 72,905, median home value $288,100; 32219 pop 14,302, $229,000; 32226 pop 21,256, $362,100 — 32226 (New Berlin / Yellow Bluff / Cedar Bay, toward the Nassau line) is the money end of the Northside.
facts.who_lives_there: Young-to-middle families and logistics/port/airport workers. ACS medians: 32218 household income $69,638, median age 36.4; 32219 $72,184, median age 39.8; 32226 $110,179, median age 40.7 with a 6.4% poverty rate (about half the metro rate). Bachelor's attainment is low-to-middling (32219 21.5%, 32218 area similar; 32226 35.1%). Standout demographic: veterans. 32219 is 18.6% veteran, 32226 13.6% — both more than double the US rate of 6.2% (Census Reporter). Employment leans JAXPORT, Jacksonville International Airport, Amazon/Wayfair-scale distribution, Anheuser-Busch, and trades. High homeownership in the new subdivisions; dog ownership is very high.
facts.golf: Honestly thin, and that is a genuine differentiator — do NOT build a golf-community page here. There is no championship course inside Oceanway or the Northside proper. Nearest: Blue Cypress Golf Course (9 holes, Arlington, opened 1960s, renovated 2003, reopened 2020 under Indigo Golf) and Blue Sky Golf Club in Arlington; then roughly 20–25 minutes north on I-95 to Golf Club at North Hampton and Amelia National Golf & Country Club in Yulee, and the Amelia Island resort courses. Practical consequence: the golf pitch on this page is the backyard putting green for someone who drives to play, not "you live on the 14th fairway."
facts.commercial_targets: Pet Paradise Resort and Day Spa, Pecan Park Road, 32218 — the flagship pet-turf target in the area. Duval County Public Schools: Oceanway Elementary and Oceanway Middle, Louis S. Sheffield Elementary, Highlands Elementary and Highlands Middle, New Berlin Elementary (New Berlin Rd, 32226), San Mateo Elementary, First Coast High School. Charters: Biscayne Elementary Leadership Academy, Biscayne High School, Somerset Academy Eagle Campus. Daycare/preschool: Victory Christian Day Care Center, Dunns Creek Baptist Church Day Care Center, Little Temples Child Care Center, Saint Martins Early Learning Center, The Little Country School. Municipal: Oceanway Community Center athletic fields. CDD common areas and amenity centers at Villages of Westport and Bainebridge Estates. Distribution-centre and airport-hotel landscaping along Airport Center Dr / Pecan Park Rd.
facts.landmarks: Jacksonville International Airport. River City Marketplace, 725 Skymarks Dr (opened 17 Nov 2006, 80+ retailers, anchored by BJ's/Walmart/Lowe's — the first real shopping north of the river, and locals still date the area's arrival to it). Jacksonville Zoo and Gardens, 370 Zoo Parkway, 32218 — 122 acres at the confluence of the Trout River and St. Johns, 1M+ visitors a year. Catty Shack Ranch Wildlife Sanctuary. The Anheuser-Busch brewery. Oceanway Community Center, Park and Pool, 12215 Sago Ave W (dog park, tennis, soccer, softball, stock pond). First Coast High School, 590 Duval Station Rd (Buccaneers, ~2,137 students). Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve and Kingsley Plantation. Dames Point Bridge.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH: "Your oaks were here first. That is why the grass is gone." Miramar is a 1926–1947 brick-bungalow tract whose canopy is now a century old, and the yards are SMALL — 30x40 to 45x55 backyards where the homeowner has already lost the grass war to permanent oak shade, surface roots and constant leaf litter. This is the shade-failure page: build the whole thing around a 400–900 sq ft full-backyard replacement at a $6k–$12k ticket, done in a day, with before-and-after photographs taken under a live oak. Different from San Marco one mile north because Miramar has no historic-district designation, no preservation society reviewing your work and no riverfront flood exposure — you sell the homeowner directly with nobody in the way. Different from San Jose two miles south because there is no Donald Ross course in the neighborhood and no estate lots — do not lead with putting greens or with luxury; lead with "nothing will grow there and it never will." Job density is the business case: tight platted streets, short drives, and one happy bungalow owner is visible to twenty neighbours with the identical dead-shade backyard.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Duval is a CONSOLIDATED city-county — no separate municipal layer the way there is in Green Cove Springs, Fernandina Beach or St. Augustine Beach. One code, Jacksonville's, applies. I could NOT reach Municode (library.municode.com returns 403) to verify any specific artificial-turf provision in Chapter 656 Part 12 landscape regulations — do NOT assert on the page that turf is expressly permitted or expressly regulated; verify first. What IS safely stateable: Miramar Terrace is not a designated historic district and has no preservation-society review (unlike San Marco a mile north), and these 1920s–40s plats carry essentially no active HOA. Statewide backstop worth knowing: Florida Statute 373.185 bars local governments and deed restrictions from prohibiting "Florida-friendly landscaping," but the statutory definition is built around plant selection, efficient watering, mulching and stormwater reduction and does NOT name synthetic turf — so it gives no protection against a covenant. Irrelevant in Miramar (no HOA), critical in Mandarin and Beauclerc. Jacksonville tree-protection rules do apply and matter here given the canopy.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: JEA (the consolidated city-county utility — one provider for the whole page, unlike Clay or St. Johns where you must name several). Regulator: St. Johns River Water Management District. STANDARD RULE: two irrigation days/week during Daylight Saving Time, ONE day/week during Eastern Standard Time; odd-numbered or no address = Wednesday and Saturday, even = Thursday and Sunday, non-residential = Tuesday and Friday; never between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. AS OF CHECK DATE 2026-09-07 A PHASE III EXTREME WATER SHORTAGE ORDER IS IN FORCE covering parts of Duval (and Baker, Bradford, Lake, Clay, Flagler, Nassau, Putnam, St. Johns, Alachua, Marion, Orange): irrigation cut to ONE day per week (odd = Saturday, even = Sunday, non-residential = Tuesday), NO irrigation between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., a hard cap of three-quarters of an inch per zone and one hour per zone, decorative fountains prohibited, tightened rules on new-planting establishment. Exemptions: micro-irrigation and hand-held hose with shut-off nozzle anytime; new landscape 30 days unrestricted then 30 days every-other-day. REBATE: I found NO rebate anywhere in SJRWMD material for which artificial turf qualifies, and JEA's conservation pages are CAPTCHA-walled and could not be verified — DO NOT claim a turf rebate on the page without calling JEA. The honest and stronger line is the restriction itself: a one-day-a-week Phase III order is exactly when St. Augustine under oak shade dies.
facts.soil_and_yard: Sandy marine-sediment soils on the St. Johns east-bank terrace. The defining Miramar condition is not soil chemistry, it is CANOPY: a 1926–1947 tract whose live oaks, water oaks and slash pines are now 80–100 years old, on a cape documented as landscaped in "oak, pine, and traditional southern" plantings. That produces the three-way failure that kills turfgrass — permanent deep shade (St. Augustine needs 4–6 hours of sun and does not get it), aggressive surface root competition drinking the top 6 inches, and year-round leaf and pine-needle litter smothering what survives. Secondary condition: the cape's creeks. Greenridge Road Park sits on a creek flowing straight into the St. Johns, and New Rose Creek runs near the Lakewood Shopping Center — lower Miramar lots on those drainage lines hold water and go to moss and bare dirt. Installation implication: shallow excavation to avoid severing oak feeder roots, permeable base that will not girdle trees, drainage tied into existing sheet flow rather than damming it.
facts.housing_stock: Miramar Terrace was platted and built out 1926–1947 and is described in the record as "a charming neighborhood of brick bungalows that culminates in the shops and restaurants of Miramar Center" — the land east of San Jose Boulevard on the Point La Vista cape, between San Marco to the north and San Jose to the south. Pre-war and immediately post-war small-lot bungalow stock, not estates: typical frontages roughly 50–75 ft with backyards in the 30x40 to 45x55 ft range (about 1,200–2,500 sq ft of usable turf area). Surrounding cape subdivisions bracket it and set context: Granada (1925, Mediterranean/Georgian brick/ranch on generous lots), Old Oak Terrace (1927), Brookwood Terrace (1937), Colonial Manor (1935–1940, Stockton Whatley & Davin), Waterman Estates (1947), Oriental Gardens (1955), South Granada (1951). Almost entirely NO HOA — 1920s–40s municipal plats inside the consolidated city, deed-restriction-light, no architectural review board. That is a sales fact: in Miramar you sell the homeowner, full stop, with no committee in the way. Verify lot dimensions against the Duval County Property Appraiser before publishing specifics. CHECK DATE 2026-09-07.
facts.who_lives_there: ZIP 32207 (ACS 2024 5-yr): ~37,000 people over 11.4 sq mi, median household income $65,234, per-capita $45,391, median age 40, 39.2% bachelor's or higher, 13% poverty, 19.8-minute average commute (about three-quarters of the metro average), 6.7% veterans. Note the split inside that ZIP: 32207 also contains rental-heavy Southbank and Philips Highway blocks that drag the median down, so Miramar's owner-occupied bungalow streets sit above the ZIP figure. Buyer profile: a professional couple or downsizer who bought a $350k–$550k bungalow for the location and the trees, not for the yard. They will spend on a 500–900 sq ft yard transformation; they will not sign a $40,000 estate job. Price the page for the $6k–$12k full-backyard ticket.
facts.golf: Miramar has NO golf course inside it and that is the point — do not lead with golf here. Nearest is San Jose Country Club (Donald Ross layout, 1925) roughly two miles south down San Jose Boulevard, and Epping Forest Yacht & Country Club off San Jose Blvd at Christopher Point. Timuquana Country Club and the Ortega/Hyde Park courses sit across the St. Johns to the west. Miramar residents are golf-adjacent, not golf-resident: the sale here is a 3-hole, 200–350 sq ft chipping-and-putting corner squeezed into a bungalow yard, not a 1,000 sq ft multi-break green. Sell the small green as a shade-tolerant use for the one part of the yard where grass has already died.
facts.commercial_targets: Hendricks Avenue Elementary School (1942, 600+ students) — playground and courtyard surfacing. Bishop Kenny High School, 1055 Kingman Avenue, 32207 — 55 riverfront acres, 1,308 students, William Johnston Stadium (football/track), John Baldwin Athletic Center, a baseball stadium, a softball field, six Abbie Lenahan tennis courts and the Roger Strickland Field House; a genuine multi-field institutional prospect about a mile from Miramar Center. Assumption Catholic School and the Hendricks Avenue church campuses. The Miramar Center tenant mix itself — restaurant patios, salons and boutiques wanting clean green frontage and small courtyards. Independent daycares and pet groomers along the San Jose Blvd / Hendricks Ave corridor. Small-scale but dense: the geography lets one crew do several jobs on the same street.
facts.landmarks: Miramar Center — the shopping and restaurant node at the southern end of Miramar Terrace where San Jose Boulevard and Hendricks Avenue converge; THE local identifier, used by every resident. Hendricks Avenue Elementary School (founded 1942, 600+ students). Granada Park, centerpiece green of adjacent Granada. Colonial Manor Park (waterfowl and fountains) and Mickey King Park on Hendricks Avenue. Greenridge Road Park on its creek. Lakewood Shopping Center at New Rose Creek. San Jose Boulevard's two-mile curved half-loop parallel to the river — the road everyone here drives daily.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH COURTYARDS AND THE REVIEW BOARD — not lawns. This is the only place in the service area where the product is a 600-square-foot walled courtyard on an HP-district lot with a 1,750 sq ft minimum and 70% building coverage, and the only place where the job has to survive a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic Architectural Review Board. The page should say: we install in the historic district, we know the COA process, and we build for a courtyard that gets salt water in it 12 to 16 times a year. The three-part argument is unique to St. Augustine: (1) there is not enough sun, soil or room downtown for real grass to have ever worked; (2) the city floods with salt water on sunny days, which kills sod and does not kill turf on a properly drained coquina-aware base; (3) HARB and the tree canopy mean this is a craft job, not a suburban rip-and-roll. Nothing next door needs any of that — St. Augustine Beach has no review board, and the mainland CDPs have no city code at all. Secondary lead: quarter-acre North City / Nelmar Terrace lots (RS-1, 10,890 sq ft, deep oak shade) as the backyard putting-green market, since the city's own Donald Ross course closed in 2005 and there is no golf inside the city limits.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE constraint is the Historic Architectural Review Board. A Certificate of Appropriateness (COA) is required for most work in any of the city's five Historic Preservation (HP) zoning districts, reviewed against the Architectural Guidelines for Historic Preservation. New construction must conform to old foundation lines to preserve scale. City tree protection applies. Statewide overlay: Fla. Stat. 125.572 (from CS/CS/HB 683 and SB 712, ch. 2025-140, signed June 2025) bars local governments from prohibiting compliant synthetic turf on single-family lots of 1 acre or less — BUT ONLY once FDEP adopts the minimum installation standards rule. As of 2026-09-07 that rule is NOT final (DEP held a workshop 8/5/2025 with comments through 8/19; proposed rules appeared January 2026 and remain subject to change). Do not tell customers the preemption is live yet. The forthcoming standards will address material type, color, permeability, stormwater, water conservation, water quality and proximity to trees; turf must be lead-free and rubber infill is out. Separately, Fla. Stat. 720.3045 bars an HOA from restricting artificial turf that is not visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel, adjacent common area, or a community golf course.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: City of St. Augustine Utilities (the city runs its own water and sewer service area and publishes a service-area map). Normal schedule under city ordinance + SJRWMD rules — Daylight Saving Time: odd addresses Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, non-residential Tue/Fri; Eastern Standard Time: odd Sat, even Sun, non-residential Tue. No watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m., max one hour per zone. AS OF 2026-09-07 THE OVERRIDE IS PHASE III: the St. Johns River Water Management District declared a Phase III Extreme Water Shortage effective May 11, 2026 covering Clay, Duval, Flagler, Nassau, Putnam and St. Johns counties — landscape irrigation is cut to ONE DAY PER WEEK (odd addresses Saturday, even addresses Sunday, non-residential Tuesday), no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m., max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone. Pressure washing and street washing also restricted. New sod gets a step-down grace period (daily for 15 days, then 3 days/week for 30 days, then 2 days/week for 15 days) — i.e. a new lawn is legal but expensive. Reclaimed water is exempt from the one-day rule. NO artificial turf rebate exists from the city or SJRWMD — do not claim one.
facts.soil_and_yard: Fine sandy soils sitting on the Anastasia Formation — a variably lithified coquina of shell and sand that outcrops close to the surface near the water and was quarried to build the Castillo de San Marcos. Seasonal high water table 0–1 ft in wet periods; slopes generally under 2%. The signature problem is salt water, not rain: the city gets 'sunny day' / king tide flooding 12 to 16 times a year, when sea water backs up through the stormwater system and into the streets. Davis Shores alone has ~21 stormwater outfalls to the Matanzas River and Salt Run. North City and Nelmar Terrace are heavily canopied — 'overhanging oaks' is how locals describe it — so shade plus salt plus periodic saltwater inundation is exactly the combination that St. Augustine grass cannot survive.
facts.housing_stock: Wildly varied by district — this is five markets under one name. The five Historic Preservation (HP-1/2/3) zoning districts downtown allow a MINIMUM lot area of just 1,750 sq ft with up to 70% lot coverage and 3 ft side/rear setbacks, so the outdoor space is a walled courtyard, not a lawn — often 20x30 ft behind a coquina or stucco wall. Standard residential zoning outside the HP districts: RS-1 = 75 ft wide / 10,890 sq ft (quarter acre) / 25% max coverage / 20-15-20 setbacks; RS-2 = 50 ft / 5,450 sq ft / 30% / 15-10-10; RG-1 = 50 ft / 5,450 sq ft / 35%. So real backyards run from a 600 sq ft courtyard downtown to roughly 60x70 ft in North City. Neighborhood eras: Lincolnville founded 1866 by newly freed people (frame vernacular, Victorian, shotgun); Model Land Company and Abbott Tract (Flagler era); Nelmar Terrace developed 1913 through the 1920s boom — Mediterranean Revival, Georgian and Dutch Colonial Revival, Craftsman bungalows, plus a Moorish Revival 'pink castle' on May Street — National Register district since 2011; Fullerwood Park same era and styles; Davis Shores (in city limits, on Anastasia Island) from the 1930s. Housing stock spans homes built from ~1909 to new construction. HOA prevalence is LOW — the binding constraint downtown is HARB, not a homeowners association.
facts.who_lives_there: Population ~15,351 (2024 est., 2026 projection 15,705). Median age 49.9. Median household income $78,151 (2024). ~4.6% of families below poverty. 84.1% White, 6.8% Hispanic, 3.6% two or more races. Mix of retirees, hospitality and tourism workers, Flagler College students and staff, second-home owners, and a heavy short-term-rental investor layer downtown.
facts.golf: No golf course inside the city limits. The Ponce de Leon Golf & Conference Resort — a Donald Ross design that opened in 1916 — CLOSED in 2005; that is a checkable local fact worth using. Nearest courses: Marsh Creek Country Club (Mark McCumber, private, Anastasia Island, 18/par 72, ~6,883 yds — the only course on the island); St. Augustine Shores Golf Club (public, 18/par 70, 5,956 yds); Royal St. Augustine Golf & Country Club (public, par 72, 6,529 yds); St. Johns Golf & Country Club (Clyde Johnston, built 2001, 7,250 yds from the tips, has hosted PGA TOUR Qualifying School); and World Golf Village's King & Bear (Palmer/Nicklaus) and Slammer & Squire (Bobby Weed). Because there is no course in town, the golf play here is backyard putting greens on quarter-acre North City lots, not course-frontage work.
facts.commercial_targets: Solomon Calhoun Community Center, 1300 Duval St — St. Johns County ALREADY converted a grass field there to high-performance artificial turf with permanent striping for lacrosse, soccer and football, funded with FY2023 Tourist Development Tax dollars, completed 2025; the county's project manager Chris Gatchell publicly cited year-round use, no flooding and 'plenty of drainage under this.' That is the single best local proof point in the whole service area — reference it. Also: the adjacent St. Augustine Little League Park; Treaty Park (1595 Wildwood Dr, 47 acres, four lighted softball fields, two multipurpose soccer fields, tennis, pickleball, bocce, basketball); Flagler College; the Florida School for the Deaf and the Blind; St. Augustine High School; Ketterlinus, John A. Crookshank and James A. Webster elementary schools; R.J. Murray and Sebastian middle schools; the St. Augustine Amphitheatre; downtown boutique hotels and B&Bs with brick or shell courtyards; short-term rental management companies.
facts.landmarks: Castillo de San Marcos; St. George Street; the Bridge of Lions; Flagler College in the former Ponce de Leon Hotel; the Lightner Museum; the Cathedral Basilica; Lincolnville; the Moorish Revival 'pink castle' on May Street in Nelmar Terrace; the Florida School for the Deaf and the Blind on San Marco Avenue; Ketterlinus Elementary; Salt Run.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE LIVE-OAK SHADE PROBLEM — AND THE ARBORIST LETTER THAT MAKES TURFING UNDER THE CANOPY LEGAL. Orange Park is a 145-year-old river town with a median age of 49, 28.7% of residents over 65, and 1950s–70s houses sitting under 80-year-old live oaks where grass has simply never grown and never will. That is a completely different sale from anywhere else in the batch. And Florida's new DEP rule turned it into a compliance problem competitors will get wrong: Rule 62-308.100(8)(b) bars installing synthetic turf inside a tree's drip line unless a certified arborist certifies in writing that it will not harm the tree — and in Orange Park most of the yards that want turf are inside a drip line. The page should lead with 'we bring the certified arborist and the written drip-line certification,' show the shade problem in photographs, and then run three offers: (1) the bare, root-choked, deep-shade patch made green and permanently usable; (2) the low-maintenance, non-slip, mower-free yard for a homeowner in their sixties or seventies who is done with a lawn; (3) senior-living, hospital and veterinary commercial work — Moosehaven, HCA Orange Park, Naval Hospital, Clay Humane. Deliberately not Fleming Island's HOA-approval page (Orange Park is largely un-covenanted), not Baldwin's acreage page, and not Beach Haven's condo-courtyard page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Orange Park maintains its own Code of Ordinances including Part III Land Development Regulations, Chapter 20 Environment and Chapter 12 Buildings, plus historic review on contributing properties in the River Road Historic District. Since 19 May 2026, however, the town cannot prohibit compliant synthetic turf on a single-family lot of 1 acre or less (s. 125.572, F.S. / DEP Rule 62-308.100).
