THE ORANGE PARK CATCH — and this is the most valuable operational fact for this page — is Rule 62-308.100(8): the installation "cannot compromise the health of nearby trees, including damage to tree roots," and turf "shall not be installed inside tree drip lines, whether on the property or adjacent properties... unless a certified arborist, using site specific information and best professional judgment, certifies that installation within that drip line would not be harmful to the tree." In a town of 80-year-old live oaks, most of the shady back yards that most want turf ARE inside a drip line. Also relevant given the older stock: the rule requires access to the septic tank for routine pumpout, and forbids in-ground irrigation over turf (heads removed, pipe capped). Low HOA prevalence in town means the real gatekeeper is the tree, not a board.
facts.water_and_rules: The Town of Orange Park runs its own water, sewer and treatment plants through its Public Works Department — it is a full-service municipality, not a Clay County Utility Authority customer inside the town limits (CCUA serves the surrounding unincorporated areas). The town publishes the SJRWMD schedule on its own site: Daylight Saving Time — odd Wednesday/Saturday, even Thursday/Sunday, nonresidential Tuesday/Friday; Eastern Standard Time — odd Saturday, even Sunday, nonresidential Tuesday; no watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m.; one hour per zone maximum. The town has also publicly posted the SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage declaration, which cuts that to one day per week with no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m. No artificial-turf rebate.
facts.soil_and_yard: The St. Johns River bluff. Better-drained relict sand ridges near River Road and the waterfront; wetter flatwoods soils inland toward Wells Road and Blanding. But the defining yard condition in Orange Park is not water — it is DEEP LIVE OAK SHADE. Clarke House Park is described as a playground "beneath a canopy of live oak trees" and the town's mid-century neighbourhoods carry 70-to-100-year-old oaks over the whole back yard. St. Augustine will not hold under that canopy at any price, and root competition takes what light does not. Riverfront lots get brackish influence: tidal range at Orange Park is about 0.7 ft and salinity at the Buckman Bridge averages 2.9 ppt, so salt reaches the soil on the lowest lots. Leaf litter and acorn drop are a year-round maintenance nuisance.
facts.housing_stock: An old river town, not a suburb. Founded 1877 by the Florida Winter Home and Improvement Company, incorporated 1879, 5.32 square miles on the west bank of the St. Johns, and Wikipedia records that it "developed primarily in the mid-to-late 20th century." Three layers: (1) a small genuinely historic core — the River Road Historic District, Grace Episcopal Church, the 1912 Clarke House on the National Register; (2) the bulk of the stock, 1950s–1970s ranch and split-level houses on generous lots under a mature live-oak canopy; (3) condos, townhomes and apartments along Kingsley Avenue and Wells Road. 3,985 housing units at a 10.7% vacancy rate (2020 census). Median property value $313,100 in 2024 (up 21.6% year on year — the fastest appreciation in this batch), but homeownership is only 55.6%, meaning roughly 45% of units are rented or vacant. HOA prevalence inside the town limits is LOW — most of this stock predates covenanted subdivision development, which is the opposite of Fleming Island four miles south.
facts.who_lives_there: Older, health-care-employed, Navy-adjacent and renter-heavy. Population 9,089 (2020) / 9,055 (2024). Median age 48.9–49.1 with 28.7% of residents aged 65 or over — the oldest population in this batch. Median household income $77,106; poverty 13.8%. Health Care & Social Assistance is the single largest employment sector (1,146 people) — HCA Florida Orange Park Hospital and Naval Hospital Jacksonville are both right here. ZIP 32073 is 17.4% veterans (6,103 people), more than double the national rate, reflecting NAS Jacksonville immediately north. Racial composition roughly 65.75% non-Hispanic White, 14.71% Black, 10.90% Hispanic.
facts.golf: Country Club of Orange Park, 2525 Country Club Boulevard — 18 holes, designed by Bobby Miller, built 1989, mature tree-lined fairways with water in play on 14 of 18 holes and an adjacent Audubon Society wildlife preserve. NAS Jacksonville Golf Course immediately north on the base. Four to eight minutes south: The Golf Club at Fleming Island (Bobby Weed) and Eagle Harbor Golf Club (Clyde B. Johnston). Magnolia Point Golf & Country Club in Green Cove Springs to the south. Solid golf access, but this is not a golf-community town — the golf pitch here is a practice green for a retiree, not a lifestyle identity.
facts.commercial_targets: Healthcare and senior living are the strongest B2B story in this batch. HCA Florida Orange Park Hospital (Kingsley Ave) and Naval Hospital Jacksonville (Child St) — courtyards, therapy gardens, rooftop and entry landscaping. Moosehaven — a 63-acre retirement campus with 400+ residents, the natural buyer for low-maintenance, trip-safe, walker- and wheelchair-friendly surfacing. Schools: St. Johns Country Day School (Pre-K–12, private, highly ranked), Grace Episcopal Day School, Orange Park High School (Kingsley Ave), Orange Park Junior High, Orange Park Elementary, Montclair Elementary, Grove Park Elementary, S. Bryan Jennings Elementary, Cherry Elementary, Charterhouse Private School of Clay County, Little Lamb Christian School, Clay Baptist Christian School. Pet: Clay Humane (Filmore Street), Allied Veterinary Specialists (Corporate Way, 32073), PetSmart (Wells Road), Banfield Pet Hospital. Childcare: Andromeda Kindergarten and Day Care, Orange Park Kindergarten. Municipal: Town Hall Park, Orange Park Sports & Recreational Park, TC Miller Community Center. Condo and apartment associations along Kingsley and Wells. Country Club of Orange Park practice green.
facts.landmarks: Clarke House Park, 1039/1047 Kingsley Avenue — the 1912 Clarke House on the National Register, home of the Orange Park Historical Society, open for tours the second Sunday of each month, with a castle-shaped wooden playground, sand volleyball court, butterfly garden and nature trails under live oaks. Club Continental (the former Mira Rio estate on the river). Grace Episcopal Church. The River Road Historic District. Moosehaven — 63 acres and 400+ residents, operating on the St. Johns since autumn 1922, one of Moose International's two philanthropic campuses. Orange Park Mall and the Wells Road corridor. HCA Florida Orange Park Hospital on Kingsley Avenue. NAS Jacksonville and Naval Hospital Jacksonville (Child Street). St. Johns Country Day School. Town Hall Park, Walter Odum Park, Orange Park Sports & Recreational Park, TC Miller Community Center on McIntosh Avenue.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE PUTTING GREEN AND THE GOLF-COURSE CLAUSE. This is the only place in the batch where the golf course is inside the neighborhood, the course is a forgiving par-70 public track built for high handicaps, roughly a third of residents are over 65, and the HOA charges $30 a month rather than policing every blade. Those four facts together say: a large, concentrated, time-rich, golf-playing population that can walk to its own course and would rather practice at home. That is a putting-green page, not a lawn page — and putting greens are where the $10–12/sq ft pricing lives. Then land the objection-killer that is unusually precise here: Fla. Stat. 720.3045 says an association may not restrict artificial turf that is not visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel, an adjacent common area, OR A COMMUNITY GOLF COURSE — St. Augustine Shores is literally a community with a golf course, so quote the statute and explain what it means for a fairway-frontage lot versus an interior lot. Third beat: the shade. The developer chose in the late 1960s to leave the native oaks and pines standing, which is why the community is beautiful and why nobody's St. Augustine grass has ever filled in under the canopy. Contrast this deliberately with St. Augustine South next door — same county, same water rules, but South is old irrigation and no HOA at all, while the Shores is golf, retirees, and a statute worth quoting.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated — St. Johns County land development code applies; no city ordinance, no architectural review board, no municipal impervious surface cap. There IS a homeowners association (single-family dues ~$30/month) plus separate condominium associations ($300–$370/month) that fund landscape maintenance. TWO STATUTES MATTER MORE HERE THAN ANYWHERE ELSE IN THE BATCH. (1) Fla. Stat. 720.3045: an association 'may not restrict parcel owners or tenants from installing, displaying, or storing items not visible from the parcel's frontage or an adjacent parcel, adjacent common area, or community golf course,' and the statute EXPLICITLY names artificial turf in its list. St. Augustine Shores is a community with a golf course, so that golf-course clause bites precisely on the frontage lots — this is the specific, checkable answer to the 'will the HOA let me?' objection. (2) Fla. Stat. 125.572 (ch. 2025-140, signed June 2025) will preempt local prohibition of compliant synthetic turf on single-family lots of 1 acre or less once FDEP adopts its minimum standards rule — NOT final as of 2026-09-07 (DEP workshop Aug 2025, proposed rules Jan 2026, still subject to change). Always confirm the individual association's own recorded covenants before promising anything.
facts.water_and_rules: Provider: St. Johns County Utility Department, with a reclaimed water program the county describes as central to its long-term conservation strategy. AS OF 2026-09-07 the SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage (effective May 11, 2026) is in force — ONE watering day per week: odd addresses Saturday, even addresses Sunday, non-residential Tuesday; no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m.; max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone. Normal schedule is twice weekly: odd Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, non-residential Tue/Fri, no watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m. New sod gets the step-down grace period (daily 15 days, 3x/week 30 days, 2x/week 15 days). Reclaimed water is EXEMPT from the one-day rule — check whether a given street is on reclaimed before making the water-savings argument. Code Enforcement: (904) 209-0734 or the SJC Connect app. County fertilizer ordinance: max 5 lb nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per year, nothing within 10 feet of a water body — directly relevant on the golf-course pond lots and the Intracoastal frontage. No artificial turf rebate exists.
facts.soil_and_yard: Elevation 26 ft — the driest ground in this batch, and worth saying so, because it means the objection here is NOT flooding. Fine sandy soils with moderate water-holding capacity, seasonal high water table 0–1 ft in wet periods, slopes under 2%. The defining yard condition is SHADE, and it is the developer's own fault in a way you can name: the community was platted in the late 1960s specifically to preserve the native trees, so live oaks and pines were left standing throughout, and 50+ miles of walking paths run under canopy. A shaded Florida yard is where St. Augustine grass thins, goes weedy and never recovers. Golf-frontage lots add cart-path traffic, ball damage, and the 10-foot no-fertilizer setback along the course ponds.
facts.housing_stock: 4.48 sq mi, elevation 26 feet — noticeably higher and drier than the beach or downtown. A master-planned community begun in the LATE 1960s along the Intracoastal, deliberately platted to leave native trees standing, with 100 acres set aside for parks and recreation (45 acres of recreation facilities plus 58 acres designated for park development). 4,737 housing units across 4,196 households; 68.6% detached single-family, the balance condos, villas and an assisted living facility. Single-family homes run 1,108–3,257 sq ft and roughly $159K to $2.1M; condos 680–2,231 sq ft and $185K–$439K. Three overlapping eras: original 1970s–80s ranch product on modest lots, 1990s–2000s infill, and newer high-end Intracoastal-front homes at the top of the price range. Fixer-uppers still trade in the low-to-mid $200s; larger homes $350K–$450K. HOA prevalence is UNIVERSAL but unusually light-touch: the single-family HOA fee is about $30 a MONTH, which locals cite as a main reason to buy here. Condo associations are a different story at $300–$370/month.
facts.who_lives_there: 8,706 at the 2020 census (up from 7,359 in 2010), with a 2026 estimate around 10,512 — the fastest-growing place in this batch. Median age 52.8–57.2 and 31.1–35.9% aged 65 or older, the OLDEST population of the five. Median household income $73,688; poverty rate 4.97%. 46.1% married-couple households and only 17.4% of households have children under 18 — this is a retiree and empty-nester community with a working-family minority. 88.8% White, 4.9% Hispanic, 4.3% two or more races. Zoned schools: W.D. Hartley Elementary, Gamble Rogers Middle, Pedro Menendez High. Buyers skew first-time, downsizing, and retiring.
facts.golf: THE ST. AUGUSTINE SHORES GOLF CLUB IS INSIDE THE COMMUNITY — this is the only place in the batch where the course IS the neighborhood. 18 holes, par 70, 5,956 yards, public access, water in play on nine holes, deliberately forgiving and beginner-friendly. That profile matters commercially: this is a course full of high-handicap retirees who play often, not scratch players — exactly the demographic that buys a backyard practice green. Nearby alternatives: Marsh Creek Country Club (Mark McCumber, private) across the Intracoastal on Anastasia Island; Royal St. Augustine Golf & Country Club (public, par 72, 6,529 yds); St. Johns Golf & Country Club (Clyde Johnston, 2001, 7,250 yds, former PGA TOUR Q-School site); World Golf Village's King & Bear (Palmer/Nicklaus) and Slammer & Squire (Bobby Weed).
facts.commercial_targets: St. Augustine Shores Golf Club — practice putting green, chipping area, tee line, clubhouse surrounds (a beginner-friendly public course with a heavy senior membership is a realistic first commercial reference). The Riverview Club grounds and its wedding/event lawn. The Shores HOA's own common areas: pool deck, kiddie park, picnic area, pier approach, the trail network's high-traffic entries. The condominium associations — Conquistador and others charging $300–$370/month, whose dues currently pay for landscape maintenance you can displace. The on-site assisted living facility, plus the broader 31–36%-over-65 population, for level, non-slip, pet-friendly walking surfaces. W.D. Hartley Elementary and Gamble Rogers Middle. Pedro Menendez High School. The US-1 corridor's vet clinics, groomers and daycares at the community entrance.
facts.landmarks: St. Augustine Shores Golf Club; the Riverview Club at 790 Christina Dr (ballroom, multipurpose rooms, conference facilities, used for weddings and events); the community fishing pier, pool, kiddie park, game room and picnic area on the Intracoastal; 50+ miles of walking and nature trails; tennis/pickleball, basketball and volleyball courts and horseshoe pits; Conquistador Condominiums; W.D. Hartley Elementary; the US-1 commercial corridor at the community entrance; roughly 7 miles from Historic Downtown and 15 minutes from Crescent Beach.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH JURISDICTION AND MARSH DRAINAGE: 'South-island turf without the city design-review process — and built for a marsh-edge water table.' Amelia City's one genuinely distinguishing, checkable fact is that it is unincorporated: a homeowner here is under Nassau County's code, NOT the City of Fernandina Beach's Historic District Council, so the permitting path is materially simpler than it is for a neighbour six miles north in the National Register district. Say that plainly — it is useful, true, and nobody else's page says it. Then pivot to the technical reality that actually decides the job on the south end: half these lots face the Amelia River across tidal marsh, on the exact west-side poorly drained soils the county's comprehensive plan calls out, with a high water table and salt intrusion; the other half take ocean salt spray and sit under permanent live-oak and palmetto canopy. Both are conditions where St. Augustine has never worked and where a cheap install fails in year three because the base was too shallow. Position the company as the crew that engineers base depth and drainage for a marsh-edge lot. Finally, borrow the corridor's credibility honestly — the Ritz-Carlton and the Golf Club of Amelia Island are at 4750 and 4700 Amelia Island Parkway, minutes away. IMPORTANT: keep this page SHORT and specific. There is not enough verified material about Amelia City to justify a long page, and padding it with invented statistics is the fastest way to make the whole site look fake. A tight, honest, geographically precise page beats a padded one.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE most useful and most differentiating fact for this page: Amelia City is UNINCORPORATED, so the City of Fernandina Beach Land Development Code and its Historic District Council Certificate of Appropriateness process DO NOT APPLY. Jurisdiction is Nassau County's land development code and building department. That is a genuinely different permitting story from Fernandina Beach a few miles north — simpler, faster, no design-review board for most residential work. Countervailing constraints: (a) Nassau County operates an Amelia Island Tree Commission concerned with tree protection on unincorporated Amelia Island — SCOPE UNVERIFIED on the check date (the county's own PDF would not parse); confirm before making claims about tree-removal or root-zone permitting. (b) Many south-island addresses still sit inside private communities (Summer Beach, Amelia Island Plantation, Amelia Surf & Racquet Club) with architectural review boards controlling turf color, pile height and edging. (c) Coastal construction control line and dune-protection rules apply on oceanfront parcels. (d) Fla. Stat. §373.185 / Ch. 720 limit HOA bans on water-conserving landscaping but do not clearly protect synthetic turf and do not override county zoning.
facts.water_and_rules: SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage, effective 11 May 2026, covers all of Nassau County including unincorporated Amelia Island: irrigation ONE day per week, never 8 a.m.–6 p.m., max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone. Residential odd-numbered or no street address = Saturday; even-numbered = Sunday; non-residential = Tuesday. Aesthetic water use is prohibited under Phase III. Normal-year baseline: two days a week during daylight saving time, one day during EST, no irrigation 10 a.m.–4 p.m. Water service on the unincorporated south island is county/JEA or private/community system rather than the City of Fernandina Beach utility — VERIFY per address; some parcels here are on wells, which changes the pitch materially (a well owner's motivation is pump wear and iron staining, not a water bill). No artificial-turf rebate is available from SJRWMD or JEA.
facts.soil_and_yard: Southern Amelia Island barrier sand with two distinct sub-conditions. West of A1A toward the Amelia River: tidal marsh edge, high water table and the poorly drained west-side soils the Nassau County comprehensive plan specifically flags — these lots need engineered base depth and positive drainage, and salt intrusion is real. East of A1A toward the ocean: better-drained higher sand, but salt spray and wind burn on anything grassy, plus dune-protection setbacks. Everywhere on the south end: dense maritime forest — live oak, palmetto and pine — meaning permanent shade, extensive shallow root plates, and yards where turfgrass has never held. The countywide problem the plan names — almost no topographic relief plus abundant poorly drained soils — is why drainage design, not the turf product, decides whether a south-island install survives.
facts.housing_stock: HONEST CAVEAT FIRST: Amelia City is a genuinely thin research subject. It is an unincorporated community with no census designation, no separate demographic data, and only a Wikipedia stub — located in the southern half of Amelia Island along State Road A1A near the Amelia River, at roughly 30.590°N, 81.457°W. There is no published housing-stock profile for it. What IS checkable is its context: it sits in the south-island corridor between Amelia Island Plantation and the Omni to the north, American Beach immediately adjacent, the Ritz-Carlton and Summer Beach nearby, and Amelia Island State Park at the island's southern tip. Housing in that corridor mixes older, unglamorous A1A-frontage and marsh-side homes on larger, irregular, wooded parcels — the pre-resort island — with newer high-value coastal construction. Lots skew larger and less regular than anything in Fernandina Beach's platted historic grid or in Yulee's subdivisions, and many are marsh- or river-facing on the Amelia River side. DO NOT publish a specific median income, median home value or lot-size figure for Amelia City; no source supports one. Build the page on geography and jurisdiction, which are verifiable, not on invented statistics.
facts.who_lives_there: No standalone data exists. Amelia City is not a CDP and is not broken out by the Census Bureau. The defensible framing is county- and island-level: Nassau County / Amelia Island, where Fernandina Beach's median household income is $97,903 and median age is 58.6, and where the south-island resort corridor runs substantially higher. Locally, the south end mixes long-tenured island families on older A1A parcels with high-net-worth buyers in the Ritz-Carlton / Summer Beach / Plantation orbit. State this qualitatively; do not fabricate numbers.
facts.golf: Amelia City's immediate neighbors are the island's golf spine. The Golf Club of Amelia Island (Mark McCumber and Gene Littler, 18 holes) is at 4700 Amelia Island Parkway, directly adjacent to the Ritz-Carlton at 4750 Amelia Island Parkway. Just north: the Omni Amelia Island Resort's Oak Marsh (Pete Dye; Beau Welling renovation completed 2025), Long Point (Tom Fazio, 1987, private/member-owned for The Amelia Island Club) at 12 Long Point Drive, and the Little Sandy 10-hole short course plus 18-hole putting course. The private Amelia River Club (TifEagle greens) is also on-island. Off-island via SR 200/A1A: Amelia National (Tom Fazio, gated) and The Golf Club at North Hampton (Arnold Palmer Signature).
facts.commercial_targets: Because there is no Amelia City commercial district to speak of, target the corridor: The Ritz-Carlton, Amelia Island — event lawns, terraces, pool surrounds, pet-relief areas. The Golf Club of Amelia Island (4700 Amelia Island Parkway) — practice greens, tee lines, clubhouse landscape. Summer Beach community common areas and villa courtyards. Vacation-rental and property-management companies operating the south-island inventory. Amelia Island State Park and Nassau County park facilities on the south end (public procurement; long cycle but a strong credential). The A.L. Lewis Museum and Burney Park at neighboring American Beach. Marsh-front and river-side private residences — small, high-margin courtyard and dock-side installs. Do not invent named daycares or pet businesses for this page; there is no verified list.
facts.landmarks: State Road A1A / Amelia Island Parkway through the south end; the Amelia River on the west side; The Ritz-Carlton, Amelia Island (4750 Amelia Island Parkway) and the adjacent Golf Club of Amelia Island (4700 Amelia Island Parkway); Summer Beach; American Beach and the 8.5-acre NaNa dune immediately adjacent; Amelia Island State Park at the island's southern tip, where you can ride horses on the beach; Nassau Sound and the south-end bridge; the Omni Amelia Island Resort and the Plantation gates to the north.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH SHADE AND THE MAYO CLINIC BUYER — the doctor who is never home. Pablo Creek Reserve is 400 wooded acres, no golf course, no resort amenities, deliberately quiet, 1.5 miles from Mayo Clinic, behind a gate that is attended around the clock. The homeowner is a physician or executive on a three-quarter-acre preserve lot under 20-year-old retained oak canopy, being told by the water district to keep an estate lawn alive on one hour per zone, one day a week, before 8 a.m. That yard has never had a full stand of St. Augustine and never will. The page should lead with the shade failure — bare, root-choked, perpetually damp ground under mature oaks — and then with zero-maintenance-while-you-travel. Second beat, and it is genuinely unique to this address: because Pablo Creek has NO community golf course, § 720.3045's golf-course carve-out never fires, so a preserve-backed rear yard here enjoys the strongest statutory HOA protection of any community in this batch. Third beat: pet turf on a big wooded lot, and a private practice green as the ONLY golf on the property. Contrast with the neighbours — Glen Kernan is loud about golf and athletes, Queen's Harbour is loud about boats, Deerwood is loud about history. Pablo Creek's whole brand is quiet, and the page should sound like that: technical, unshowy, root-competition and drainage engineering explained properly to an audience that is professionally trained to check work.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: City of Jacksonville consolidated code; no separate municipality, so permitting is the same as everywhere else in this batch. § 125.572, Fla. Stat. (HB 683 / Ch. 2025-140, effective 2025-07-01) preempts local prohibition of DEP-compliant synthetic turf on single-family lots ONE ACRE OR LESS — most Pablo Creek lots qualify, but the largest estate parcels may not, and the DEP standards rule was still in development at the check date. § 720.3045, Fla. Stat. protects turf not visible from the frontage, an adjacent parcel or an adjacent common area — and here the statute is MORE useful than it is at Glen Kernan or Deerwood, because Pablo Creek has NO community golf course to trigger that carve-out, and estate lots back to preserve rather than to shared common area. A wooded, preserve-backed, three-quarter-acre rear yard behind a 24/7 attended gate is close to the ideal statutory fact pattern. That is a real, checkable, community-specific legal advantage worth putting on the page. HONEST GAP: the Pablo Creek Reserve HOA architectural guidelines are not published publicly and no turf-specific standard could be retrieved.
facts.water_and_rules: JEA, under the SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage covering Duval at the 2026-09-07 check: one irrigation day per week, no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m., ¾ inch per zone maximum, one hour per zone maximum; odd addresses Saturday, even Sunday, non-residential Tuesday. Duval went Phase I in February 2026, Phase II by late April 2026 (explicitly covering JEA potable, reuse and reclaimed customers), and Phase III thereafter. The angle that lands hardest with this specific buyer: a Mayo physician on call, or an executive who travels, on a three-quarter-acre lot is being asked to keep a large estate lawn alive on one hour per zone, one day a week, watering only in the dark. HONEST GAP: no artificial-turf rebate from JEA or SJRWMD.
facts.soil_and_yard: This is the SHADE page. 400 wooded acres means retained mature live oak, laurel oak and pine canopy, and estate lots are sold on their preserve views — the same canopy that makes St. Augustine grass fail permanently. Underneath: Duval's Pomona-series poorly drained acidic sand, organic matter under 1.2%, seasonal high water table, flat terrain, zone 9a/9b. Lakefront and water-feature lots add pond-bank drainage and edge-retention requirements. Root competition from mature oaks is a real base-construction constraint on three-quarter-acre wooded lots, and it is the technical detail that separates a competent installer from a cheap one in this gate.
facts.housing_stock: 275 single-family homesites on 400 WOODED acres, developed by The PARC Group from the mid-2000s (site references both 'mid-2000s' and a 2008 start). Two lot classes: COTTAGE lots and ESTATE lots; featured estate listings sit on roughly three-quarter-acre preserve lots. Every home was CUSTOM built — there is no production product here — with living areas from about 3,000 sq ft to over 10,000 sq ft, by builders including Elwood Collier and Fox Construction. Every home has a preserve view, a water view, or both. Landscaped common areas, sidewalks, trails, water features and parks throughout. Pricing: entry 'cottage' product around $1.6M, the bulk of the market $2.2M–$3.5M, premium lakefront and larger-acreage estates $4.5M+ (current listings quoted $3M–$4.6M; $530–$700+ per sq ft). HOA yes; NO CDD. Gated and ATTENDED 24/7. Located in the comparatively rare 'south of JTB on San Pablo' pocket. Backyards are big, wooded and private — three-quarter-acre preserve lots under mature canopy is a very different install from a 40ft Nocatee rear yard.
facts.who_lives_there: The defining fact: Pablo Creek Reserve sits roughly 1.5 miles (about 7 minutes) from MAYO CLINIC FLORIDA on San Pablo Rd, and multiple neighbourhood guides identify it as a hotspot for Mayo physicians and for downtown commuters. Add executives and professionals in the $1.6M–$4.6M bracket. Community marketing points buyers at The Bolles School and Episcopal School of Jacksonville, indicating private-school families rather than a retiree profile. ZIP 32224 median household income is $88,259 with 52% holding a bachelor's or higher, but as with Glen Kernan that figure is diluted by UNF students and dramatically understates this gate — do not put the ZIP income on the page. HONEST GAP: no community-level income figure is published; the Mayo-physician characterisation comes from real-estate marketing, not census data, so phrase it as 'popular with Mayo Clinic physicians' rather than as a statistic.
facts.golf: Pablo Creek Reserve has NO golf course of its own — and that is worth saying plainly rather than padding. It deliberately favours 'privacy and tranquility over resort-style amenities'. Golf is all adjacent: Glen Kernan Club (Robert C. Walker 1999 / Jim Furyk 2024) and Jacksonville Golf & Country Club just north of JTB, Queen's Harbour (Mark McCumber) to the northeast, Windsor Parke Golf Club on Hodges Blvd, Deerwood Country Club to the west, and the Ponte Vedra Beach cluster including TPC Sawgrass about 4.5 miles southeast. Because there is no home course, a private backyard practice green here is not a redundancy — it is the only golf on the property, and residents are club members elsewhere.
facts.commercial_targets: Inside: the fitness centre, swimming pool deck surround, tennis courts, and the community parks and green spaces along the trail network — HOA-controlled and all subject to the Tuesday-only non-residential irrigation rule. Immediately outside: MAYO CLINIC FLORIDA's San Pablo Rd campus — courtyards, healing gardens, rooftop and terrace spaces, and pet-therapy areas — is the single highest-value commercial prospect adjacent to any community in this batch, and the community's own residents are the warm introduction. Private schools named in the community's marketing: The Bolles School and Episcopal School of Jacksonville. Nearby Duval schools and the UNF athletics complex on Kernan Blvd. Veterinary and pet-boarding businesses along the San Pablo / JTB corridor serving a high-income, large-lot, dog-owning demographic.
facts.landmarks: Mayo Clinic Florida, 4500 San Pablo Rd — about 1.5 miles / 7 minutes, and the reason the community exists in the form it does. The 24/7 attended gate on San Pablo Rd south of JTB (SR 202), one of the few residential addresses in that pocket. 400 acres of retained woodland with internal lakes, water features, parks and walking trails. Roughly 10 minutes to Atlantic Beach, about 4.5 miles to Ponte Vedra Beach, about 20 minutes to St. Johns Town Center. The Brumos Collection and Castaway Island Preserve are both on San Pablo Rd nearby.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE ABSENTEE OWNER AND THE 0.40 IMPERVIOUS CAP. This is the richest place in the batch ($100,802 median household income), the second-oldest (median age 53–56, ~30% over 65), and roughly half the housing stock is seasonal or rented out — these are people who are not here to mow, are paying $3,000+ in homeowners insurance plus flood, and have watched salt and sand kill three lawns. The pitch is 'the yard maintains itself between visits and the renters can't kill it.' Then the technical differentiator no competitor is leading with: St. Augustine Beach caps low-density residential impervious surface at 0.40 with only a 465 sq ft pool allowance, so the install has to be specced as a permeable system that does not eat the property's impervious budget — and it has to work around a mandatory Tree Removal Permit and the city's Urban Forestry manual. That combination — beach-town money, absentee owners, salt, and a numeric impervious ratio — exists nowhere else in the service area. It is NOT the courtyards-and-HARB story of St. Augustine city, and it is NOT the no-rules story of the mainland CDPs.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE hard number to lead with is the impervious surface ratio in the city's Land Development Regulations, Article VI: Low Density Residential 0.40, Medium Density Residential 0.50, High Density Residential 0.70, Commercial 0.70 — with a 465 sq ft allowance in low density 'for the construction and installation of a pool and pool decking only.' Whether a given turf system counts against that 0.40 is the design question on every single job in this city, and it is the argument for an open-graded, genuinely free-draining base rather than a compacted-fines build. The city also requires a Tree Removal Permit before cutting, destroying or moving any tree and has formally adopted the 'St. Augustine Beach Urban Forestry Standards and Specifications Manual.' Fla. Stat. 125.572 will preempt the city from prohibiting compliant synthetic turf on single-family lots of 1 acre or less once FDEP finalizes its rule — NOT final as of 2026-09-07 (workshop Aug 2025, proposed rules Jan 2026, still subject to change), so the city's existing rules still govern today. For the gated/HOA pockets, Fla. Stat. 720.3045 bars an association from restricting artificial turf not visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel, adjacent common area, or a community golf course.
facts.water_and_rules: The Anastasia Sanitary District is the special district providing water and wastewater on Anastasia Island — its area starts at the St. Augustine city limits at the ocean and runs south to the county line, west to the Matanzas River and back north. St. Johns County Utility also operates in parts of the island. Whoever bills you, the SJRWMD rules are the same. AS OF 2026-09-07: Phase III Extreme Water Shortage, effective May 11, 2026 — ONE watering day per week, odd addresses Saturday, even addresses Sunday, non-residential Tuesday, no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m., max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone. Normal (non-shortage) schedule is twice a week: odd Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, non-residential Tue/Fri, no watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m. New sod gets a step-down grace window (daily 15 days, 3x/week 30 days, 2x/week 15 days). Reclaimed water is exempt from the one-day rule. No artificial turf rebate identified — do not claim one.
facts.soil_and_yard: Barrier-island sand sitting directly on the Anastasia Formation coquina — variably lithified shell rock that in places is shallow enough to matter during excavation. Seasonal high water table 0–1 ft in wet periods; slopes under 2%; essentially flat. The specific killers here are salt aerosol blowing off the Atlantic, wind-driven sand burying the crown of the grass, and full unshaded sun. Irrigation water drains straight through beach sand, so a sod lawn here needs the most water in the county and returns the worst result. Flood insurance in high-risk zones runs well over $1,000/year and homeowners insurance commonly starts around $3,000/year — households here are already paying a premium just to be here.
facts.housing_stock: 2.17 sq mi total (2.12 sq mi land), bounded by the Atlantic on the east, State Road A1A on the west, and Pope Road on the north. 4,553 housing units: ~49.9% detached single-family, 3.4% attached (duplex/townhouse), the rest multifamily, 0.9% mobile. Median construction year 1987 — a late-20th-century beach town, NOT new build and NOT historic. Development waves: most of the build-out in the second half of the 20th century, then 21.8% of homes added 2000–2009, only 5.4% 2010–2019, and 0.5% since. Zoning: Low Density Residential min lot 7,500 sq ft, max 4 units/acre, min floor area 1,400 sq ft one-story; setbacks 25 ft front / 10 ft side / 20 ft rear — but the older platted 50 ft x 93 ft lots get 20 / 7.5 / 20, which leaves a back yard on the order of 35 x 25 ft. Medium Density Residential runs duplex (75 ft frontage, 12,444 sq ft) up to four-plex (122.5 ft, 24,888 sq ft). So there are two distinct job types: the narrow 50-footer with a small usable rear yard, and the 7,500+ sq ft lot with a real back yard. HOA prevalence is mixed — much of the older grid is unassociated, but the gated and association-governed pockets are significant: Sea Colony (the city's only private gated oceanfront neighborhood), Marsh Creek, Anastasia Dunes, Island Hammock, Ocean Palms, Seagate, Ocean Walk, Ocean Woods, Sea Grove, Commodores Club.
facts.who_lives_there: 6,803 at the 2020 census (up 10.2% from 6,176 in 2010; it was 396 people in 1960). Roughly 6,860 currently. Median age 53.4–55.7. 29.9–30.3% are 65 or older. Median household income $100,802 (2024) — the HIGHEST of the five places in this batch and materially above St. Augustine city ($78,151), the Shores ($73,688) and St. Augustine South ($75,996). 88.6–90.5% White, 4.6–5.5% Hispanic. Retirees, second-home owners, and a very heavy short-term/vacation rental layer. Former U.S. National Security Advisor Mike Waltz is a resident.
facts.golf: Marsh Creek Country Club — the ONLY golf course on Anastasia Island and the course closest to the beach. Private. 18 holes, par 72, ~6,883–6,888 yards, designed by Mark McCumber, six sets of tees, oak trees and marsh views, 10 Har-Tru tennis courts, two dining venues over the marsh. 169 Marshside Dr, St. Augustine FL 32080. Every other course requires crossing a bridge: St. Augustine Shores Golf Club, Royal St. Augustine, St. Johns G&CC, World Golf Village's King & Bear and Slammer & Squire.
facts.commercial_targets: St. Johns County Parks (Pier Park pavilion surrounds, splash-pad perimeter, event/market area); beachfront and near-beach condo and HOA common areas and pool decks — Sea Colony, Ocean Walk, Ocean Woods, Sea Grove, Anastasia Dunes, Island Hammock, Ocean Palms, Seagate, Commodores Club; Marsh Creek Country Club practice green, short-game area and tennis surrounds; hotel and resort pool decks and rooftop bars along A1A Beach Blvd; R.B. Hunt Elementary and Sebastian Middle School; the vacation-rental management companies that run the city's large short-term rental inventory; pet-friendly rentals (pet turf as an amenity upsell); the Anastasia Island Branch Library grounds.
facts.landmarks: St. Johns County Ocean Pier Park, 350 A1A Beach Blvd — splash pad, covered pavilion, volleyball courts, free beach access and parking, gift shop, visitor information center; the Wednesday Pier Farmers Market; 'Music & Art by the Sea' free concerts Wednesdays 7–9 p.m.; New Year's fireworks; the Santa Suits 5K. NOTE for accuracy: the fishing pier itself has been CLOSED for construction repairs since May 13, expected to run through November 2026, though the splash park and beach access stay open. Also: Anastasia State Park (1,600 acres); the St. Augustine Lighthouse; the St. Augustine Alligator Farm; the Anastasia Island Branch Library; City Hall at 2200 A1A South; Mayor Beth Sweeny's 'Mondays with the Mayor' local-business series.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE GROUND AND THE JURISDICTIONAL MAZE — the island install nobody else specs correctly. Two things are true here and nowhere else in the service area. First, the ground: this is the type locality of the Anastasia Formation, so you are excavating sand over coquina shell rock at unpredictable depth, with the water table inches down, with salt aerosol above and periodic tidal saltwater below. That means the base is a design decision, not a default — and it is a legitimate reason to charge $10–12/sq ft instead of $7. Second, the paperwork: an 'Anastasia Island' address can be governed by the City of St. Augustine (HARB and a Certificate of Appropriateness), the City of St. Augustine Beach (a 0.40 impervious cap plus a Tree Removal Permit), or St. Johns County (neither) — depending literally on which side of a street it sits. The page should be the resource that sorts out which rules apply to your address, then quotes the right base build for coquina. That is a genuinely different lead from the St. Augustine city page (courtyards) and the St. Augustine Beach page (absentee owners and money), even though the island contains both. Secondary lead: Marsh Creek is the only course on 14 miles of island, so backyard putting greens have no local substitute.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Three regulatory regimes on one island — this is the island's defining complication and the page's best service angle. (A) City of St. Augustine governs Davis Shores and Lighthouse Park: Certificate of Appropriateness through HARB for the HP districts, city tree rules, RS-1/RS-2 lot standards. (B) City of St. Augustine Beach governs the incorporated beach: impervious surface ratio 0.40 low density / 0.50 medium / 0.70 high and commercial, with only a 465 sq ft pool-and-decking allowance; mandatory Tree Removal Permit; adopted Urban Forestry Standards and Specifications Manual. (C) St. Johns County land development code governs Butler Beach, Crescent Beach and the unincorporated remainder — no municipal architectural review, no city impervious cap. On top of that, private deed restrictions at Marsh Creek and Sea Colony. Statewide: Fla. Stat. 125.572 (ch. 2025-140) will preempt local prohibition of compliant turf on single-family lots of 1 acre or less once FDEP adopts its rule — NOT final as of 2026-09-07. Fla. Stat. 720.3045 already bars an HOA from restricting artificial turf not visible from the frontage, an adjacent parcel, adjacent common area, or a community golf course.
facts.water_and_rules: Three providers depending on where you stand: the City of St. Augustine Utilities serves the in-city portion (Davis Shores, Lighthouse Park); the Anastasia Sanitary District — a special district established 1951 — serves from the city limits at the ocean south to the county line, ocean to Matanzas River; St. Johns County Utility Department covers other pockets. All are under the same SJRWMD order. AS OF 2026-09-07: Phase III Extreme Water Shortage, effective May 11, 2026 — ONE day per week, odd addresses Saturday, even Sunday, non-residential Tuesday, none 8 a.m.–6 p.m., max 3/4 inch and one hour per zone. Normal schedule twice weekly (odd Wed/Sat, even Thu/Sun, non-res Tue/Fri, no watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m. in the city). Reclaimed water exempt from the one-day rule. No turf rebate exists.
facts.soil_and_yard: This is the island the geology is named after. Beneath the sand lies the Anastasia Formation — a variably lithified coquina of shell and sand, quarried here by the Spanish and British to build the Castillo de San Marcos, with the old quarries still visible in Anastasia State Park. Practical consequence: excavation depth is not predictable — you can hit shell rock shallow. Above it, fine sand with a seasonal high water table of 0–1 ft in wet periods and slopes under 2%. Layer on salt aerosol off the Atlantic, blowing sand, and elevation: parts of Davis Shores were built at 6-foot elevation and flooded in Hurricanes Matthew and Irma, while Lighthouse Park sits higher and is largely out of the flood zone. The city side experiences sunny-day/king-tide flooding 12–16 times a year with roughly 21 stormwater outfalls draining Davis Shores to the Matanzas River and Salt Run. The island has three access points and bridges may close when winds exceed 40 mph.
facts.housing_stock: A 14-mile barrier island averaging about 1 mile wide, running south from the St. Augustine inlet to Matanzas Inlet. Treat it as a market area, not a jurisdiction — it contains at least five distinct housing products. (1) DAVIS SHORES: developed from the 1930s by D.P. Davis (the Tampa developer who vanished at sea in 1926), inside St. Augustine city limits, split north/south by Anastasia Boulevard — cottages, mid-century modern, Spanish style and newer infill on large lots with winding streets; homes from the high $200s up; Inlet Drive in North Davis Shores is the waterfront-glimpse street. (2) LIGHTHOUSE PARK: older, quainter, some cottages fronting Salt Run, higher elevation, walkable to town, mid-$300s up, also inside city limits. (3) CITY OF ST. AUGUSTINE BEACH: 1970s–90s beach-town grid, median build year 1987, 7,500 sq ft low-density minimum plus older 50x93 ft lots. (4) UNINCORPORATED ST. JOHNS COUNTY: Butler Beach, Crescent Beach, Coquina Gables, Treasure Beach (canal-front). (5) GATED/HOA COMMUNITIES: Marsh Creek across 800+ acres, Sea Colony (the only private gated oceanfront neighborhood), Anastasia Dunes, Island Hammock, Ocean Palms, Seagate, Ocean Walk, Ocean Woods, Sea Grove, Commodores Club. HOA prevalence therefore ranges from zero (Davis Shores, Lighthouse Park, most of Butler Beach) to strict (Marsh Creek, Sea Colony).
facts.who_lives_there: No single census figure covers the island. The best proxies: St. Augustine Beach 6,803 residents, median age 53.4, ~30% over 65, median household income $100,802; the in-city Davis Shores / Lighthouse Park portion falls under St. Augustine's $78,151 median and 49.9 median age. Practically: a blend of affluent retirees and second-home owners at the north and in the gated communities, year-round working households in Davis Shores and Butler Beach, and a very large seasonal and short-term-rental population everywhere. Cost of ownership defines the mindset — flood insurance in high-risk zones runs well over $1,000/year and homeowners insurance commonly starts around $3,000/year.
facts.golf: Marsh Creek Country Club is the ONLY golf course on the entire 14-mile island, and the closest course to the beach in the region. Private. Mark McCumber design, 18 holes, par 72, ~6,883–6,888 yards, six tee sets, oaks and marsh, 10 Har-Tru tennis courts, 169 Marshside Dr, 32080. Everything else requires crossing the Bridge of Lions or the SR 312 bridge — St. Augustine Shores Golf Club, Royal St. Augustine, St. Johns Golf & Country Club, World Golf Village. That scarcity is the whole island golf story and it makes backyard putting greens a genuinely strong sell here.
facts.commercial_targets: Marsh Creek Country Club (practice green, short game, tennis court surrounds); Sea Colony and the gated HOA common areas, entry features and pool decks; St. Johns County Parks at Ocean Pier Park and Frank Butler Park; the St. Augustine Amphitheatre lawn and VIP areas; Anastasia State Park campground and concession areas; the St. Augustine Alligator Farm (exhibit landscaping and animal-safe surfacing); R.B. Hunt Elementary; the Anastasia Island Branch Library; the very large pet-friendly vacation rental inventory along A1A South (pet turf); kayak, surf and paddleboard outfitters; beachfront hotel and condo pool decks.
facts.landmarks: St. Augustine Lighthouse & Maritime Museum (current 1874 tower, replacing an earlier coquina structure); Anastasia State Park (1,600 acres) and the historic coquina quarries; the St. Augustine Alligator Farm Zoological Park; the St. Augustine Amphitheatre; Fort Matanzas National Monument (built 1740–42) at the south end; the Bridge of Lions; Salt Run; Anastasia Boulevard; Sea Colony; Inlet Drive in North Davis Shores.

facts.strongest_angle: Lead the Jacksonville Beach page as a GOLF page. It is the only one of the five with a city-owned 18-hole course inside the city limits — Jacksonville Beach Golf Club, expanded and renovated by the city from January 2018 — and it also has the highest concentration of high-income households in the batch ($115,825 median). The story writes itself: you already play a municipal 18 four minutes from your driveway; the part of your game that actually costs you strokes is the part you can build in your own backyard. Put the backyard putting green above the fold, price it as a golf product rather than a landscaping product, and use the Ponte Vedra / Marsh Landing / Atlantic Beach Country Club names as the aspirational frame without claiming them. Then run a clear second section that no other town in this batch needs: a job-type menu, because Jax Beach is the volume town with four genuinely different yards — the tight 1920s Pablo Beach cottage backyard, the shaded mid-century ranch lot west of 3rd, the Isle of Palms canal lot ending at a seawall, and the gated Sanctuary yard that needs HOA architectural approval. That combination — municipal golf plus four distinct job types at scale — is what Neptune Beach next door cannot run: same money, a quarter of the land, no course, and one yard type.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Jacksonville Beach kept municipal independence through the 1968 Duval consolidation, so its own Land Development Code and its own building department govern — NOT the City of Jacksonville's ordinance code — even though residents still vote in Jacksonville mayoral elections. Be honest on the page: I could not confirm a Jacksonville Beach synthetic-turf provision or a specific residential impervious/lot-coverage percentage from public sources. The LDC's Article VI (Zoning Districts) and Article VII (Site Development Standards) are where lot coverage, setbacks and landscape requirements live, and those should be verified with the city's planning department before the page makes any compliance claim. Private governance is the more predictable gate: The Sanctuary and similar gated communities run architectural review that will approve or reject turf on aesthetic grounds regardless of city code.
facts.water_and_rules: The City of Jacksonville Beach runs its own water utility — it is NOT a JEA customer, and the page must not say JEA. Live discrepancy to resolve before publishing: the city's own watering page posts a 'Modified Phase II Severe Water Shortage' effective March 2, 2026, while SJRWMD escalated the region to Phase III Extreme Water Shortage in mid-May 2026. Both land in the same place operationally: irrigation ONE day per week, odd-numbered addresses Saturday, even Sunday, non-residential Tuesday, maximum 3/4 inch and one hour per zone, and no daytime watering (the city page says no watering 10 a.m.–4 p.m.; the District says 8 a.m.–6 p.m. — cite the District's window, it's stricter and current). Applies to private wells and pumps as well as utility water. Phase III also tightened irrigation allowances for new plantings including sod. No turf rebate identified — do not claim one. FS 125.572 (Ch. 2025-140) preempts inconsistent local synthetic-turf rules once FDEP adopts standards.
facts.soil_and_yard: San Pablo Island barrier sand, with about 52.44 inches of rain a year. The beach blocks drain fast and burn in salt wind. The interior grid and the Isle of Palms canal fringe sit low, close to a high water table and under tidal influence, so those yards hold water and stay soggy — a drainage-first install, not a decorative one. Live oaks and cabbage palms shade the older streets west of 3rd, thinning St. Augustine grass under canopy. (Soil character inferred from the confirmed barrier-island geography and rainfall figure rather than a survey.)
facts.housing_stock: The widest range of housing in this batch, and the page has to reflect that rather than pick one hero job. Four distinct products: (1) the original Pablo Beach grid near the boardwalk and pier — small 1920s–1950s cottages and bungalows on tight beach-block lots, many now scraped and rebuilt tall, with minimal backyards; (2) mid-century ranch neighborhoods west of 3rd Street on more generous lots with mature canopy; (3) Isle of Palms, platted from 1960 — roughly 500 homes on a man-made canal system off the Intracoastal, one of very few canal communities anywhere in Jacksonville, most with private docks and marsh frontage, so the yard runs to a seawall or bulkhead; (4) The Sanctuary, from 1990 — gated, 218 homes from 1,583 to 4,353 sq ft with community pool, tennis courts and nature trails, and an active HOA with architectural review. 2020 population 23,830 on just 7.316 sq mi of land — the largest and densest of the beaches. Median sold price $643,700 in May 2025 at ~$393/sq ft, rising to roughly $686K over the three months to June 2026; homes average 2 offers and about 70 days on market.
facts.who_lives_there: Median household income $115,825 (2023 ACS) — high, and the largest high-income population of the five by a wide margin. 86.7% White. Incorporated as Pablo Beach in 1907, renamed Jacksonville Beach in 1925. A young-professional and family renter base clusters near downtown Jax Beach and the boardwalk; established owners hold the ground west of A1A, the Intracoastal canal lots and the gated communities. This is the volume market of the batch — the town where the same page can support a $4,000 cottage backyard and a $40,000 canal-front install.
facts.golf: Jacksonville Beach Golf Club (locally 'Jax Beach Golf Club') — PUBLIC/MUNICIPAL, owned by the City of Jacksonville Beach, which purchased the club and expanded it to 18 holes, then ran an extensive renovation beginning January 2018. This is the only city-owned golf course inside any of the five towns in this batch, and it is the single most exploitable fact on the page. Adjacent named private and resort courses for the aspirational frame: Atlantic Beach Country Club just north; Marsh Landing Country Club, and the Ocean and Lagoon courses at Ponte Vedra Inn & Club to the south; Jacksonville Golf & Country Club and Windsor Parke inland. Roughly 40 courses sit within 20 miles of Jacksonville Beach (about 13 public, 3 municipal, 23 private).
facts.commercial_targets: Jacksonville Beach Golf Club — city-owned, so there is a municipal procurement path, and practice-green / short-game / chipping-area work is a natural fit for a course that already renovated in 2018. Beaches Museum & History Park grounds at 381 Beach Boulevard. Boardwalk-district bars, restaurants and rooftop/patio venues where outdoor square footage is revenue-generating and sod never survives foot traffic. Oceanfront hotels. The Sanctuary HOA common areas (pool surround, tennis area, entry). Isle of Palms dock-side and seawall yards. Short-term-rental management companies. Daycares and pet businesses along Beach Boulevard and 3rd Street. Also worth noting for cross-selling: Jack Russell Park's athletic fields are in Atlantic Beach, not Jax Beach — do not mis-attribute it.
facts.landmarks: Jacksonville Beach Pier (rebuilt following hurricane damage). The boardwalk entertainment district, running since about 1915–16 under Martin Williams Sr. Beaches Museum & History Park at 381 Beach Boulevard — regional history with a restored 1911 train engine, an 1873 cabin and an 1886 chapel. The lifeguard corps lineage — established 1912, current station structure from 1948. The 1922 historical marker for Lt. James H. Doolittle's transcontinental speed-record flight launched from Pablo Beach. The San Pablo River, which divides the island from the mainland and gave Pablo Beach its 1886 name. Kathryn Abbey Hanna Park (447 acres) sits just north at Atlantic Beach's tip and is the shared regional landmark.

facts.strongest_angle: THE SMALL FENCED HOA BACKYARD PLUS THE APARTMENT DOG PARK — a two-headed page, and neither head exists anywhere else in this batch. Residential lead: 'Your backyard is thirty feet deep, your dog has killed the sod, the back fence ponds after every storm, and your HOA wants a form.' Answer all four in the fold: pet-rated turf with a drainage base, a fix for the settled fill pad, and — the differentiator competitors will not offer — 'we prepare and submit your ARC package for you.' Commercial lead: Bartram Park has more brand-new large apartment communities per square mile than anywhere on the client's map, and multifamily dog parks and courtyards are the single most repeatable, spec-driven synthetic turf line of business in Northeast Florida. Get on the property-management approved-vendor lists. This lead is the exact inverse of Julington Creek two miles west (big unregulated acreage), of Baymeadows to the north (mature golf-community credibility and 1980s condo common areas), and of Riverside (century-old shade and drainage craftsmanship).
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: This is the most rule-bound place in the batch and the page must be built around that. Governance is typically stacked three deep: a Community Development District (Bartram Springs CDD has its own Board of Supervisors plus District Management, Operations and Amenity Management arms), a Master HOA (Bartram Springs' master HOA is administered by Trinity Property Services Group), and often a sub-association for a specific pod of townhomes. Practical effect: any exterior change including synthetic turf normally requires an architectural review submittal, and because artificial turf is not protected under Florida's Florida-Friendly Landscaping statutes, a refusal is enforceable. Duval is a consolidated city-county so City of Jacksonville code applies directly with no separate municipality — but I could NOT verify whether COJ Chapter 656 addresses artificial turf specifically (Municode returned 403 on every attempt). Have the client confirm with COJ Planning & Development before publishing any permit claim.
facts.water_and_rules: JEA water and sewer. St. Johns River Water Management District irrigation rule applies: Daylight Saving Time, up to two days per week — odd addresses Wednesday and Saturday, even addresses Thursday and Sunday, nonresidential Tuesday and Friday — before 10 a.m. or after 4 p.m. only. Reclaimed water exempt unless locally restricted. I could not verify the Eastern Standard Time winter schedule or JEA's own page (CAPTCHA-gated); confirm before publishing. No artificial-turf rebate found. Critically for this page: Florida Statute 373.185(3)(b) and 720.3075 protect Florida-Friendly Landscaping from local and HOA prohibition, but artificial turf falls OUTSIDE the statutory definition of Florida-Friendly Landscaping. That means Bartram Park HOAs and ARCs can lawfully restrict or refuse synthetic turf — so the honest, valuable service offer on this page is 'we prepare and submit your ARC package,' not 'state law is on your side.'
facts.soil_and_yard: Flatwoods sand over a shallow seasonal water table on fill-pad construction — the standard northeast Florida new-build profile. Bartram Springs alone dedicates 471 of its 1,025 acres to wetlands and open space, which means an unusually high share of lots back directly onto a stormwater pond or preserve edge. Consequences the homeowner already knows: the back fence line ponds after every storm, the fill pad has settled since closing, and the swale between houses never dries. Jacksonville takes roughly 52 inches of rain a year, concentrated May–September in short violent downpours, on ground about 3 ft above sea level with sand-and-clay rather than limestone soils. Add small-yard dog traffic and urine burn and a young St. Augustine lawn simply cannot hold. Shade is less of a factor than in Riverside or Julington Creek — these are new lots with immature trees — but fence-line and house-shadow strips still fail.
facts.housing_stock: Checked 2026-09-07. The Bartram Park corridor runs along Bartram Park Blvd and Old St. Augustine Road between I-95 and Philips Highway, at the extreme southern edge of Duval County against the St. Johns line, zip 32258. Built out almost entirely 2000s–2020s — this is the newest housing stock in the batch and the most apartment-and-townhome-dense new suburb in Jacksonville. Three distinct product types: (1) CDD master-planned single family, exemplified by Bartram Springs — 1,025 acres, roughly 1,700 residences, 471 acres of wetlands and open space, 20 acres of parks and recreation, with a Junior Olympic pool, athletic fields, tennis and volleyball courts and a picnic gazebo with dock access; (2) large institutional apartment communities, e.g. Avana Bartram Springs at 14951 Walden Springs Way — 15 buildings on 23.7 acres, sold for $39.65 million in July 2026; (3) townhomes and small-lot detached on roughly 40–60 ft wide lots. Backyards are typically 20–40 ft deep, fully vinyl-fenced, with a dead shade strip along the fence line where sod never establishes. New-build, not historic.
facts.who_lives_there: ZIP 32258 (Census Reporter / ACS): population 40,408; median household income $102,204; median home value $370,700; median age 36.2; 47% bachelor's or higher; 11.6% veterans. Bartram Park itself skews younger and more renter-heavy than the ZIP aggregate — this is relocation country: dual-income young professionals and young families drawn by St. Johns County school proximity, the Baptist South employment base and I-95 access to both downtown Jacksonville and St. Augustine. High household income, high mortgage, small yard, one or two dogs, and very little free weekend time. That last point is the whole sales thesis.
facts.golf: No golf course inside Bartram Park, and the page should say so rather than imply adjacency. The neighborhood sits between the St. Johns County courses (Julington Creek Golf Club, Cimarrone Golf Club, St. Johns Golf & Country Club) and the Duval clubs to the north (Deerwood Country Club at 10239 Golf Club Drive 32256, mid-Erik-Larsen-redesign with a new par-3 short course opening mid-2026; Deercreek Country Club, gated, 700+ homes). The correct golf offer here is a SMALL backyard putting green engineered to fit a 30x40 ft yard — two or three cups, a short fringe, no approach length. That is a genuinely different product from the Julington Creek acreage green and should be photographed and priced as such.
facts.commercial_targets: This is the batch's best MULTIFAMILY market and that should drive the commercial half of the page. Named and near-named targets: Avana Bartram Springs (15 buildings, 23.7 acres, 14951 Walden Springs Way) and the cluster of peer Class-A apartment communities along Bartram Park Blvd — every one has or wants a dog park, a courtyard, and a pool deck, and synthetic turf is the standard specification for all three. Baptist Medical Center South courtyards and healing-garden areas. Bartram Springs CDD amenity center — athletic fields, playground surrounds, volleyball. Daycares and preschools along Old St. Augustine Road. Veterinary clinics, groomers and pet resorts on the corridor. Bartram Village and Bartram Market tenant patios.
facts.landmarks: Baptist Medical Center South, 14550 Old St. Augustine Road, Jacksonville FL 32258 — opened February 2005, includes a Wolfson Children's ER, labor and delivery with NICU, heart and vascular, orthopedics; ranked by U.S. News among the top 5% of Florida hospitals. Bartram Park Publix and the Bartram Village retail district (Lucky Goat Coffee Co. was permitted there in April 2026). Bartram Market shopping center just over the line in St. Johns County, where a Chick-fil-A on 2.38 acres was permitted in April 2026 at a $2.5 million valuation. The I-95 / Old St. Augustine Road interchange. Race Track Road. The Bartram Springs amenity center. Note for accuracy: The Bolles School's 'Bartram Campus' at 2264 Bartram Road is in 32207 (San Marco / St. Nicholas), NOT Bartram Park — do not conflate them on the page.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH WATER — the lagoon, the lock, the dock, the bulkhead. Queen's Harbour is not 'a Jacksonville golf community'; it is the only community in northeast Florida where you keep a boat in a private FRESHWATER lagoon behind a lock and a gate. The page should open on the lagoon-front lot: turf that runs cleanly to a bulkhead, drains without scouring, survives salt-air and dock traffic, and — the argument that only works here — stops fertiliser and irrigation runoff from entering the lagoon your neighbours fish and swim in. That is an environmental-neighbourliness pitch, and it is genuine. Glen Kernan next door sells golf performance and Pablo Creek sells physician-grade low maintenance; Queen's Harbour sells SHORELINE COMPETENCE. Second beat: the § 720.3045 golf-course-and-common-area carve-out, framed as 'we handle your POA architectural review' — because on a lagoon or fairway lot the statute does not save the homeowner and they need someone who has been through the ARB before. Third beat: a lagoon-view putting green on a McCumber-course address.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Consolidated City of Jacksonville code applies — no separate municipality. § 125.572, Fla. Stat. (from CS/CS/CS/HB 683, Ch. 2025-140, effective 2025-07-01) preempts local prohibition of DEP-compliant synthetic turf on single-family lots of one acre or less; DEP rulemaking was still pending at the check date. § 720.3045, Fla. Stat. protects turf NOT visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel, an adjacent common area, OR A COMMUNITY GOLF COURSE — which means the statutory protection is thinner here than a homeowner assumes: a fairway-facing or lagoon-facing rear yard visible from common area or from the McCumber course still falls under the association's architectural standards. That is the single most useful, checkable, differentiating thing to put on this page. Bulkhead work and anything touching the shoreline may also trigger separate review. HONEST GAP: the Queen's Harbour POA architectural guidelines are not published publicly — I could not retrieve a turf-specific ARB standard. Advise the client to get the ARB packet from the POA office (904-221-8859) and build the page around 'we submit your ARB application for you'.
facts.water_and_rules: JEA service, and the community is inside the same SJRWMD Phase III Extreme Water Shortage as the rest of Duval as of 2026-09-07: one irrigation day per week, no irrigation 8 a.m.–6 p.m., ¾ inch per zone maximum, one hour per zone maximum. Odd addresses Saturday, even addresses Sunday, non-residential (which includes the club and POA common areas) Tuesday. Phase II in April 2026 explicitly swept in JEA reuse and reclaimed customers, so a homeowner on reclaimed water has no workaround. The site-specific twist that makes this page different: the community's identity is a 120-acre FRESHWATER lagoon that homeowners boat and fish in. Fertiliser and irrigation runoff from lagoon-front lawns goes straight into that lagoon. A turf lawn on a bulkhead lot eliminates the fertiliser input entirely — that is a neighbour-facing, community-benefit argument no other page in this batch can make. HONEST GAP: no artificial-turf rebate exists from JEA or SJRWMD; do not claim one.
facts.soil_and_yard: Duval's dominant poorly-drained acidic Pomona sand with a seasonally high water table, plus the specific hazards of a community with water on three sides: brackish and salt influence at the Intracoastal and Greenfield Creek margins, near-zero natural grade, tidal marsh edges, and shoreline/bulkhead transitions where a lawn meets a seawall or dock apron. Mature oak and palm canopy across the interior — the club's own marketing describes homes 'among oak and palm trees' — so shade-killed St. Augustine is a common condition. Lagoon-front installs need a base and drainage design that will not scour, settle at the bulkhead, or wash fines into the water; that engineering competence, demonstrated in photos, is what justifies $10–12/sq ft here.
facts.housing_stock: Roughly 925 residences (marketing figures range 925–1,017; one neighbourhood guide says ~350, which appears to count only a section — flag the discrepancy, do not publish a single hard number) on over 1,000 acres, bounded by water on three sides: the St. Johns River, Greenfield Creek and the Intracoastal Waterway. Development start is reported as both 1990 and 1997 depending on source, so the dominant era is safely stated as 'mid-1990s through 2010s custom and semi-custom'. Product mix: townhomes, single-family, custom estates and remaining vacant homesites for ground-up builds. Lot sizes are quoted across a very wide band (roughly 1,834 sq ft footprint-scale lots up to 12,000+ sq ft), meaning small townhome courtyards and half-acre-plus lagoon estates sit in the same gate. The turf-relevant split is three ways: (a) LAGOON-FRONT lots, many with private docks, where the yard runs to a bulkhead — the premium job; (b) GOLF-FRONT lots on the McCumber course; (c) interior preserve lots under oak and palm. Homes range from roughly the $600Ks to $4M; current listings quoted $874,000–$2.9M. POA/association fees apply; NO CDD. Named streets a local will recognise: Charter Court, Shipwatch Drive, Admirals Bend Drive, Barony Drive. Club address: 1131 Queens Harbor Blvd.
facts.who_lives_there: Boaters first — that is the organising principle of the community and the thing residents self-identify by. The 120-acre freshwater lagoon reaches the Intracoastal through a navigational lock, and dock-owning homeowners keep vessels in fresh water behind a gate, which is the community's unique selling point regionally. Population skews established-affluent rather than young-professional: ZIP 32225 median household income $90,559 with 44.5% bachelor's or higher, but Queen's Harbour sits far above its ZIP average given a $874K–$4M listing band. Expect physicians (Mayo Clinic is a short drive south), business owners, senior Navy and retired military given Mayport proximity, and second-home boaters. No community-level income data is published; do not invent one.
facts.golf: Queen's Harbour Golf & Country Club — 18 holes, par 72, designed by MARK McCUMBER, bordered by the Intracoastal and tidal marshland; operated within the Invited (formerly ClubCorp) network, so members get reciprocal access to 300+ clubs. Marketing cites past hosting of a PGA Tour Qualifier and the Mercedes Collegiate Championships. Also on site: a 65-slip marina in the freshwater lagoon, junior-Olympic pool, tennis and pickleball, basketball court, fitness centre, low-country clubhouse. Adjacent golf within a short drive: Glen Kernan Club, Jacksonville Golf & Country Club, Windsor Parke Golf Club, and the Atlantic Beach/Ponte Vedra clubs.
facts.commercial_targets: POA-owned common areas are the cluster: the playground, pavilion, multipurpose room, basketball court, tennis and pickleball courts, and the junior-Olympic pool deck surround. The country club's practice area and tee surrounds. Marina and dock aprons — high-traffic, constantly wet, salt-exposed, and a natural turf application. Outside the gate but in the same catchment: Neptune Beach Elementary, Landmark Middle and Sandalwood High athletic fields; Mayo Clinic Florida on San Pablo Rd; and the boat/marine services businesses along the Intracoastal that would benefit from durable showroom-grade surfacing. Note the POA is a non-residential water customer restricted to Tuesday irrigation under Phase III — its own common areas are a live turf prospect for the same reason its residents are.
facts.landmarks: The LOCK — a navigational lock connecting a 120-acre freshwater lagoon to the Intracoastal Waterway, with 8+ feet average depth in the basin. The 65-slip marina. The low-country-style clubhouse at 1131 Queens Harbor Blvd. Greenfield Creek and the St. Johns River as the northern and western boundaries. Streets: Charter Court, Shipwatch Drive, Admirals Bend Drive, Barony Drive. Roughly 10 miles from downtown Jacksonville, about 7 minutes to Atlantic Beach Town Center. Assigned schools reported as Neptune Beach Elementary, Landmark Middle, Sandalwood High.

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH ACREAGE, MUD AND INDEPENDENCE — THE ANTI-HOA PAGE. Baldwin is the only place in Duval County that still has its own town hall, its own water plant and its own ordinance book, because it kept independent government through the 1968 consolidation. Out here nobody has to file an architectural review application, and the constraint isn't a board — it's your septic tank and your well. The page should NOT sell a manicured putting green to a $47,500-median household inside the two-square-mile town. It should target the 32234 acreage owner, where the median household income is $87,331 and the poverty rate is 3.9%: fenced dog yards that stop being mud pits, horse-property high-traffic zones, a shaded oak-canopy patch where grass has never grown, and a private chipping green on a five-acre parcel with no course within twenty minutes. Two technical hooks give the page credibility no competitor will have: (1) the state preemption stops at one acre, so on most Baldwin parcels the town's own code still applies and you know it; (2) DEP Rule 62-308.100 requires the install to preserve septic-tank pumpout access, which is exactly the mistake a Jacksonville installer will make out here. Deliberately the mirror image of Fleming Island's HOA-approval page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Baldwin maintains its own Code of Ordinances (Municode, codified through Ordinance No. 2025-03, enacted 16 September 2025), including Chapter 22 zoning, land use and landscaping. Since 19 May 2026 the town cannot prohibit compliant synthetic turf on a single-family residential lot of 1 acre or less, or regulate it inconsistently with DEP Rule 62-308.100 (s. 125.572, F.S.). BUT here is the Baldwin-specific catch nobody else's page has: a great many properties in and around Baldwin exceed one acre, and the preemption does not reach them — on those lots the town's own code (or, outside town limits, Jacksonville's) still governs in full. Second Baldwin-specific point: Rule 62-308.100(9)(c) requires that any installation "must provide for access to the septic tank for routine pumpout," which is a live design constraint on the septic-served majority out here. HOAs are effectively a non-issue in Baldwin — a genuine selling point versus Fleming Island.
facts.water_and_rules: Unusual and worth saying out loud: Baldwin runs its OWN water and wastewater treatment plants (Water Plant Manager Eddie Smith, Wastewater Plant Manager CJ Hunt, Town Foreman Roger Smith) and publishes its own Annual Drinking Water Report — one of the only places in Duval County not served by JEA, a legacy of retaining independent government through the 1968 consolidation. The town posts the SJRWMD schedule directly: odd-numbered homes Saturday, even-numbered Sunday, non-residential Tuesday, none between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. (as posted April 2026 — note SJRWMD's Phase III Extreme Water Shortage order sets the prohibited window at 8 a.m.–6 p.m. and one day per week, so verify which is being enforced before quoting). Outside town limits most 32234 properties draw from private wells and discharge to septic — no utility bill, so 'save on your water bill' is a weak pitch out there; 'stop fighting the mud and the mower' is the strong one. No rebate of any kind for artificial turf.
facts.soil_and_yard: Pine flatwoods and hardwood uplands. Leon-series-type fine sands — USDA classes Leon as poorly to very poorly drained with a spodic hardpan within 30 inches and a water table at 6–18 inches for months of the year. The Jacksonville–Baldwin Rail Trail corridor is described as running through "hardwood uplands, wetlands and pine flatwoods" with dense canopy. Practically: big flat lots that hold water through the wet season and go to loose dry sand in spring; live oaks around the older town core; Brandy Branch and the Trail Ridge sand country to the west. Horse paddocks, dog yards and equipment areas churn to mud — that is the real problem to solve here, not lawn aesthetics.
facts.housing_stock: Small, modest and old — and the town and the ZIP are two completely different markets, which is the single most useful fact on this page. TOWN: 2.02 square miles, 1,396 residents at the 2020 census (1,298 in 2024 per DataUSA), 588 households, median property value $180,700, homeownership 57.9%, poverty 16.3%. Stock is mostly mid-century frame and concrete-block houses, older cottages near the depot, and manufactured homes, on deep, generous lots with almost no HOAs. ZIP 32234 wraps 152.1 square miles of rural west Duval around that 2-square-mile town and reads as a different place entirely: 9,678 residents at 63.6 people per square mile, median household income $87,331, median home value $262,800, poverty just 3.9% (Census Reporter ACS). That outer ring is small farms, horse property, hunting land and 2-to-20-acre homesteads with real disposable income. A meaningful share of properties outside town limits are on private wells and septic. Median age 41.3 in town, 32.8 across the ZIP; average commute 27.3 minutes in town, 35.1 across the ZIP — this is a place people drive out of.
facts.who_lives_there: In town: working households — retail trade, food services and healthcare are the largest employment sectors — with a 16.3% poverty rate and a median household income of $47,500 (DataUSA 2024, down 15% year on year). 2020 census racial composition 67.19% White, 22.06% Black, 4.87% multiracial, 4.58% Hispanic; 24.5% under 18, 19.8% aged 65+. Across ZIP 32234: 13.3% veterans (more than double the US rate), 91.5% high-school attainment but only 20% with bachelor's degrees, and the long commutes of people who chose land over convenience. Practical read for a turf business: the town core is not the customer; the acreage owners in the surrounding ZIP are.
facts.golf: None. There is no golf course in Baldwin and none adjacent — genuinely nothing. The nearest options are on Jacksonville's Westside or up in Nassau County. Do not build a golf page here; a chipping/putting green sold to an acreage owner as a private practice amenity is the only realistic golf product.
facts.commercial_targets: Genuinely limited, and worth being straight about. Duval County Public Schools operates exactly two campuses: Mamie Agnes Jones Elementary (K–5) and Baldwin Middle-Senior High School — one athletic-field opportunity, not a district's worth. The Community/Seniors Building at 850 N Center Street. Baldwin Skatepark. The Rail Trail depot trailhead and Camp Milton Historic Preserve trailhead landscaping. The truck stops (Pilot, Love's) — pet-relief areas are a real and under-served synthetic-turf product category at interstate travel centres, and Baldwin has two on a major freight corridor. Horse properties, boarding barns and small farms across 32234 — wash racks, run-in areas and mud-control matting rather than decorative lawn.
facts.landmarks: The Jacksonville–Baldwin Rail Trail — 14.5 miles on a 100-foot right-of-way of the former Atlantic Coast Line/CSX corridor abandoned in 1992, a 12-ft paved path plus a parallel unpaved equestrian trail, western terminus at the old Baldwin train depot, with Camp Milton Historic Preserve as the midpoint trailhead and about 8.5 miles of spur trails. The I-10 / US 90 / US 301 crossroads. The truck stops that define the town's economy — Pilot Travel Center, Love's on Brandy Branch Road, and the CAT Scale. Everybody's Restaurant and the Waffle House. Town Hall at 10 US Highway 90 West. The Community/Seniors Building at 850 N Center Street. Baldwin Skatepark.
